**Surah al-Ra'd** has forty-three verses and is Meccan and Medinan in parts.

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.) ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the verses of the Book. And what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most people do not believe.﴾ ﴿It is Allah who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see, then established Himself above the Throne, and subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. He manages the affair and details the signs, that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord.﴾ ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth, placed in it firm mountains and rivers, and of every fruit He made in it two mates, two. He covers the night with the day. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3] ﴿And in the earth are adjoining tracts, gardens of grapevines, crops, and palm trees, some with multiple stems and some with single stems, all watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4] ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord; those have shackles around their necks; those are the companions of the Fire, wherein they will abide forever.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5] ﴿They ask you to hasten evil before good, though exemplary punishments have already passed before them. Indeed your Lord is Full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6] ﴿Those who disbelieve say: "Why was a sign not sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7] ﴿Allah knows what every female carries, what the wombs diminish and what they increase. And everything with Him is in measure.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8] ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Exalted.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 9] ﴿It is the same whether one of you conceals speech or declares it, and whether one hides by night or goes forth by day.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10] ﴿For him there are successive angels before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah. Indeed Allah does not change a people's condition until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah intends harm for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have besides Him no protector.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11] ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, causing fear and hope, and produces the heavy clouds.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12] ﴿The thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and the angels, out of awe of Him. He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, while they dispute about Allah, and He is severe in might.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 13] ﴿To Him is the true supplication. And those they invoke besides Him do not respond to them with anything, except like one who stretches out his hands toward water to reach his mouth, but it will not reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is but in error.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 14] ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and their shadows in the mornings and evenings.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15] ﴿Say: "Who is Lord of the heavens and the earth?" Say: "Allah." Say: "Have you then taken besides Him protectors who possess neither benefit nor harm for themselves?" Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are darknesses and light equal? Or have they attributed to Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed alike to them?" Say: "Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Subduer."﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16] ﴿He sent down water from the sky, and valleys flowed according to their capacity, and the torrent carried a swelling foam. And from what they heat in the fire seeking ornament or goods there is a foam like it. Thus Allah strikes the example of truth and falsehood: as for the foam, it passes away as scum, but as for what benefits people, it remains in the earth. Thus Allah sets forth examples.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17] ﴿For those who responded to their Lord is the best; but for those who did not respond to Him, even if they had all that is in the earth and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves with it. Those will have a terrible reckoning, and their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 18].

**Al-'Amad** (the pillars): it is a collective noun. Whoever treats it as a plural does so because it conveys the meaning of a plural, and it means supporting columns. The poet said:

*"And the host of jinn, indeed I have permitted them / to seek Tadmur with swords and pillars."*

Its singular is *'imad* and *'amad*, like *ihab* and *ahab*. It is also said that its singular is *'amud* and its plural *'amad*, like *adim* and *adam*, and *qadim* and *qadam*. The *'imad* and *'amud* are that by which something is propped up. One says: "I propped up the wall (*'amadtu al-ha'it*), I prop it up (*a'muduhu*) with *'amdan*, when you buttress it," so the wall "leaned on the pillar," meaning it held onto it. One says: "So-and-so is the *'umda* (mainstay) of his people," when they rely on him in what troubles them. *'Imad* is pluralised as *'umud* with two dammas, like *shihab* and *shuhub*. *'Amud* is also pluralised as *'umud*, like *rasul* and *rusul*, and *zabur* and *zubur*. This is for the plural of abundance. Both are pluralised in the plural of paucity as *a'mida*.

**Al-Sinw** (the offshoot): it is a branch that grows from a root, and the other is from a single root. Its basic meaning is "like," and from this one says of the paternal uncle that he is a *sinw*. Its plural in the dialect of the Hijaz is *sinwan*, with a kasra on the *sad*, like *qinw* and *qinwan*. In the dialect of Tamim and Qays it is pronounced with a damma, like *dhi'b* and *dhu'ban*. It is also said *sanwan* with a fatha on the *sad*, which is a collective noun, not a broken plural, because it is not of its pattern.

**Al-Jadid** is the opposite of the worn and the old. One says "a new garment," meaning as if it has just been finished from its making. It is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*, as if it has been cut from the weaving.

**Al-Mathulah** is punishment, and it is pluralised with the suffix *alif* and *ta'* as *samawat* from *sama*. The dialect of the Hijaz pronounces it *mathla* with a fatha on the *mim* and a sukun on the *tha'*; the dialect of Tamim pronounces it with a damma on the *mim* and a sukun on the *tha'*. It was called punishment because of the likeness between the penalty and the one punished, as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. Or it is from *mithal* in the sense of retribution: one says "I made the man equal to his companion (*amthaltu*) and I retaliated against him (*aqassatuhu*)." Or it is because, because of the greatness of its punishment, a proverb is struck with it.

**Al-Sarib** is an active participle from *sarab*, meaning he acts as he wishes. The poet said:

*"I have wandered, and I was not one who wanders much, / and dreams bring near what is not near."*

Another said:

*"Every people have tied the fetter of their stallion, / and we have loosed its fetter, so it is a wanderer."*

That is, it goes wherever it wishes, not repelled from a direction, boasting of the might of its people. 

**Al-Mihal** means strength and destruction. Al-A'sha said:

*"A branch of a nabk tree that sways in the branch of the ... / abundant in generosity, strong in might."*

And 'Abd al-Muttalib said:

*"Let their cross and their might never overcome / your might, forever."*

It is said: "The man schemed (*mahala*) against the man," meaning he plotted against him and seized him with severe pursuit. *Al-mumahalah* is contrivance and deception, and from it: "He made an effort (*tamahhala*) for such and such," meaning he took pains to employ a stratagem and strove for it. Abu Zayd said: *al-mihal* is vengeance. Ibn 'Arafa said: *al-mihal* is argument, "what turns from its matter," that is, he argued. Al-Qutaybi said: it means "severe in cunning," and its root is from strategy; its *mim* is treated like the *mim* of a place, and its root is from existence, then one says "I established (*tamakkantu*)." Al-Azhari criticised him for adding the *mim*, saying: "If it were *mif'al*, it would have shown the *waw* like *mirwad*, *mihwal* and *mihwar*. It is actually a pattern like *mihad* and *mirас*." [Note: the Arabic *mirās* is rendered here as the pattern noted by al-Azhari.]

**Al-Kaff** is a known limb. Its plural in the paucity pattern is *akuff*, like *sakk* and *asuk*, and in the abundance pattern *kufuf*, like *sukuk*. Its root is the verbal noun of *kaffa*.

**The shadow of a thing** is what appears of its image in light, and what is similar to it in brightness.

**Al-Zabad** (foam): Abu al-Hajjaj al-A'lam said it is what the valley throws out when its water surges and its waves become agitated. Ibn 'Atiyya said it is what the torrent carries of debris and the like, and what it throws onto its banks from the tangled bubbles. Ibn 'Isa said: *al-zabad* is the scum of boiling and its impurity. The poet said:

*"What is the Euphrates when the winds blow on it, / its waves throw the two banks with foam."*

**Al-Juffa'** is the name for what the torrent casts away, that is, throws out. One says: "The pot cast off (*jaffa'at*) its foam," and "the torrent cast off its foam (*jaffa al-sayl bi-zabadihi*)," and "it removed and fled." Ibn al-Anbari said: *juffa'an* means scattered, from *jaffa'at al-rih al-ghaym*, when the wind cut the clouds, and *jaffa'at al-rajul*, when it threw the man down. It is also said: "The valley dried up (*jaffa al-wadi*)" when it was soaked dry.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the verses of the Book. And what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most people do not believe.﴾ ﴿Allah, who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see, then established Himself above the Throne, and subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. He manages the affair and details the signs, that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord.﴾

This surah is Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' and Ibn Jubayr. According to 'Ata', it is Meccan except His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "You are not a messenger"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43]. According to others, it is Meccan except His saying: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12] up to His saying: ﴿To Him is the true supplication﴾ [al-Ra'd: 14]. It is Medinan according to al-Kalbi, Muqatil, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, and they excepted two verses, saying: they were revealed in Mecca, and they are: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which mountains were moved﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31] up to the end of the two. According to Ibn 'Abbas, except His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31] up to the end of the verse. According to Qatada, it is Meccan except His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], the verse, related by al-Mahdawi. It is also said: the surah is Medinan, related by al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'd al-Ballut and Makki ibn Abi Talib.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Tilka*" (these) is a reference to the verses of the surah, and by "the Book" is meant the surah; that is, these are the verses of the complete surah, wondrous in its kind. Ibn 'Atiyya said: whoever says the opening letters of the surahs are examples of the letters of the alphabet, says: the reference here by "*tilka*" is to the letters of the alphabet. It is valid on this view for "the Book" to mean the Qur'an, and it is valid for it to mean the Torah and the Gospel. On this view, *Alif Lam Mim Ra* is a beginning, "*tilka*" is a second beginning, "*ayat*" is the predicate of the second, and the sentence is the predicate of the first, end of quotation.

The link is the demonstrative *tilka*. It is also said: the reference by "*tilka*" is to what was narrated of the accounts of the messengers, referred to by His saying: ﴿These are among the tidings of the unseen﴾. What he said, "it is valid for it to mean the Torah and the Gospel," is close to the saying of Mujahid and Qatada, and the reference by "*tilka*" is to all the books of Allah the Exalted that were sent down. The meaning is: these are the verses whose account I have related to you, and they are verses of the Book that I sent down before this Book which I have sent down to you.

Apparently, His saying "*wa-alladhi*" (and what) is the subject, "*al-haqq*" (the truth) is its predicate, and ﴿from your Lord﴾ is linked to "*unzila*" (was sent down). Al-Hawfi permitted that ﴿from your Lord﴾ be the predicate and "*al-haqq*" a deleted subject, or a predicate after a predicate, or both a single predicate, end of quotation. This is a forced grammatical analysis (*i'rab*). Al-Hawfi also permitted that "*wa-alladhi*" be in the nominative position, coordinated with "*ayat*," and both he and Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that it be in the genitive position. On these two analyses, "*al-haqq*" is the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: "it is the truth," and ﴿and what has been sent down﴾ is one of those in which a descriptive is coordinated with a descriptive, both referring to one thing, as you say: "The witty, intelligent one came to me," while you mean one person. From this is the poet's saying:

*"To the stately king and the son of the lofty one / and the lion of the battalion in the crowd."*

Al-Hawfi permitted that "*al-haqq*" be an attribute of "*alladhi*," meaning: if you make "*wa-alladhi*" coordinated with "*ayat*."

"And most people": it has been said the reference is to the disbelievers of Mecca, who do not affirm that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah the Exalted. It has also been said the reference is to the Jews and Christians, but the more apt view is that it is general. When He mentioned the absence of faith in most people, He next mentioned what indicates the validity of Tawhid (the oneness of God) and the Return, and what draws them to faith, in what the intellect reflects upon and observes of great power and wondrous craftsmanship.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verses 1–2 (part 2 of 2):

The word *al-Jalalah* (Allah) is the *mubtada'* (subject, the topic of the sentence), and *alladhi* (the One who) is the *khabar* (predicate, the comment about the subject). The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And He is the One who spread out the earth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3]. It is also permissible for *alladhi* to be an adjective (*sifah*), and His saying ﴿He arranges the affair, He details the signs﴾ is a second predicate after the first. Al-Zamakhshari said this is supported by what precedes it, namely the mention of the signs.

The majority of readers read *'amad* (pillars) with two *fathahs*. Abu Hayah and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with two *dammahs*. The phrase *bi-ghayri 'amadin* (without pillars) is in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), meaning: free of any pillars.

The pronoun in ﴿you see it﴾ refers to the heavens; that is, you see the heavens free of pillars. This construction allows that ﴿you see it﴾ be a new independent statement, or that it be a circumstantial clause, meaning: He raised them visible to you without pillars. It is a *hal muqaddarah* (a circumstantial clause with a delayed or anticipated state), because when He raised them, we were not yet created.

It has also been said that the object pronoun in ﴿you see it﴾ refers to *'amad*, meaning: without visible pillars. In this case ﴿you see it﴾ is an adjective of *'amad*. What indicates that it is an adjective of *'amad* is the reading of Ubayy: (*tarawnahu*, you see it, masculine), where the pronoun returns in the masculine form in agreement with the wording *'amad*, since it is a *ism jam'* (a collective noun, a noun that denotes a plurality but is not its regular plural).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is the plural of *'amud* (pillar), and the regular pattern for its plural is *'umud*, with the three letters vowelled with *dammah*, like *rasul* and *rusul*." End of quote. This is an error, and the correct statement is: with the two letters vowelled with *dammah*, because the third letter is *harf al-i'rab* (the letter that carries the case-ending), so its vowel is not considered in the pattern of the plural.

This interpretation allows two meanings. The first is that the heavens do have pillars, but these pillars are not seen. This view was held by Mujahid and Qatadah. Ibn 'Abbas said: "What makes you sure that they have pillars that are not seen?" Some have reported that the pillars are the mountain of Qaf that surrounds the earth, and the sky is above it like a dome.

The second meaning is that the sentence is a negation of pillars, and what is intended is the negation of seeing the pillars. So there are no pillars, and therefore nothing is seen; that is, the heavens have no pillars by which they could be seen. The majority hold that the heavens have absolutely no pillars. If they had pillars, those pillars would themselves need pillars, and the matter would go on endlessly. Therefore the apparent meaning is that they are held up by the divine power, as in His saying: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ [al-Hajj: 65], and similar verses.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: *al-'Imad* is that on which something relies. These bodies stand in the high space by the power of Allah, so their pillar is the power of Allah. Therefore they have a pillar in reality, except that this pillar is Allah's holding, preservation, management, and sustaining of them in the high space. You do not see that management, nor do you know the manner of that holding. End of quote.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "There is no support beneath them that props them up, nor is there any suspension above them that holds them." Those who held that ﴿you see it﴾ is a declarative in wording but an imperative in meaning, that is, "look at them and see whether they have pillars," are far from the correct understanding.

The explanation of ﴿Then He established Himself on the Throne﴾ has already been given. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "*Thumma* (then) here is for conjoining sentences, not for sequence, because the establishment on the Throne was before the raising of the heavens." In the Sahih it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah existed, and nothing existed before Him, and His Throne was upon the water, then He created the heavens and the earth." End of quote.

﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾: that is, He made them subservient for what He wills from them. It has also been said: for the benefit of the servants. He expressed their motion by *al-jaryan* (running), which is a motion with speed. The word *kull* (each) is in the grammatical construction of an added noun (*mudafah*) in the implied sense. The apparent view is that the omitted element is the pronoun of the sun and the moon, meaning: both of them run until a specified term. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The sun and the moon, by including their mention, include the mention of the stars, and that is why He said: ﴿each runs for a specified term﴾, meaning: each of what is in the sense of the sun and the moon among the subjugated things." And *kull* is a word that requires an added noun, whether stated or implied. End of quote. He explained *kull* by his words "meaning: each of what is in the sense of the sun and the moon," which excludes the sun and the moon from the mention of running until a specified term. Its clarification is that one should say, according to his view: the stars are included in their mention; that is, and of what is in their sense, until a specified term.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The stations of the sun and the moon are the limits they do not exceed. He determined for each of them a particular course towards a particular direction, with a particular measure of speed and slowness." It has also been said: the specified term is the Day of Resurrection. At its coming that running and driving will cease, as He said: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1], and He said: ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9].

The meaning of *tadbir al-amr* (arranging the affair) is carrying it out and finalizing it. He expressed it with *tadbir* to bring it closer to understanding, since *tadbir* is only the consideration of the outcomes and consequences of affairs, and that is among the attributes of human beings. The affair belongs to His dominion and lordship, and it is general for all affairs: bringing into existence and annihilation, giving life and causing death, sending down revelation, sending messengers, imposing obligations, and other things.

Mujahid said: ﴿He arranges the affair﴾ means He decrees it alone, and ﴿He details the signs﴾ means He makes them distinct clarifications, distinguishing some from others. The *ayat* (signs) here are His proofs and indications in His heavens of His oneness, or the signs of the revealed books, or the signs of the Qur'an; these are the views.

The readers al-Nakha'i, Abu Razin, and Aban ibn Tha'lab, from Qatadah, read (*nudabbiru al-amra nufassilu*, We arrange the affair, We detail) with *nun* in both. Likewise Abu 'Amr al-Dani reported from al-Hasan that both were read with *nun*. Abd al-Wahid, from Abu 'Amr, and Hubayrah, from Hafs, agreed on *nufassilu* with *nun* in the light reading (*al-khifaf*). The author of al-Lawami' said: "It came from al-Hasan and al-A'mash, (*nufassilu*) with *nun* only." Al-Mahdawi said: "There is no disagreement about (*yudabbiru*)," or, it is not as he said, since the reading of Aban has already been mentioned. Al-Dani reported from al-Hasan: "What eloquence requires is that these two clauses be an interrogative of information about Allah, the Exalted." It has also been said: (*yudabbiru*) is a *hal* from the pronoun in (*wa sakhkhara*), and (*nufassilu*) is a *hal* from the pronoun in (*yudabbiru*). The address in (*la'allakum*, so that you) is to the disbelievers, and (*tuqinun*, you may be certain) means with regard to the recompense, or that this Arranger and Detailer is surely the One to whom you must return.

This is for the plural of abundance. Both are pluralised in the plural of paucity as *a'mida*.

**Al-Sinw** (the offshoot): it is a branch that grows from a root, and the other is from a single root. Its basic meaning is "like," and from this one says of the paternal uncle that he is a *sinw*. Its plural in the dialect of the Hijaz is *sinwan*, with a kasra on the *sad*, like *qinw* and *qinwan*. In the dialect of Tamim and Qays it is pronounced with a damma, like *dhi'b* and *dhu'ban*. It is also said *sanwan* with a fatha on the *sad*, which is a collective noun, not a broken plural, because it is not of its pattern.

**Al-Jadid** is the opposite of the worn and the old. One says "a new garment," meaning as if it has just been finished from its making. It is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*, as if it has been cut from the weaving.

**Al-Mathulah** is punishment, and it is pluralised with the suffix *alif* and *ta'* as *samawat* from *sama*. The dialect of the Hijaz pronounces it *mathla* with a fatha on the *mim* and a sukun on the *tha'*; the dialect of Tamim pronounces it with a damma on the *mim* and a sukun on the *tha'*. It was called punishment because of the likeness between the penalty and the one punished, as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. Or it is from *mithal* in the sense of retribution: one says "I made the man equal to his companion (*amthaltu*) and I retaliated against him (*aqassatuhu*)." Or it is because, because of the greatness of its punishment, a proverb is struck with it.

**Al-Sarib** is an active participle from *sarab*, meaning he acts as he wishes. The poet said:

*"I have wandered, and I was not one who wanders much, / and dreams bring near what is not near."*

Another said:

*"Every people have tied the fetter of their stallion, / and we have loosed its fetter, so it is a wanderer."*

That is, it goes wherever it wishes, not repelled from a direction, boasting of the might of its people. 

**Al-Mihal** means strength and destruction. Al-A'sha said:

*"A branch of a nabk tree that sways in the branch of the ... / abundant in generosity, strong in might."*

And 'Abd al-Muttalib said:

*"Let their cross and their might never overcome / your might, forever."*

It is said: "The man schemed (*mahala*) against the man," meaning he plotted against him and seized him with severe pursuit. *Al-mumahalah* is contrivance and deception, and from it: "He made an effort (*tamahhala*) for such and such," meaning he took pains to employ a stratagem and strove for it. Abu Zayd said: *al-mihal* is vengeance. Ibn 'Arafa said: *al-mihal* is argument, "what turns from its matter," that is, he argued. Al-Qutaybi said: it means "severe in cunning," and its root is from strategy; its *mim* is treated like the *mim* of a place, and its root is from existence, then one says "I established (*tamakkantu*)." Al-Azhari criticised him for adding the *mim*, saying: "If it were *mif'al*, it would have shown the *waw* like *mirwad*, *mihwal* and *mihwar*. It is actually a pattern like *mihad* and *mirас*." [Note: the Arabic *mirās* is rendered here as the pattern noted by al-Azhari.]

**Al-Kaff** is a known limb. Its plural in the paucity pattern is *akuff*, like *sakk* and *asuk*, and in the abundance pattern *kufuf*, like *sukuk*. Its root is the verbal noun of *kaffa*.

**The shadow of a thing** is what appears of its image in light, and what is similar to it in brightness.

**Al-Zabad** (foam): Abu al-Hajjaj al-A'lam said it is what the valley throws out when its water surges and its waves become agitated. Ibn 'Atiyya said it is what the torrent carries of debris and the like, and what it throws onto its banks from the tangled bubbles. Ibn 'Isa said: *al-zabad* is the scum of boiling and its impurity. The poet said:

*"What is the Euphrates when the winds blow on it, / its waves throw the two banks with foam."*

**Al-Juffa'** is the name for what the torrent casts away, that is, throws out. One says: "The pot cast off (*jaffa'at*) its foam," and "the torrent cast off its foam (*jaffa al-sayl bi-zabadihi*)," and "it removed and fled." Ibn al-Anbari said: *juffa'an* means scattered, from *jaffa'at al-rih al-ghaym*, when the wind cut the clouds, and *jaffa'at al-rajul*, when it threw the man down. It is also said: "The valley dried up (*jaffa al-wadi*)" when it was soaked dry.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the verses of the Book. And what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most people do not believe.﴾ ﴿Allah, who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see, then established Himself above the Throne, and subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. He manages the affair and details the signs, that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord.﴾

This surah is Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' and Ibn Jubayr. According to 'Ata', it is Meccan except His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "You are not a messenger"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43]. According to others, it is Meccan except His saying: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12] up to His saying: ﴿To Him is the true supplication﴾ [al-Ra'd: 14]. It is Medinan according to al-Kalbi, Muqatil, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, and they excepted two verses, saying: they were revealed in Mecca, and they are: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which mountains were moved﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31] up to the end of the two. According to Ibn 'Abbas, except His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31] up to the end of the verse. According to Qatada, it is Meccan except His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], the verse, related by al-Mahdawi. It is also said: the surah is Medinan, related by al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'd al-Ballut and Makki ibn Abi Talib.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Tilka*" (these) is a reference to the verses of the surah, and by "the Book" is meant the surah; that is, these are the verses of the complete surah, wondrous in its kind. Ibn 'Atiyya said: whoever says the opening letters of the surahs are examples of the letters of the alphabet, says: the reference here by "*tilka*" is to the letters of the alphabet. It is valid on this view for "the Book" to mean the Qur'an, and it is valid for it to mean the Torah and the Gospel. On this view, *Alif Lam Mim Ra* is a beginning, "*tilka*" is a second beginning, "*ayat*" is the predicate of the second, and the sentence is the predicate of the first, end of quotation.

The link is the demonstrative *tilka*. It is also said: the reference by "*tilka*" is to what was narrated of the accounts of the messengers, referred to by His saying: ﴿These are among the tidings of the unseen﴾. What he said, "it is valid for it to mean the Torah and the Gospel," is close to the saying of Mujahid and Qatada, and the reference by "*tilka*" is to all the books of Allah the Exalted that were sent down. The meaning is: these are the verses whose account I have related to you, and they are verses of the Book that I sent down before this Book which I have sent down to you.

Apparently, His saying "*wa-alladhi*" (and what) is the subject, "*al-haqq*" (the truth) is its predicate, and ﴿from your Lord﴾ is linked to "*unzila*" (was sent down). Al-Hawfi permitted that ﴿from your Lord﴾ be the predicate and "*al-haqq*" a deleted subject, or a predicate after a predicate, or both a single predicate, end of quotation. This is a forced grammatical analysis (*i'rab*). Al-Hawfi also permitted that "*wa-alladhi*" be in the nominative position, coordinated with "*ayat*," and both he and Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that it be in the genitive position. On these two analyses, "*al-haqq*" is the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: "it is the truth," and ﴿and what has been sent down﴾ is one of those in which a descriptive is coordinated with a descriptive, both referring to one thing, as you say: "The witty, intelligent one came to me," while you mean one person. From this is the poet's saying:

*"To the stately king and the son of the lofty one / and the lion of the battalion in the crowd."*

Al-Hawfi permitted that "*al-haqq*" be an attribute of "*alladhi*," meaning: if you make "*wa-alladhi*" coordinated with "*ayat*."

"And most people": it has been said the reference is to the disbelievers of Mecca, who do not affirm that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah the Exalted. It has also been said the reference is to the Jews and Christians, but the more apt view is that it is general. When He mentioned the absence of faith in most people, He next mentioned what indicates the validity of Tawhid (the oneness of God) and the Return, and what draws them to faith, in what the intellect reflects upon and observes of great power and wondrous craftsmanship.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verses 1–2 (part 2 of 2):

The word *al-Jalalah* (Allah) is the *mubtada'* (subject, the topic of the sentence), and *alladhi* (the One who) is the *khabar* (predicate, the comment about the subject). The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And He is the One who spread out the earth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3]. It is also permissible for *alladhi* to be an adjective (*sifah*), and His saying ﴿He arranges the affair, He details the signs﴾ is a second predicate after the first. Al-Zamakhshari said this is supported by what precedes it, namely the mention of the signs.

The majority of readers read *'amad* (pillars) with two *fathahs*. Abu Hayah and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with two *dammahs*. The phrase *bi-ghayri 'amadin* (without pillars) is in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), meaning: free of any pillars.

The pronoun in ﴿you see it﴾ refers to the heavens; that is, you see the heavens free of pillars. This construction allows that ﴿you see it﴾ be a new independent statement, or that it be a circumstantial clause, meaning: He raised them visible to you without pillars. It is a *hal muqaddarah* (a circumstantial clause with a delayed or anticipated state), because when He raised them, we were not yet created.

It has also been said that the object pronoun in ﴿you see it﴾ refers to *'amad*, meaning: without visible pillars. In this case ﴿you see it﴾ is an adjective of *'amad*. What indicates that it is an adjective of *'amad* is the reading of Ubayy: (*tarawnahu*, you see it, masculine), where the pronoun returns in the masculine form in agreement with the wording *'amad*, since it is a *ism jam'* (a collective noun, a noun that denotes a plurality but is not its regular plural).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is the plural of *'amud* (pillar), and the regular pattern for its plural is *'umud*, with the three letters vowelled with *dammah*, like *rasul* and *rusul*." End of quote. This is an error, and the correct statement is: with the two letters vowelled with *dammah*, because the third letter is *harf al-i'rab* (the letter that carries the case-ending), so its vowel is not considered in the pattern of the plural.

This interpretation allows two meanings. The first is that the heavens do have pillars, but these pillars are not seen. This view was held by Mujahid and Qatadah. Ibn 'Abbas said: "What makes you sure that they have pillars that are not seen?" Some have reported that the pillars are the mountain of Qaf that surrounds the earth, and the sky is above it like a dome.

The second meaning is that the sentence is a negation of pillars, and what is intended is the negation of seeing the pillars. So there are no pillars, and therefore nothing is seen; that is, the heavens have no pillars by which they could be seen. The majority hold that the heavens have absolutely no pillars. If they had pillars, those pillars would themselves need pillars, and the matter would go on endlessly. Therefore the apparent meaning is that they are held up by the divine power, as in His saying: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ [al-Hajj: 65], and similar verses.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: *al-'Imad* is that on which something relies. These bodies stand in the high space by the power of Allah, so their pillar is the power of Allah. Therefore they have a pillar in reality, except that this pillar is Allah's holding, preservation, management, and sustaining of them in the high space. You do not see that management, nor do you know the manner of that holding. End of quote.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "There is no support beneath them that props them up, nor is there any suspension above them that holds them." Those who held that ﴿you see it﴾ is a declarative in wording but an imperative in meaning, that is, "look at them and see whether they have pillars," are far from the correct understanding.

The explanation of ﴿Then He established Himself on the Throne﴾ has already been given. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "*Thumma* (then) here is for conjoining sentences, not for sequence, because the establishment on the Throne was before the raising of the heavens." In the Sahih it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah existed, and nothing existed before Him, and His Throne was upon the water, then He created the heavens and the earth." End of quote.

﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾: that is, He made them subservient for what He wills from them. It has also been said: for the benefit of the servants. He expressed their motion by *al-jaryan* (running), which is a motion with speed. The word *kull* (each) is in the grammatical construction of an added noun (*mudafah*) in the implied sense. The apparent view is that the omitted element is the pronoun of the sun and the moon, meaning: both of them run until a specified term. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The sun and the moon, by including their mention, include the mention of the stars, and that is why He said: ﴿each runs for a specified term﴾, meaning: each of what is in the sense of the sun and the moon among the subjugated things." And *kull* is a word that requires an added noun, whether stated or implied. End of quote. He explained *kull* by his words "meaning: each of what is in the sense of the sun and the moon," which excludes the sun and the moon from the mention of running until a specified term. Its clarification is that one should say, according to his view: the stars are included in their mention; that is, and of what is in their sense, until a specified term.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The stations of the sun and the moon are the limits they do not exceed. He determined for each of them a particular course towards a particular direction, with a particular measure of speed and slowness." It has also been said: the specified term is the Day of Resurrection. At its coming that running and driving will cease, as He said: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1], and He said: ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9].

The meaning of *tadbir al-amr* (arranging the affair) is carrying it out and finalizing it. He expressed it with *tadbir* to bring it closer to understanding, since *tadbir* is only the consideration of the outcomes and consequences of affairs, and that is among the attributes of human beings. The affair belongs to His dominion and lordship, and it is general for all affairs: bringing into existence and annihilation, giving life and causing death, sending down revelation, sending messengers, imposing obligations, and other things.

Mujahid said: ﴿He arranges the affair﴾ means He decrees it alone, and ﴿He details the signs﴾ means He makes them distinct clarifications, distinguishing some from others. The *ayat* (signs) here are His proofs and indications in His heavens of His oneness, or the signs of the revealed books, or the signs of the Qur'an; these are the views.

The readers al-Nakha'i, Abu Razin, and Aban ibn Tha'lab, from Qatadah, read (*nudabbiru al-amra nufassilu*, We arrange the affair, We detail) with *nun* in both. Likewise Abu 'Amr al-Dani reported from al-Hasan that both were read with *nun*. Abd al-Wahid, from Abu 'Amr, and Hubayrah, from Hafs, agreed on *nufassilu* with *nun* in the light reading (*al-khifaf*). The author of al-Lawami' said: "It came from al-Hasan and al-A'mash, (*nufassilu*) with *nun* only." Al-Mahdawi said: "There is no disagreement about (*yudabbiru*)," or, it is not as he said, since the reading of Aban has already been mentioned. Al-Dani reported from al-Hasan: "What eloquence requires is that these two clauses be an interrogative of information about Allah, the Exalted." It has also been said: (*yudabbiru*) is a *hal* from the pronoun in (*wa sakhkhara*), and (*nufassilu*) is a *hal* from the pronoun in (*yudabbiru*). The address in (*la'allakum*, so that you) is to the disbelievers, and (*tuqinun*, you may be certain) means with regard to the recompense, or that this Arranger and Detailer is surely the One to whom you must return.

(p-361)﴿It is He who spread out the earth and placed in it firm mountains and rivers, and of all the fruits He placed in it two pairs. He covers the night with the day. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾ When he had established the celestial proofs, he followed them with establishing the terrestrial proofs. ﴿Spread out the earth﴾ means He extended it in length and breadth, so that it could be worked and settled upon. It was said: He spread it out and flattened it from Makkah, from beneath the House, and so it went such-and-such. And it was said: it had been gathered together at Bayt al-Maqdis, and He said to it: "Go such-and-such." Ibn 'Atiyya said: His words ﴿spread out the earth﴾ imply that it is flat, not a sphere, and this is the apparent meaning of the Shari'ah. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Darani said: It has been established by proof that the earth is a sphere, and this does not contradict His words ﴿spread out the earth﴾, because the earth is a vast body, and when a sphere is extremely large, a part of it is seen as a surface, and the difference between it and a surface does not become apparent except in the knowledge of God, exalted is He. Do you not see that He said: ﴿and the mountains as pegs﴾ [al-Naba' 78:7], although the world and people walk upon them? Thus it is here too. Furthermore, He mentioned the spreading of the earth so that it would be used as evidence for the existence of the Creator, and that it is gathered together beneath the House is not something observed or perceptible, so it cannot be used as evidence for the existence of the Creator. Therefore the interpretation of ﴿spread out the earth﴾ is that He made it according to a specific measure, and that it is capable of increase and decrease is something permissible and possible in itself. So the specification of that particular measure must be due to the specification of one who specifies and the determination of one who determines, and by this the proof of the existence of the Creator is attained. End of quotation, summarized.

Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: ''al-madd'' is extension to an extent whose end cannot be seen. The meaning is: He made the earth a small volume, such that the eye does not reach its limit, for if the earth were smaller in size than it is now, benefit from it would not be complete. End of quotation. What he mentioned, that if it were smaller... to the end of it, is not accepted, because the benefit derived from the earth is the inhabited part, and the inhabited part is far less than the uninhabited part. So if God had wished to make it the measure of the inhabited part that is benefited from, that would not have been impossible. Thus three interpretations arise from His words ﴿spread out the earth﴾: that He spread it after it had been gathered together; that it is specified by a particular measure; and that He made its volume large, so that its limit cannot be seen.

Al-rawasi means the firmly fixed ones, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Upon it are everlasting ones that do not move, and a dusty one, set firm by the girl with the pestle."

The meaning is: mountains that are firmly fixed. The feminine form of the attributive pattern (fawa'il) is not regular except for feminines, but the broken plural of a non-rational masculine noun follows the pattern of feminine plurals. Also, the mountains have come to be described as al-rawasi, and the attribute has come to stand in for the noun, so it was pluralized as a noun, like ha'it / hawa'it and kahil / kawahil. It was said: ﴿rawasi﴾ is the plural of rasiyah, with the ha' for emphasis, and it is an attribute of the mountain. The earth was unstable, so God made it firm with mountains in its regions, and its instability ceased. The evidence of the existence of the Creator, the Mighty and Wise, is found in the existence of the mountains. It was said: this is because the nature of the earth is one, so the presence of a mountain in some of its parts and not others must be by the creation of a Wise and Powerful One. Also, from the mineral and metallic substances produced from it, such as petroleum and sulphur, the mountain is one in nature, and the influence of the sun is one; this is evidence that this is by the decree of a Powerful, Dominant One, exalted above resemblance to contingent beings. And also from the generation of rivers from them. It was said: this is because the mountain is a solid body, and its vapour rises from the depths of the earth toward it and is retained there, so it continues to accumulate within it, and thereby abundant waters are produced; by their force they break forth and flow over the surface of the earth. For this reason, in most cases when God mentions the mountains, He mentions the rivers, as in this verse, and as in His words: ﴿And We placed in it firm mountains, rising high, and gave you sweet water to drink﴾ [al-Mursalat 77:27], and ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and rivers﴾ [al-Nahl 16:15]. The commentators said: the rivers are the flowing waters in the earth. al-Kirmani said: they are the channels of water. The discussion of the rivers has already preceded at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah.

The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿of all the fruits﴾ are connected to ﴿He placed﴾. When He mentioned the rivers, He mentioned what arises from them, which is the fruits. Here zawj means a single kind, which is the opposite of two; that is, (p-362) when He spread out the earth, He made this, then it multiplied and diversified. It was said: by the two pairs He meant the black and the white, the sweet and the sour, the small and the large, and similar varieties of differing kinds.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This verse implies that every fruit has two kinds present in it; if it happens that more than two kinds are found in one fruit, that does not conflict with the meaning of the verse. al-Kirmani said: zawj is one, and zawj is two, and for this reason it was restricted so that it would be known that the intended meaning of zawj here is the single item, not the pair, so that there would be four; and He singled out two for mention, although among the kinds of fruits there are more than that, because it is the least, for there is no type whose varieties are fewer than two. End of quotation.

It is said that in every fruit there is a male and a female, and al-Farra' pointed to this. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: When God created the world and created trees in it, He created from each kind two only. So if He had said "He created two pairs," it would not be known whether the intended meaning was the kind or the individual; but when He said "two," we know that He first created from each pair two, neither fewer nor more. Thus trees and crops are like the children of Adam: many came from them, and their beginning was from two, a pair, as individuals, namely Adam and Eve. The evidence from the creation of the fruits for what God mentioned is from the aspect of the garden's mound in the earth, and the splitting of its upper and lower parts: from the upper split comes the rising tree, and from the lower the sunken roots. The nature of that garden is one, and the influences of natures, spheres and stars upon it are one. Then from the upper part there emerges what rises upward into the air, and from the lower what sinks into the soil. It is impossible that two opposing natures should arise from one nature; so we know that this is by the decree of a Wise and Powerful One. Then that tree becomes partly timber, partly almonds, partly fruit; and then in that fruit substances of differing natures come into being, by the decree of the Wise and Powerful One. End of quotation, with some summarization.

It was said: the sentence is complete at His words ﴿and of all the fruits﴾, so it is conjoined to what precedes it by the conjunction of single items, and it is connected to His words ﴿and placed in it firm mountains﴾. The meaning is that He placed in the earth from every male and female two. It was said: the two pairs are the sun and the moon; it was said: the night and the day. ﴿He covers the night with the day.﴾ The explanation of this sentence and its readings has already been given in al-A'raf. He singled out those who reflect, because the wondrous craftsmanship contained in these signs cannot be grasped except through reflection.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 13, verse 4:**

﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts, and gardens of vines, and crops, and palm trees, both single and multiple, watered with one water; yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾

﴿Qit'a﴾ is the plural of ﻗِﻄْﻌَﺔ (qit'ah), which means a portion. ﴿Mutajawirat﴾ means adjoining, close together, near to one another. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak said: some land is good and some is saline (sabakhah, salt-laden and barren), and these grow while the one beside them does not grow. Ibn Qutaybah and Qatadah said: it means neighbouring towns. It was also said: they are adjoining in place but differ in quality, some hard and some soft, some sandy and some smooth, or some fertile and some barren, some suitable for crops but not for trees, and the reverse, while all of them share the same kind of ground. It was also said: there is an elision in the speech, a coordinated omission, meaning: "and [tracts that are] not adjoining."

(p. 363) The ﴿mutajawirat﴾ are the cities and whatever is inhabited, and the non-adjoining ones are the deserts and whatever is uninhabited. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: what appears from describing them as adjoining is that they come from one soil and one type. The point of the lesson here is clearer, because although they agree in soil and water, power and will make some of their produce excel others, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) said when he was asked about this verse: "The inferior dates (al-daql) and the al-qaris, the sweet and the sour." Ibn 'Atiyyah also said: in this example he restricted it to those that are adjacent and close to one another, because difference in produce among them is more remarkable.

In some copies of the Qur'an the reading is ﴿qit'an mutajawirat﴾ with the accusative, governed by "made" (ja'ala). Al-Jumhur read ﴿wa-jannatun﴾ in the nominative, while al-Hasan read it in the accusative by supposing a verb. It was also said that it is coordinated with ﴿rawasiya﴾ [13:3]. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is coordinated with ﴿zawjayni ithnayn﴾ [13:3], or in the genitive with ﴿kulli al-thamarat﴾ [13:3], end of quote. The better view is to supply a verb, because the two conjoined elements are far apart in these readings and are separated by many clauses.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read ﴿wa-zar'un wa-nakhilun sinwanun wa-ghayru sinwanin﴾ in the nominative throughout, in agreement with ﴿qit'un﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: coordinated with ﴿a'nab﴾; this is also not a precise statement, because it includes what is not coordination, namely ﴿sinwan﴾. The remaining seven read them in the genitive throughout, in agreement with ﴿min a'nab﴾. He said: making the garden of vines an element coordinated with the crops is a figurative usage; strictly speaking a garden is the land in which the vines are. A poet said:

"As if my eye, in the western direction, were coming toward me from the water-carriers, irrigating a garden of distant palms."

That is, the palms of a garden, since only palm trees are described as distant (suhuq). Whoever reads ﴿zar'.﴾ in the genitive takes the gardens as the whole of this, not the crops alone, because a plot is not called a garden unless fruit trees are mixed with it.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿sinwan﴾ with a kasrah on the ṣād in both places. Ibn Musarrif, al-Sulami and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a ḍammah. Al-Hasan and Qatadah read it with a fathah, and with the fathah it is a collective noun, like al-sa'dan.

'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿yusqa﴾ with the yā' (masculine), meaning: what has been mentioned is watered. The remaining seven read it with the tā' (feminine), which is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and the people of Makkah; they used the feminine because the pronoun refers to the wording of what came before, and because of His saying ﴿nufaddilu﴾ with the nūn. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the yā'; Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿yusqa﴾ and ﴿nufaddilu﴾ with the yā'. Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Haywah and al-Halabi, on the authority of 'Abd al-Warith, read ﴿yufaddalu﴾ with the yā' and a fathah on the ḍād, and some of them with a ḍammah. Abu Hatim said: I found it like that in the copy of the Qur'an of Yahya ibn Ya'mar, who was the first to add dots to the Qur'an copies. The disagreement of the reciters over the ḍammah and sukun of the kāf in ﴿al-ukul﴾ has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah. ﴿Al-ukul﴾ with a ḍammah on the hamzah means the thing eaten, like naqḍ in the sense of the thing broken; with a fathah it is the verbal noun.

The most apparent reading of most exegetes regarding ﴿sinwan﴾ is that the word ﴿sinwan﴾ is an attribute of ﴿wa-nakhil﴾. Those exegetes who explained it as "like" made it an attribute of everything mentioned before, meaning: of similar forms and of dissimilar forms. It is said that the counterpart of this word is qinw and qinwan, and no third form is found for them. He mentioned the 'unwan (a term for a sort of title) because it is in the pattern of the adjoining plots, so the strangeness of the difference in produce becomes evident in it.

The meaning of ﴿with one water﴾ is rain water, or sea water, or river water, or spring water, or the water of a source that does not flow over the surface of the earth. He singled out the difference in produce, although they differ in other respects, because it is the predominant aspect of benefit from fruits. Do you not see how they are close in shape, colour, scent, benefit and what is similar to these? It was said: God, exalted is He, drew attention in this verse to His power and wisdom, and that He is the one who arranges all things. That is because the tree puts forth its branches and fruit at a known time, neither delayed nor advanced. Then the water rises at that time, rising high, though its nature is only to descend. That water spreads through the leaves, branches and fruit, each receiving its share and the amount in which its welfare lies. Then the flavours of the fruits differ, though the water is one and the tree is one kind; all of this is evidence of a Manager who arranged and perfected it, who is not like created things. The rajaz poet said:

"The earth has a lesson for one who takes heed;
it tells of the workmanship of a sovereign, mighty King.
Its trees are watered with one water,
and its ground is one plot.
The sun and the air do not differ,
yet its produce differs and does not agree.
If this were from the works of nature alone, or
the handiwork of a non-maker, it would not differ,
and would be one single thing. Does anything resemble its offspring except its parent?
The sun and the air, O obstinate one,
and the water and the dust, are one thing.
So what caused this difference
except a Wise One who did not will it in vain?"

(p. 364) al-Hasan said: this is a parable God struck for the hearts of the children of Adam. The earth was one clay, and He spread it out, and it became adjoining plots. Then one water came down upon it from the sky, and this one brings forth a flower and a fruit, while that one brings forth a salt marsh, brine and filth. Likewise people were created from Adam: there came down upon them from the sky a reminder. Some hearts drew near, some hearts humbled themselves, some hearts hardened, and some hearts were heedless. al-Hasan also said: no one sits with the Qur'an without rising from it with an increase or a decrease. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it adds nothing for the wrongdoers but loss﴾ [17:82]. This is similar to the speech of the Sufis.

﴿Indeed in that﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: in the difference of colours, scents and flavours. ﴿Are signs﴾: proofs and indications. ﴿For a people who use their reason﴾: who know the evidences and so reason from them to the oneness of the Creator, the Powerful. Since the inference in this verse rests on things that are most evident, namely the observable adjoining of plots and gardens, their being watered, and their being made to excel one another, the verse closes with ﴿for a people who use their reason﴾. This is unlike the verse before it, whose inference requires reflection and further consideration; its closing is ﴿for a people who reflect﴾ [13:3].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verse 5–7 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord; those have shackles upon their necks; those are the companions of the Fire, wherein they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good, though exemplary punishments have already passed before them. Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment.﴾ (p-365) When He had established the proofs of His great power through the wonders He placed in His dominion, which none other than Him can bring about, the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) was amazed at the denial of the polytheists of His oneness and their belittling of His power, owing to the weakness of their intellects. So it was revealed: ﴿And if you are amazed﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "And if you are amazed at their denying you, after they had judged you to be among the truthful, then this is more amazing." It was also said: "And if you are amazed, O Muhammad, at their worship of what does not possess for them any harm or benefit, after they have come to know the proofs indicating monotheism, then this is more amazing." Al-Zamakhshari said: "And if you are amazed at their saying, O Muhammad, in denying the Resurrection, then their saying is amazing and worthy of being wondered at, because He who is able to originate what He has enumerated for you of the great creations, and was not wearied by creating them, the restoration is easier and simpler for Him. So their denial is one of the marvels among marvels." End of quote. The meaning of the wording is not what was mentioned, because he made the object of the Prophet's (ﷺ) amazement their saying in denying the Resurrection, so the response and the condition become identical, since the sense becomes: "And if you are amazed at their saying in denying the Resurrection, then be amazed at their saying in denying the Resurrection." Rather, the literal meaning is that amazement should occur from you, so let it be from their saying: ﴿When we are dust﴾, to the end of the verse. And the meaning that ought to be wondered at is the denial of the Resurrection, because He, exalted is He, is the originator of things, and whoever is able to bring them forth from pure non-existence is able to restore them, as the Exalted said: ﴿And He it is who begins the creation and then repeats it, and it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27], meaning: it is easy for Him.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This verse is a rebuke to the disbelievers; that is: "And if you are amazed, O Muhammad, at their ignorance and their turning away from the truth, they are deserving of that. And it is strange and amazing that their hearts deny return after we have become a new creation." The wording may also bear another sense: "If you intend a marvel, then come, for among the most marvelous marvels is their saying." End of quote. The readers differed regarding the two interrogatives when they come together, in eleven places: here is one place, and likewise in al-Mu'minun, in al-ʿAnkabut, in al-Naml, in al-Sajda, in al-Waqiʿa, in al-Naziʿat, and in Bani Isra'il there are two places, and likewise in al-Saffat.

Nafiʿ and al-Kisaʾi read the first as an interrogative and the second as a declarative, except in al-ʿAnkabut and al-Naml, where it is the reverse of Nafiʿ's reading. Al-Kisaʾi combined the two interrogatives in al-ʿAnkabut, and in al-Naml he followed his own principle, except that he added a nun, so he read: (innana lamukhrajun). Ibn ʿAmir read the first as a declarative and the second as an interrogative, except in al-Naml and al-Naziʿat, where it is reversed; and in al-Naml he added a nun like al-Kisaʾi. Except in al-Waqiʿa, where he read both as interrogatives; this is the reading of the rest of the Seven in this category, except that Ibn Kathir and Hafs read in al-ʿAnkabut the first as declarative and the second as interrogative, and they follow their own principles regarding the meeting of two hamzas, whether by easing, by making clear, by separating the two hamzas, or by omitting that.

And their saying: (fa-ʿajabun) is a fronted predicate, and there must necessarily be an estimated qualifier in it, because the meaning is not complete with an unqualified noun, so it must be restricted. Its estimate, God knows best, is: "then amazement, i.e., a [certain] amazement," or "then a strange amazement." When we estimate it as qualified, it is permissible to parse it as a subject, because it is indefinite, with a qualifier that justifies its being a subject, which is the adjective, and it has come in the position of a subject. The fact that the predicate is definite does no harm, as Sibawayh permitted in "kam malikun?" because of the justifier of the subject in it, which is the interrogative, and in such as "qsid rajulan khayrun minhu abuhu," also because of a justifier of the subject, which is that it governs what follows it. Abu al-Baqa' said: "It has been said that ʿajab means muʿajjab (one who is amazed at), and so on this basis it is permissible for their saying to be raised by it." End of quote. What he permitted is not permissible, because it does not follow that if one thing has the meaning of another, its operation in governing is the same as its; so muʿajjab governs, but ʿajab does not govern. Do you not see that the pattern fiʿl like dhabaḥa, the pattern fiʿl like qabaḍa, and the pattern fuʿla like ghurfa, have the meaning of maf'ul, yet do not govern as it does? So one does not say: "I passed by a man who slaughtered his ram," nor "by a man who seized his wealth," nor "by a man who scooped his water," meaning "whose ram is slaughtered," "whose wealth is seized," or "whose water is known." They have indeed stated that these substitute for the passive participle in signification, not in governing. The grammarians have confined what raises the agent, and the apparent view is that "ʾa-idha" is an element governed by their saying, spoken as a quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿When we are dust﴾ up to the end of their saying may be in the position of nominative as a substitute for their saying. End of quote. This is a strained parsing and a departure from the apparent. And "idha" is purely a temporal adverb and has no sense of condition, so its governing element is an omitted verb that is explained by what the second clause indicates, and its estimate is: "Shall we be raised?" or "Shall we be gathered?"

(Ulaika) is a reference to the speaker of that statement, and it is an affirmation firmly set upon denying the Resurrection; therefore He judged them to be disbelievers, since they had made His power incapable of restoring what He had originated and invented at the beginning. And when He judged them to be disbelievers in this world, He mentioned what they will come to in the Hereafter as a threat, and He expressed that in an independent clause, with them as those pointed to. The apparent view is that the shackles are literally upon their necks like shackles, and then He mentioned what they will be settled in during the Hereafter, as He said: ﴿When the shackles are upon their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71]. It has been said: it may be figurative, meaning: they are shackled from faith, so "idha" takes the place of sealing and stamping upon the hearts, as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed We have placed shackles upon their necks﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8], and as the poet said:

"For them, away from right guidance, are shackles and fetters."

It has also been said: the shackles here are an expression for their corrupt deeds upon their necks like shackles, and then He mentioned what they will be settled in during the Hereafter, and expressed that in an independent clause, with them as those pointed to, returning upon them what they denied of the Resurrection, since the companions of the Fire exist only after the gathering. And since they were threatened with punishment if they persisted in disbelief, and were denying what they had been warned of regarding punishment, they asked and sought hastily in demanding that punishment come upon them, and that was by way of mockery, as they said: ﴿Then rain upon us stones﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and they said: ﴿Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim﴾ [al-Isra: 92].

Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-sayyi'a is the punishment, and al-hasana is well-being. Qatada said: "with evil before good." It has been said: with affliction and punishment before ease and well-being. These sayings are close in meaning.

﴿And exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾: that is, they ask you to hasten the evil while knowing what befell others among the deniers of the messengers in earlier nations. This indicates the feebleness of their minds, since they seek to hasten punishment in this state. Had the punishment of their like not preceded, they might have had an excuse, but they do not take heed, so they mock. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-mathulat are the uprooting punishments, like the mutilation of nose and ear and the like. al-Suddi said: the vengeances. Qatada said: the manifest events of God, like the transformation into apes and swine. Mujahid said: the parables that are struck. The majority read: with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the ta', while Mujahid and al-Aʿmash read with fatha on both. Ibn ʿUmayr Isa, and in a narration from al-Aʿmash and Abu Bakr, read with damma on both. Ibn Wathhab read with damma on the mim and sukun on the tha'. Ibn Musarrif read with fatha on the mim and sukun on the tha'.

﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ is an expression of hope for forgiveness, and ﴿despite their wrongdoing﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the meaning is: He forgives them despite their wronging themselves by committing sins; that is, wronging themselves. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful than this one." (p-367) Al-Tabari said: "that He may forgive them in the Hereafter." Al-Qasim ibn Yahya and a group said: "that He may forgive them the past wrong by their repentance in the present." It has been said: "that He may forgive the minor sins of one who avoids the major ones." It has been said: "that He may forgive them by His concealing and granting them respite, so He does not hasten punishment for them despite their hastening in disobedience." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "The apparent meaning of forgiveness here is His concealing it in this world and granting respite to the disbelievers. Do you not see the facilitation in the wording 'forgiveness,' that it is indefinite and restricted, and there is no intensification in it as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82]? The sense of the verse gives this its ruling against them, that they are for the Fire." Then he said: "And they ask you to hasten"; so when the evil of their conduct became apparent, the punishment of them became obligatory in the mind of the hearer, so He informed of His way with the nations, and that He grants respite despite the wrongdoing of the disbelievers." End of quote.

﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾ is a warning and an anticipation of punishment after a hope. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Were it not for God's pardon and His forgiveness, no one would enjoy a life, and were it not for His punishment, everyone would become complacent." In another hadith: "If the servant knew the extent of God's pardon, he would not refrain from sin; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would suppress his self in the worship of God, Mighty and Majestic."

﴿And those who disbelieved say: "Why has not a sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide﴾. From Ibn ʿAbbas: when it was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) placed his hand upon his chest and said: "I am a warner," and he gestured with his hand toward the shoulder of ʿAli and said: "You are the guide, O ʿAli; through you will be guided whoever comes after me." Al-Qushayri said: It was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. And "those who disbelieved" are the polytheists of the Arabs, or whoever among their polytheists and disbelievers denied his prophethood, and they did not count the extraordinary signs sent down, such as the splitting of the moon, the yielding of trees, the turning of the staff into a sword, the gushing of water from between the fingers, and similar things. Out of obstinacy they proposed signs like those mentioned in Subhan, and in al-Furqan, like the gushing of a spring, the ascent to heaven, a kingdom, and a treasure. So God, Exalted, said to His Prophet: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, frightening them of the evil consequence, and a counselor like other messengers; it is not for you to bring what they propose, since he has already brought signs numbering the pebbles, and all signs are alike in the soundness of the claim, with no difference among them. So the proposing is only obstinacy, and God has not established the custom of manifesting the proposed signs except for a sign whose punishment He has decreed and whose uprooting He has determined.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 13, verses 5–7 (part 2 of 2):

The word (hadin) ("a guide") may be understood as being conjoined to (mundhirun) ("a warner"), with the phrase (li-kulli qawmin) ("for every people") placed between them. This is the view of ʿIkrimah and Abu al-Duha. If you take ﴿wa-li-kulli qawmin hadin﴾ ("and for every people there is a guide") in its general sense, its meaning is: "and one who calls to guidance," as in his saying: "I have been sent to the red and the black." If, however, you take hadin in its literal sense, then (li-kulli qawmin) is specific: that is, "for every people there is a guide among those who speak." It has also been said: "for every nation that has passed away there was a guide," meaning a prophet calling them. The intent is: your matter is not novel or unprecedented. This is the view of Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: "a prophet who calls them with the signs that are given to him, not with the proposals they dictate." Al-Zamakhshari followed them and said: "a guide is one of the prophets who guides them to the religion and calls them to God by a way of guidance and a sign specific to him, and [God] did not make all things a single law in specific signs."

A group said: the guide in this verse is God Most High. It is narrated that this is from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. On this reading, (hadin) means "one who originates guidance." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "There are expressions connected to this meaning, and it is known that God Most High is the Guide from other places in the Qur'an."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "In this view there is another aspect: the meaning is that they deny that what has been sent down to you is signs, and they obstinately resist. So let that not concern you; you are only a warner, and it is incumbent upon you only to warn, not to establish faith by compulsion. The one who establishes faith by compulsion is God Most High." End of quote. His words indicate Muʿtazili doctrine.

In explaining the view he followed from Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, he wrote the following: "By what He has added of the mention of the signs of His knowledge and His measuring out of things, He has indicated the principles of His wisdom: that giving every warner signs is a matter arranged by all-pervading knowledge and determined by divine wisdom. Had He known in granting their proposal any good or benefit, He would have granted it to them."

Al-Zamakhshari also said, regarding the view that the guide is God Most High, that is, by compulsion according to his claim (p. 368): "As for this second aspect, by it He has indicated that among this power is His power and this is His knowledge; He alone is capable of guiding them, knowing by which way He guides them, and there is no path to that for anyone else." End of quote.

A group said: the guide is ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. Even if what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, which we mentioned at the start of this verse, is sound, the Messenger (ﷺ) made ʿAli ibn Abi Talib an example of the scholars of the community and its guides to the religion. It is as if he said: "You, O ʿAli, are this description," so that Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman and the rest of the scholars among the Companions (may God be pleased with them) enter into it, and then likewise the scholars of every age. The meaning according to this is: "You, O Muhammad, are only a warner, and for every people, past and present, there are callers who are guides to good."

Abu al-ʿAliyah said: the guide is the deed. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: "for every people there is one who preceded them to guidance, the prophet of those people." It has also been said: (hadin) means a leader toward good or toward evil. God Most High said regarding good: ﴿And they were guided to the good of speech, and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Hajj: 24], and He said regarding evil: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 23]. This was said by Abu Salih.

Ibn Kathir paused on (hadin) and (waqin) wherever they occur, and on (wali) here and (baqin) in al-Nahl, with the yaʾ retained. The rest of the Seven omitted it. In al-Iqna' by Abu Jaʿfar Ibn al-Baadhish, from Ibn Mujahid: pausing on the whole category with the yaʾ is for Ibn Kathir, and the Meccans do not know this. In the same work, from Abu Yaʿqub al-Azraq, from Warsh, that he gave him the choice in pausing on the whole category between pausing with the yaʾ and pausing with it omitted. The category is every defective noun that takes tanwin and is not diptote.

And "idha" is purely a temporal adverb and has no sense of condition, so its governing element is an omitted verb that is explained by what the second clause indicates, and its estimate is: "Shall we be raised?" or "Shall we be gathered?"

(Ulaika) is a reference to the speaker of that statement, and it is an affirmation firmly set upon denying the Resurrection; therefore He judged them to be disbelievers, since they had made His power incapable of restoring what He had originated and invented at the beginning. And when He judged them to be disbelievers in this world, He mentioned what they will come to in the Hereafter as a threat, and He expressed that in an independent clause, with them as those pointed to. The apparent view is that the shackles are literally upon their necks like shackles, and then He mentioned what they will be settled in during the Hereafter, as He said: ﴿When the shackles are upon their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71]. It has been said: it may be figurative, meaning: they are shackled from faith, so "idha" takes the place of sealing and stamping upon the hearts, as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed We have placed shackles upon their necks﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8], and as the poet said:

"For them, away from right guidance, are shackles and fetters."

It has also been said: the shackles here are an expression for their corrupt deeds upon their necks like shackles, and then He mentioned what they will be settled in during the Hereafter, and expressed that in an independent clause, with them as those pointed to, returning upon them what they denied of the Resurrection, since the companions of the Fire exist only after the gathering. And since they were threatened with punishment if they persisted in disbelief, and were denying what they had been warned of regarding punishment, they asked and sought hastily in demanding that punishment come upon them, and that was by way of mockery, as they said: ﴿Then rain upon us stones﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and they said: ﴿Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim﴾ [al-Isra: 92].

Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-sayyi'a is the punishment, and al-hasana is well-being. Qatada said: "with evil before good." It has been said: with affliction and punishment before ease and well-being. These sayings are close in meaning.

﴿And exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾: that is, they ask you to hasten the evil while knowing what befell others among the deniers of the messengers in earlier nations. This indicates the feebleness of their minds, since they seek to hasten punishment in this state. Had the punishment of their like not preceded, they might have had an excuse, but they do not take heed, so they mock. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-mathulat are the uprooting punishments, like the mutilation of nose and ear and the like. al-Suddi said: the vengeances. Qatada said: the manifest events of God, like the transformation into apes and swine. Mujahid said: the parables that are struck. The majority read: with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the ta', while Mujahid and al-Aʿmash read with fatha on both. Ibn ʿUmayr Isa, and in a narration from al-Aʿmash and Abu Bakr, read with damma on both. Ibn Wathhab read with damma on the mim and sukun on the tha'. Ibn Musarrif read with fatha on the mim and sukun on the tha'.

﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ is an expression of hope for forgiveness, and ﴿despite their wrongdoing﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the meaning is: He forgives them despite their wronging themselves by committing sins; that is, wronging themselves. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful than this one." (p-367) Al-Tabari said: "that He may forgive them in the Hereafter." Al-Qasim ibn Yahya and a group said: "that He may forgive them the past wrong by their repentance in the present." It has been said: "that He may forgive the minor sins of one who avoids the major ones." It has been said: "that He may forgive them by His concealing and granting them respite, so He does not hasten punishment for them despite their hastening in disobedience." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "The apparent meaning of forgiveness here is His concealing it in this world and granting respite to the disbelievers. Do you not see the facilitation in the wording 'forgiveness,' that it is indefinite and restricted, and there is no intensification in it as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82]? The sense of the verse gives this its ruling against them, that they are for the Fire." Then he said: "And they ask you to hasten"; so when the evil of their conduct became apparent, the punishment of them became obligatory in the mind of the hearer, so He informed of His way with the nations, and that He grants respite despite the wrongdoing of the disbelievers." End of quote.

﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾ is a warning and an anticipation of punishment after a hope. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Were it not for God's pardon and His forgiveness, no one would enjoy a life, and were it not for His punishment, everyone would become complacent." In another hadith: "If the servant knew the extent of God's pardon, he would not refrain from sin; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would suppress his self in the worship of God, Mighty and Majestic."
