Rather, the mu'aqqibāt are described by three attributes apparently: the first: "min bayni yadayhi wa-min khalfihi," that is, occurring from before him. The second: "yaḥfaẓūnahu," that is, they are guarding him. The third: their being "min amri Allāh," that is, occurring by the command of God. And if we make "min bayni yadayhi wa-min khalfihi" connected to "yaḥfaẓūnahu," then the mu'aqqibāt are described by two attributes: one, "they guard him from before him and behind him," and the second, His saying, "min amri Allāh," that is, occurring by the command of God. The most that can be said about this is that the description by a clause was mentioned before the description by a prepositional phrase, and that is common and eloquent; and the description by a clause indicating permanence is more emphatic in guarding, so he put the description by it first.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī mentioned, concerning the angels appointed over us and among the scribes, opinions drawn from the astrologers and the people of the talismans, and some people whom the scholars of Islam named; one can learn about that from his tafsir. When He, Exalted, mentioned the encompassing of His knowledge over the hidden and the manifest things, and that the angels follow up on the accountable to record what proceeds from them, whether good or evil, He mentioned that the blessings He has bestowed on them and the favors He has lavished on them are not removed from them to punishment except through disbelief in those blessings, neglect of His command to obey, and exchanging them for disobedience. So in mentioning that there is an admonition to hold to obedience and a warning of the consequence of disobedience. The apparent meaning is that the change of blessings does not befall a people until they themselves change through acts of disobedience. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this place requires interpretation, because it is established by report that the Sharīʿa has ordained that the common people may be taken for the sins of the elite, and the reverse, as in His saying: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike only those of you who have wronged﴾ [al-Anfāl: 25], and their question to the Messenger (ﷺ): "Shall we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases." So the meaning of the verse is: until a change takes place, either from them, or from one who observes them, or from one who is a cause of it among them, just as God, Exalted, changed the fleeing ones on the day of Uhud through the cause of the archers' change of what was in themselves, and other examples in the rules of the Sharīʿa. So the meaning of the verse is not that no punishment descends on anyone except by a prior sin on his part; rather, calamities may descend because of the sins of others. There are also calamities by which God increases the reward of the one afflicted, and those are not a change. End of quote. In a hadith: "When they see the wrongdoer and do not seize his hand, God is about to encompass them all with punishment." It was also said: this refers back to His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten evil before good﴾ [al-Raʿd: 6]. God thus clarified that the punishment of uprooting does not descend upon them except when it is known of them that they persist in disbelief and sins, unless God's knowledge is that among them, or among their descendants, there is one who will believe; in that case He does not send down upon them the punishment of uprooting.

"Mā" is a relative pronoun whose complement is (bi-qawmin), and likewise (mā bi-anfusihim). In "mā" there is an ambiguity whose intended meaning is not determined except by the context of the statement and by supposing an omitted element through which the meaning becomes clear. The estimate is: God does not change what is with a people of blessing and goodness into its opposite until they change what is in themselves of obedience to Him into continual disobedience.

"Evil" (sūʾ) encompasses everything that is distressing, whether illness, harm, punishment, or other tribulation. Since the context of the statement concerns vengeance against the disobedient, He mentioned only "evil" (sūʾan). Otherwise, evil and good, when God, Exalted, wills something of them, there is no repelling it; He mentioned evil for emphasis in causing fear. al-Suddī said: "min wāl" means "from one who takes refuge." al-Zamakhsharī said: "from one who manages their affairs and wards off from them." It was also said: "from a helper who prevents from His punishment."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verses 8–11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah knows what every female carries, and what the wombs diminish and what they increase. And everything with Him is in a measure.﴾ ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Exalted.﴾ ﴿It is the same for you whether one of you conceals speech or openly speaks it, and whether one hides by night or goes forth freely by day.﴾ ﴿For him there are successive watchers before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of Allah. Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah wills misfortune for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have no protector other than Him.﴾

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is what al-Zamakhshari pointed out: when the disbelievers asked that a sign be sent down to the Messenger ﷺ (and how many signs had been sent down), He followed that with a mention of the signs of His dazzling knowledge, His penetrating power and His eloquent wisdom, and that the signs already sent down to him are sufficient for whoever reflects, so they should not demand others, and that the sending down of signs is only in accordance with what Allah, exalted is He, decrees. It was also said: the connection is that, since their denial of resurrection had preceded, on the grounds that the parts disperse and become mixed with one another such that they cannot be distinguished, He drew attention to the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, and that whoever knows all that is known is able to restore what He originated. It was also said: the connection is that, since they hastened the evil (the punishment), He drew attention to His knowledge of all that is known, and that the punishment is only sent down according to what He knows to be a benefit. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: In this example, which draws attention to the power of Allah that necessitates the possibility of resurrection, He recounts "the one" of the kind that are "the keys of the unseen" (i.e., that none knows except Him), and what females carry of the sperm-drop of every kind of animal. This beginning shows that restoration is not difficult for the One who is capable of it. And ﴿Allah knows﴾ is a resumptive statement (mustaʾnaf, one that begins a new sentence), a subject and predicate (mubtadaʾ wa khabar). Whoever interprets "the guide" (al-Hadi) as Allah may allow that ﴿Allah﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is Allah, exalted is He, then he began to inform about Him saying: ﴿knows﴾. Here ﴿yaʿlamu﴾ (knows) is transitive to one object, because the meaning here is not attribution but a connection to the objects themselves. As for ﴿mā﴾ (what), they permitted that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (that which), in which case the returning pronoun in its relative clause is omitted; ﴿taghīḍu﴾ (diminishes) would then be transitive, and ﴿an﴾ would be verbal (maṣdariyyah, forming a verbal noun), so that ﴿taghīḍu wa tazdādu﴾ would both be intransitive. The usage of both transitivity and intransitivity is attested in the speech of the Arabs. ﴿Mā﴾ may also be an interrogative subject (mubtadaʾ), with ﴿taḥmilu﴾ its predicate and ﴿yaʿlamu﴾ its complement, and the clause is in the place of the object. ﴿Taḥmilu﴾ here is from carrying in the belly, not from carrying on the back. In the codex of Ubayy: ﴿mā taḍaʿu wa taḥmilu﴾ ("what every female bears and bears"), which is an explanatory addition, since it was not part of the body of the codex (sawād al-muṣḥaf, the written text of the codex).

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿taghīḍu﴾ means "diminishes in its creation," and ﴿tazdādu﴾ means "completes."

Mujahid said: the diminishing of the womb is that it bleeds upon the pregnancy, so the child becomes weak in the belly and is drawn back; but if the child remains in her belly after nine months, a period in which it would have been completed from five (months), and what was lost through the bleeding accompanies it. End of Ibn ʿAbbas's statement.

ʿIkrimah said: ﴿taghīḍu﴾ is by the cessation of menstruation during pregnancy, and ﴿tazdādu﴾ is by postpartum bleeding after birth.

Qatadah said: the diminishing is the miscarriage, and the increase is remaining beyond nine months. Al-Dahhak said: the diminishing of the womb is that the woman miscarries the child, and the increase is that she bears it for a full and complete term. And also from al-Dahhak: the diminishing is the deficiency from nine months, and the increase is up to two years. It was also said: (the increase is) in the number of children, for she may carry one and she may carry more.

The majority said: the diminishing of the womb is the blood upon the pregnancy. Al-Zamakhshari said: If ﴿mā﴾ is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), then the meaning is: He knows what she carries of the child, in whatever state it is, whether male or female, complete or premature, beautiful or ugly, tall or short, and other states that are present and progressing. And He knows what the wombs diminish, that is, what they reduce; and ﴿mā tazdādu﴾ means what they take in excess. You say: "I took my right from him and I took from him such-and-such in excess." And from this: ﴿and they increased by nine﴾ (Qur'an 18:25). It is also said: "I increased it, and it increased on its own (zāda binafsihi) and increased (izdāda)." What the womb diminishes and what it increases is the number of children, for it may contain one, and it may contain two, three or four. It is narrated that Shurayk was the fourth of four in his mother's belly. And from this: the body of the child, for it may be complete or premature. And from this: the period of its birth, for it may be less than nine months, or more than that, up to a year according to Abu Hanifah, up to four years according to al-Shafiʿi, and up to five years according to Malik. It was said: al-Dahhak was born after two years, and Harim ibn Hibban remained in his mother's belly for four years, which is why he was named Harim (the aged one). And from this: the blood, for it may decrease and increase. If ﴿mā﴾ is verbal (maṣdariyyah), then the meaning is: He knows the pregnancy of every female, and He knows the diminishing of the wombs and their increase, so nothing of that is hidden from Him, from its times and its states. It may also be intended that the diminishing and increase are of what is in the wombs, so the verb is attributed to the wombs while it actually belongs to what is in them, on the basis that the verb is intransitive. This is strengthened by the saying of al-Hasan: "al-ghaydūḍa" is when a child is born at eight months or less, and "al-izdiyād" is when it exceeds nine months. He also said: "al-ghayḍ" is a miscarriage that is not complete, and "al-izdiyād" is a child of full term. End of the quotation. These are the statements of the exegetes gathered together after being scattered.

﴿Bi-miqdār﴾ means "by a measure that is determined." The term ﴿miqdār﴾ is used to mean "quantity" and also "that by which a thing is measured." The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and everything with Him is in a measure﴾ is general: that is, with a limit that it does not exceed and from which it does not fall short. Ibn ʿAbbas said: everything of reward and punishment is with Him in a measure, that is, according to the measure of obedience and disobedience. Al-Dahhak said: of diminishing and increasing. Qatadah said: of provision and term. It was also said: the health of the fetus and its sickness, its death and its life, its provision and its term.

The better view is to take these statements as examples rather than as specifications, since there is no proof for specifying them.

By "being with Him" is meant knowledge: that is, He, exalted is He, knows the quantity of everything and its manner, in the detailed and clear way, so confusion about those known things is impossible. It was also said that by "being with Him" is meant that He, exalted is He, specified each event to its exact time and a particular state by His eternal will and everlasting determination. Having mentioned that He knows hidden things that none but He knows, and that minute particulars are among the secrets of His knowledge, He mentioned that His knowledge encompasses all things. So His knowledge, exalted is He, relates to what is witnessed by the knower in the same way that it relates to what is hidden from them. It was said: "the unseen" is that which is non-existent, and "the witnessed" is that which exists. It was also said: "the unseen" is what is absent from the senses, and "the witnessed" is what is present to the senses. Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿ʿĀlima al-ghayb﴾ with the accusative case. ﴿Al-Kabīr﴾ (the Great) is the one of great status, beneath whom everything is; ﴿al-Mutaʿāl﴾ (the Exalted) is the one who is elevated above everything by His power, or the one who is too great for the attributes of created beings and is exalted above them. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr, in one narration, kept the final yāʾ of ﴿al-Mutaʿāl﴾ both in pause and in continuous recitation, and this is the more common in the Arabic language; the rest omitted it both in continuous recitation and in pause, because it is written that way in the orthography. Sibawayh cited its omission in the rhyme-endings of verses (fawāṣil) and in the rhyme of poetry (qawāfī), and others permitted its omission absolutely. The reason for its omission, even though it is omitted with tanwīn (nunation), is that when the nunation is replaced, the yāʾ is omitted together with the replacing element, treating it as its substitute.

Since He mentioned that He, exalted is He, is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed in general, He then mentioned the connection of His knowledge with a particular matter of the conduct of the responsible persons, saying: ﴿It is the same for you﴾ and so on. The meaning is: in His knowledge, the one who conceals speech and the one who speaks it openly are equal; nothing of their words is hidden from Him. ﴿Sawāʾ﴾ (the same) has been discussed before, along with its meanings; here it means "equal," and in the most common dialects it is not dualized. Abu Zayd transmitted its dual form, so one says: "they two are sawāʾān." It was also said: it has an omission; that is: "It is the same among you: the secret of the one who conceals speech and the open speech of the one who speaks it." They parsed ﴿sawāʾ﴾ as the predicate of a subject (khabar mubtadaʾ), or as the subject, with "man asarra" in the place of the one it is coordinated with. Ibn ʿAtiyyah's statement that Sibawayh deemed this weak because it begins with an indefinite noun is not correct. Sibawayh himself parsed the Arabs' saying "sawāʾun ʿalayhi al-khayru wa al-sharru" in this way. It may be that ﴿sawāʾ﴾ is the subject (mubtadaʾ), because it is qualified by His saying ﴿minkum﴾ (among you), and "man" is the predicate coordinated with it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿mustakhfin﴾ means "hidden," and ﴿sārib﴾ means "visible." Mujahid said: "mustakhfin" means one who hides his sins. The interpretation of al-Akhfash and Qutrub is that the one who hides here is by the outward appearance; and even if it is present in the language, the context of its being joined with "by night" and the context of "sārib" with "by day" repels it. The two descriptions correspond in His saying ﴿and whoever is one who hides﴾, since it corresponds to ﴿whoever conceals speech﴾, and in His saying ﴿sārib bi-l-nahār﴾ (goes forth by day), since it corresponds to ﴿and whoever speaks it openly﴾. The meaning, and Allah knows best, is that His knowledge, exalted is He, encompasses the speech and deeds of the responsible persons, and nothing of that escapes Him. The apparent division requires repeating "man" but it was omitted because it is known, since His saying ﴿whoever conceals speech and whoever speaks it﴾ came before. But that is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans, while the Kufans permitted it. It is also permitted that ﴿wa sārib﴾ (and one who goes forth) be coordinated with "man" and not with "mustakhfin," so that the division is sound, as if it were said: "It is the same: a person who is one who hides by night, and a person who is one who goes forth by day." It is also permitted that it be coordinated with "mustakhfin," and "man" is intended as two persons, and the verb is construed according to the meaning in the division of the predicate of the subject that is the same, and according to the wording of "man" in the singular "huwa" (he). The meaning is: "It is the same: the two who are one who hides by night and one who goes forth by day," being one man who hides by night and goes forth by day, and so that his conduct among people is seen. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This is one category, which Allah has made the day of his ease. The meaning is: this one, and the one whose whole affair is one, free of doubt, are equal in Allah's full awareness of all of them. The coordination of "sārib" without repeating "man" supports this interpretation, and its omission is not found except in poetry. The verse may also contain three categories: one who conceals is one extreme, one who speaks openly is an extreme opposed to the first, and the third is an intermediate, inconstant person who disobeys by night in secret and displays innocence by day. End of quotation. It was also said: ﴿wa man huwa mustakhfin bi-l-layl﴾ means: by its darkness, intending to conceal his deed in it, as he said: "I visit them while the darkness of night intercedes for me," and as he said:

"How many a favour the darkness of night has done for me."

The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿lahu﴾ (for him) is to "man," as if it were said: "for whoever conceals, and whoever speaks openly, and whoever hides, and whoever goes forth, there are successive watchers." Ibn ʿAbbas said: it refers to "man" in His saying ﴿wa man huwa mustakhfin﴾, and likewise for the rest of the pronouns in the verse.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The muʿaqqibāt, on this view, are the man's guards and bodyguards who protect him. He said: 'On this view, the verse concerns the disbelieving leaders.' al-Ṭabarī chose this opinion, and it is the opinion of ʿIkrima and a group of others. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: 'It is the ruler who is guarded from the command of God.' al-Māwardī mentioned that the sense of the statement on this interpretation negates its affirmation: (they do not guard him from the command of God). End of quote." The "lā" (not) is omitted in the answer to an oath, which is a remote usage.

al-Mahdawī said: "Whoever makes the muʿaqqibāt the guards, the meaning is: they guard him from God, according to his assumption and claim."

It was also said: the pronoun in "lahu" (for him) refers to God, Exalted; that is, for God there are mu'aqqibāt, angels, from before the servant and behind him. The mu'aqqibāt on this view are the angels who record the deeds of the servants, and the guardians are also for them. A hadith has been transmitted on this from ʿUthmān, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is the opinion of Mujāhid and al-Nakhaʿī.

It was also said: the pronoun in "lahu" refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), even though no nearby mention of him has preceded, although his mention has occurred in His saying: ﴿They say, "Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾ [Yunus: 20]. The meaning is that God, Exalted, appointed for His Prophet guardians from the rebellious jinn and humans. Abū Zayd said: the verse about the Prophet (ﷺ) was revealed concerning God's protection of him from Arbad ibn Qays and ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl, from the story that we will mention later in the mention of the thunderbolts.

The first opinion regarding the return of the pronoun is the preferred one, which should be adopted, and on it the verse is interpreted.

[The author] says: Since it has been stated that whoever conceals speech and whoever speaks aloud, and whoever hides by night and goes forth by day, are equal in God's knowledge, nothing about their conditions is hidden from Him, He also mentioned that for that person there are mu'aqqibāt: groups of angels who follow one another in guarding and protecting him.

Muʿaqqib: its form is mufaʿʿil, from ʿaqqaba al-rajulu, when a man comes after another, because some of them follow others, or because they follow what he says and write it down.

al-Zamakhsharī said: the original is mu'taqibāt, so the tāʾ was assimilated into the qāf, as in His saying: ﴿And those who make excuses came﴾ [al-Tawba: 90], meaning the al-muʿtadhirūn. It is permissible to read mu'iqqibāt with a kasra on the ʿayn, though it has not been read with it. End of quote. This is a gross error: the tāʾ is not assimilated into the qāf, nor the qāf into the tāʾ, neither within one word nor across two words. The morphologists have stated explicitly that the qāf and the kāf each assimilate into the other, and they are not assimilated into anything else, nor is anything else assimilated into them. As for his comparing it to His saying ﴿And those who make excuses came﴾ [al-Tawba: 90], it is not necessary that its origin be al-muʿtadhirūn; this was already explained in (Barāʾa), and that it is not necessarily so there. As for his statement that mu'iqqibāt with a kasra on the ʿayn is permissible, this is not permissible, because he based it on the assumption that the original is mu'taqibāt, with the tāʾ assimilated into the qāf. We have already mentioned that this is a gross error.

Al-Muʿaqqibāt is the plural of muʿaqqiba. It was also said: the hāʾ in muʿaqqiba is for emphasis, so it is like rajulun nassāba (a man who is very knowledgeable in genealogy). It was also said: it is the plural of muʿaqqiba, which means a group that comes after another, collectively formed in view of the multiplicity of groups; muʿaqqiba is not the plural of muʿaqqib as al-Ṭabarī mentioned. He compared that to rajul, rijāl, rijālāt, but the matter is not as he stated, because that is like jamal, jimāl, jimālāt, whereas muʿaqqiba and muʿaqqibāt are only like ḍārib and ḍāribāt. This was said by Ibn ʿAṭiyya.

It should be understood that al-Ṭabarī's statement, "the plural of muʿaqqib," means that he applied it, in terms of usage, to the plural of muʿaqqib, although its original application is to the feminine of muʿaqqib, and it became like al-wāridah for the group who come (al-wāridūn). And although its original application is to the feminine of wārid, since it is collectively formed as a broken plural, it may be treated as a feminine singular in predicates and in the return of pronouns, as with: al-ʿulamāʾ qāʾilatun kadhā (the scholars say so), and their saying al-rijāl wa-aʿḍāduhā. Al-Ṭabarī's comparison of that to rajul and rijālāt is in terms of meaning, not in terms of the grammarians' technical practice. He thus clarified that muʿaqqiba, when meant as a collective, is like rijāl in being used for the collective, and that muʿaqqibāt, when used as the plural of muʿaqqiba used collectively, is like rijālāt, which is the plural of rijāl.

ʿUbayd ibn Ziyād read from the pulpit: lahu (al-maʿāqib), and it is the reading of Ubayy and Ibrāhīm. al-Zamakhsharī said: it was read (lahu maʿāqīb). Abū al-Fatḥ said: it is the broken plural of muʿqib with a sukūn on the ʿayn and a kasra on the qāf, like muṭʿim and maṭāʿim, and muqdim and maqādīm. Muʿaqqib was a plural of muʿāqaba, then the yāʾ in maʿāqīb was made a substitute for the omitted hāʾ in muʿāqaba. al-Zamakhsharī said: the plural of muʿaqqib or muʿaqqiba, and the yāʾ is a substitute for the deletion of one of the two qāfs in the broken plural. It was read lahu (mu'taqibāt) from iʿtaqaba. Ubayy read: min bayni yadayhi, and raqīb min khalfihi. Ibn ʿAbbās read: wa-ruqabāʾu min khalfihi, and Abū Ḥātim reported from him that he read (muʿaqqibāt min khalfihi wa-raqīb min bayni yadayhi). These readings should be understood as interpretation, not as Qur'an, because they contradict the written text of the codex on which the Muslims agreed.

Apparently, His saying, Exalted: ﴿min amri Allāh﴾ (by the command of God) is connected to His saying: ﴿yaḥfaẓūnahu﴾ (they guard him). It was said: min here expresses causation, as in your saying: "I broke it from ʿurā" (from a cause), and its meaning and the meaning of bi are the same, as if it were said: they guard him by the command of God and His permission, so their guarding of him is caused by God's command to them to do so. Ibn Jurayj said: they guard his deeds for him, so the genitive has been omitted. Qatāda said: they write down his sayings and his actions. The reading of ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Zayd ibn ʿAlī and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad: (yaḥfaẓūnahu bi-amri Allāh) supports the causal interpretation of min and this interpretation. al-Zamakhsharī said: they guard him on account of God's command, that is, because God commanded them to guard him. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qatāda said: the meaning of min amri Allāh is bi-amri Allāh, that is, they guard him by what God commanded. This is an arbitrary interpretation. End of quote. It is not arbitrary, and the occurrence of min for causation is established in the language of the Arabs.

It was also said: they guard him from the might and vengeance of God, as in your saying: "I guarded Zayd from the lion." The meaning of that is: when God permits them, in their supplication, to delay him, hoping that he will repent and turn back, as in His saying: ﴿Say, "Who protects you by night and day from the Most Merciful?"﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 42]. The meaning of the statement reverts to implication, that is: they pray for him to be guarded from God's punishments, hoping for his repentance.

As for whoever makes the mu'aqqibāt the guards, and makes them the leaders of the disbelievers, then "they guard him" means: in his assumption and imagination, from God's destruction, and they pray for his decree according to his opinion, and that is due to his ignorance of God, Exalted; or it may be meant in the sense of mockery toward him. The essence of mockery is that one reports something whose outward appearance is the affirmation of a certain attribute, while in reality it is the opposite. For this reason some have taken (yaḥfaẓūnahu) to mean that what is intended is: they do not guard him, so "lā" is omitted. On this interpretation, min is connected, as we have mentioned, to yaḥfaẓūnahu, and it is in the accusative position.

al-Farrāʾ and a group said: there is a reordering in the statement: for him are mu'aqqibāt from the command of God, guarding him from before him and behind him. This was reported from Mujāhid, al-Nakhaʿī and Ibn Jurayj. Then "min amri Allāh" is in the nominative position, since it is an attribute of a nominative noun, and it is then connected to an omitted element, meaning: occurring by the command of God, Exalted, and this meaning does not need the assumption of reordering. Rather, the mu'aqqibāt are described by three attributes apparently: the first: "min bayni yadayhi wa-min khalfihi," that is, occurring from before him. The second: "yaḥfaẓūnahu," that is, they are guarding him. The third: their being "min amri Allāh," that is, occurring by the command of God. And if we make "min bayni yadayhi wa-min khalfihi" connected to "yaḥfaẓūnahu," then the mu'aqqibāt are described by two attributes: one, "they guard him from before him and behind him," and the second, His saying, "min amri Allāh," that is, occurring by the command of God. The most that can be said about this is that the description by a clause was mentioned before the description by a prepositional phrase, and that is common and eloquent; and the description by a clause indicating permanence is more emphatic in guarding, so he put the description by it first.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī mentioned, concerning the angels appointed over us and among the scribes, opinions drawn from the astrologers and the people of the talismans, and some people whom the scholars of Islam named; one can learn about that from his tafsir. When He, Exalted, mentioned the encompassing of His knowledge over the hidden and the manifest things, and that the angels follow up on the accountable to record what proceeds from them, whether good or evil, He mentioned that the blessings He has bestowed on them and the favors He has lavished on them are not removed from them to punishment except through disbelief in those blessings, neglect of His command to obey, and exchanging them for disobedience. So in mentioning that there is an admonition to hold to obedience and a warning of the consequence of disobedience. The apparent meaning is that the change of blessings does not befall a people until they themselves change through acts of disobedience. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this place requires interpretation, because it is established by report that the Sharīʿa has ordained that the common people may be taken for the sins of the elite, and the reverse, as in His saying: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike only those of you who have wronged﴾ [al-Anfāl: 25], and their question to the Messenger (ﷺ): "Shall we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases." So the meaning of the verse is: until a change takes place, either from them, or from one who observes them, or from one who is a cause of it among them, just as God, Exalted, changed the fleeing ones on the day of Uhud through the cause of the archers' change of what was in themselves, and other examples in the rules of the Sharīʿa. So the meaning of the verse is not that no punishment descends on anyone except by a prior sin on his part; rather, calamities may descend because of the sins of others. There are also calamities by which God increases the reward of the one afflicted, and those are not a change. End of quote. In a hadith: "When they see the wrongdoer and do not seize his hand, God is about to encompass them all with punishment." It was also said: this refers back to His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten evil before good﴾ [al-Raʿd: 6]. God thus clarified that the punishment of uprooting does not descend upon them except when it is known of them that they persist in disbelief and sins, unless God's knowledge is that among them, or among their descendants, there is one who will believe; in that case He does not send down upon them the punishment of uprooting.

"Mā" is a relative pronoun whose complement is (bi-qawmin), and likewise (mā bi-anfusihim). In "mā" there is an ambiguity whose intended meaning is not determined except by the context of the statement and by supposing an omitted element through which the meaning becomes clear. The estimate is: God does not change what is with a people of blessing and goodness into its opposite until they change what is in themselves of obedience to Him into continual disobedience.

"Evil" (sūʾ) encompasses everything that is distressing, whether illness, harm, punishment, or other tribulation. Since the context of the statement concerns vengeance against the disobedient, He mentioned only "evil" (sūʾan). Otherwise, evil and good, when God, Exalted, wills something of them, there is no repelling it; He mentioned evil for emphasis in causing fear. al-Suddī said: "min wāl" means "from one who takes refuge." al-Zamakhsharī said: "from one who manages their affairs and wards off from them." It was also said: "from a helper who prevents from His punishment."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verses 12–14 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿He it is who shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and produces the heavy clouds.﴾ ﴿The thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and so do the angels, out of awe of Him. He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whomever He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength.﴾ ﴿To Him is the true call. Those they call upon besides Him do not respond to them with anything, except like one who stretches his hands out to water so that it may reach his mouth, but it does not reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ (p-374) When the Exalted lliminated the servants with His saying: ﴿And when God wills evil for a people, there is no turning it back﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], He followed it with what includes matters indicating the power and wisdom of God the Exalted, which resemble blessings in one respect and punishments in another. The discussion of the lightning, the thunder, the thunderbolts and the clouds has already appeared in al-Baqara.

Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: "a fear of the thunderbolts, and a hope for the rain." Qatada said: "a fear for travelers of the harm of rain, and a hope for the resident of its benefit." Close to this is what al-Zajjaj mentioned: "a fear for the land that fears the harm of rain upon it, and a hope for one who hopes to benefit from it." Al-Mawardi mentioned: "a fear of punishment, and a hope for reward."

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and others that he used "the lightning" as a metonym for the water, since rain usually accompanies it, and this is of the type of applying a thing figuratively to what usually accompanies it. Al-Hawfi said: "fear and hope" are two verbal nouns (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun of address. Al-Zamakhshari permitted this, meaning: "fearing and hoping." He said: "The meaning of fear and hope is that the falling of thunderbolts causes fear at the flash of lightning, and gives hope of the rain." Abu al-Tayyib said:

*A youth like the dark cloud: he is feared and hoped for;*
*the rain is hoped for from him, and the thunderbolts are feared.*

It has been said: whoever has harm from it fears the lightning and the rain, like the traveler, and whoever has dates and raisins drying in his threshing-floor, and whoever has a house that leaks. Some lands do not benefit their people from rain, like the people of Egypt. End of quotation.

As for his first statement on the explanation of fear and hope, it is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan that preceded. As for his saying "like the people of Egypt," it is not as he mentioned. Rather, they benefit from rain during many periods of the growth of crops, and by it the crops grow and flourish. Indeed, periods pass over the crops when they are harmed and their growth is diminished by the withholding of rain.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the two words be in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative from the lightning, as if it in itself is fear and hope, or as "possessing fear and hope." Abu al-Baqa said: ﴿fear and hope﴾ is an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is not valid for them to be an object of purpose, because they are not the act of the agent in the causative verb, except by assuming an elided genitive (muḍāf), meaning 'the will of fear and hope,' or in the sense of 'causing fear and causing hope.'" End of quotation. The reason they are not taken at face value is that the agent of the causative verb is not the agent of the fear and hope: the will is God's act, while the fear and the hope are an act of those addressed. So the agent does not unite in the verb with the verbal noun. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that the agent must be the same in both, is not agreed upon; rather, some grammarians do not stipulate this, and this is the view of Ibn Kharuf.

The word ﴿al-saḥāb﴾ (the clouds) is a collective noun which may be masculine or feminine, singular or plural. He said: ﴿and the palm trees, tall with fruit﴾ [Qaf: 10]. For this reason it was made plural in His saying ﴿al-thiqāl﴾ (the heavy), meaning "with water." It is the plural of *thaqīla* (heavy). Mujahid and Qatada said: its meaning is that they bear the water, and the Arabs describe them with this. Qays ibn Akhtam said:

*How many a garden of the sand-grouse's gardens,*
*whose blossoms are like lamps,*
*is none more beautiful than it, nor a cloud*
*or a sheet that uncovers its valleys.*

The heavy buckets are those laden (with water). The apparent sense is that the glorifying (tasbīḥ) is attributed to the thunder. If the thunder can truly glorify, the attribution is literal; if it cannot, the attribution is figurative. His indefinite use of it in His saying ﴿in it are darknesses, thunder and lightning﴾ [al-Baqara: 19] denies that it is the proper name of an angel. Ibn al-Anbari said: the reporting of the sound as glorification is figurative, as when one says, "your speech has grieved me."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And the hearers of the thunder among the servants, who hope for rain, glorify, praising Him": that is, they cry out "Glory be to God" and "Praise be to God." In a hadith: "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise." And from ʿAli: "Glory be to Him for whom it glorifies." When the thunder grew intense, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O God, do not kill us with Your anger, do not destroy us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that." Among the innovations of the Sufis is: the thunder is the shrieks of the angels, the lightning is the sighs of their hearts, and the rain is their weeping. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it has been said regarding the thunder that it is a wind choking between the clouds, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. But in my view this is not valid, because this is the babble of the naturalists and other atheists. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: Know that the investigating philosophers mention that these upper phenomena are only completed by spiritual, celestial powers; the cloud has a particular spirit from the celestial spirits that directs it, and likewise with the winds and all upper phenomena. This is exactly what we have said: that the thunder is the name of an angel among the angels who glorifies God the Exalted. So what the commentators said in this expression is exactly what the investigating philosophers mentioned, so how can an intelligent person deny it? End of quotation.

Even supposing it were the name of an angel, it does not follow that this angel directs the cloud or anything else, since such knowledge is not derived except from the Prophet (ﷺ), who is attested to be protected from error, not from the misguided philosophers.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in His saying ﴿out of His awe﴾ (*min khīfatihi*) is to God the Exalted, just as it refers to Him in ﴿with His praise﴾ (*bi-ḥamdihi*). The angels are His helpers; God made this (awe) for them, so they are fearful, submissive, and obedient to Him. He said: "Tell me about the God of Muhammad: is He made of pearl or of gold?" Then a thunderbolt fell upon him, and the verse was revealed concerning him. His brother Labid has several verses about him, among them:

*I fear for Arbad the calamities of death,*
*and I do not dread the star-rising of al-Simak or of al-Asad.*

*The lightning and the thunderbolts have bereaved me of the horsemen*
*on the day of the disaster, the brave ones.*

These four attributes (ṣilāt) that the relative pronoun *alladhī* is joined to indicate overpowering capability and complete control over the upper and lower worlds. Whoever possesses them should not be disputed about, and one should believe in the lofty attributes he has.

The pronoun in ﴿وهم يُجادِلُونَ﴾ ("while they dispute") refers to the disbelievers who denied the Messenger ﷺ and rejected the signs. They dispute about God's power over resurrection and the recreation of creation, by their saying: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Yā-Sīn 36:78], and about His oneness by taking partners and equals to Him. They also attribute offspring to Him by saying: "The angels are the daughters of God, exalted is He." The meaning is that He, mighty and majestic, possesses these attributes, yet they applied to them something other than their requirement by disputing about Him and His attributes, when their requirement was submission to what the prophets brought.

It has also been said that ﴿وهم يُجادِلُونَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object of *yashā'* ("He wills"), meaning: "He strikes with it whom He wills while they are disputing," as happened to the Jew. Likewise [it happened to] al-Jabbār and to Arbad.

﴿وهُوَ شَدِيدُ المِحالِ﴾ ("and He is severe in might") is a circumstantial nominal clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah) from the divine name (al-jalālah). The majority read *al-miḥāl* with a kasra on the *mīm*. From Ibn ʿAbbās: *al-miḥāl* means enmity; and from him also: rancor. From ʿAlī: seizing. From Mujāhid: strength. From Qutrub: anger. From al-Ḥasan: destruction by the *maḥall*, which is famine.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Aʿraj read *al-maḥāl* with a fatḥah on the *mīm*. From Ibn ʿAbbās: power/strength (*al-ḥawl*). From ʿUbaydah: stratagem (*al-ḥīlah*). It is said: *al-maḥāl* and *al-maḥālah*, which is stratagem; and from it is the Arab proverb: "The man is helpless, not the stratagem (*al-maḥālah*)."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also possible that the meaning is "severe in punishment," and that it is a figure of speech for strength and power, as in the saying: "The arm of God is stronger, and His cutting is sharper," because an animal that is extremely strong is described as possessing intense strength and the ability to undertake what others cannot. Do you not see their saying: "The calamities broke his backbone (*faqarathu al-fawāqir*)"? That is because the *fiqār* is the spine of the back and its support.

The pronoun in *lahu* ("to Him") refers to God, exalted is He. "The call of truth" (*da'wat al-ḥaqq*): Ibn ʿAbbās said: the call of truth is "There is no god but God," and whatever is in the Sharīʿah in its meaning. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: the call of truth is monotheism (*al-tawḥīd*). al-Ḥasan said: God is the Truth (*al-Ḥaqq*), so calling upon Him is the call of truth. It has also been said: the call of truth is supplication to Him at the time of fear, for in that state none is called upon except Him, as He said: ﴿Those whom you call upon vanish, except Him﴾ [al-Isrā' 17:67]. al-Māwardī said: this is more fitting to the context of the verse.

It has been said: "the call of truth" means the call of seeking, the true one, i.e., the one whose answer is hoped for, whereas calling upon other than God is not answered.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: In it there are two aspects. The first: the call is attributed to *al-ḥaqq*, which is the opposite of falsehood, just as the word is attributed to it in His saying: "the word of truth" (*kalimat al-ḥaqq*), to indicate that the call is associated with truth and specific to it, and that it is far from falsehood. The meaning is that God, glorified is He, is called upon, and He answers the call and gives the caller his request if it is in his interest; so His call is associated with the truth because He is worthy that supplication be directed to Him, for in calling upon Him there is benefit and advantage, unlike what does not benefit and whose call is of no use. The second: that it is attributed to *al-ḥaqq*, who is God, mighty and majestic, in the sense of "the call to the Truth who hears and answers."

On the authority of al-Ḥasan, may God have mercy on him: the Truth is God the Exalted, and every call to Him is the call of truth, end of quote. This second aspect that al-Zamakhsharī mentioned does not appear sound, because its end result is the estimate: "To God is a call to God," just as you say: "To Zayd is the call of Zayd," and this construction is not valid. What appears to be the case is that this idafah is of the type of attributing a noun to its adjective, as in His saying: ﴿and the home of the Hereafter﴾ [Yūsuf 12:109] according to one of the two views, and the estimate is: "To God belongs the true call" (*al-da'wah al-ḥaqq*), in contrast to others, for their calling is false. The meaning is that the call to God, exalted is He, is the true call.

When God mentioned the disputing of the disbelievers about God, and their dispute was about establishing gods alongside Him, He mentioned that to Him belongs the true call, i.e., whoever calls upon Him, his call is the truth, unlike their idols for whose sake they disputed about God, for calling upon them is false and nothing comes of it. So He said: ﴿And those who call upon﴾.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The gods whom the disbelievers call upon besides God do not answer them with anything of their requests except with an answer like that of (*bāsiṭ kaffayhi*, "one who stretches out his two palms"), i.e., like the answer of water to one who stretches out his two palms to it, asking it to reach his mouth. Water is an inanimate thing that does not perceive his stretching out his palms, nor his thirst and need for it, and cannot answer his call and reach his mouth. Likewise, what they call upon is an inanimate thing that does not perceive their call, cannot answer them, and cannot benefit them.

It has also been said: they were likened, in the futility of their call to their gods, to one who wants to scoop water with his hands in order to drink it, so he spreads them, extending his fingers, but his palms retain none of it, and he does not reach his goal of drinking, end of quote.

So the pronoun in *yad'ūna* ("they call") refers to the disbelievers, and the returning pronoun for *alladhīna* is omitted, i.e., *yad'ūnahum* ("they call upon them"). This is supported by the reading of those who read *tad'ūna* with a *tā'*, which is the reading of al-Yazīdī from Abū ʿAmr.

It has also been said: *alladhīna* means the disbelievers who call upon, and the object of *yad'ūna* is omitted, i.e., they call upon the idols. The returning pronoun for *alladhīna* is the *wāw* in *yad'ūna*, and the *wāw* in *lā yastajībūna* ("they do not answer") refers in this view to the omitted object of *yad'ūna*, while in the first view it refers to *alladhīna*.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: [the disbeliever is] like one who looks at his reflection in the water, wanting to take hold of it; so too the one in need imagines in his need the image of his need.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: like one who stretches his hands out to the water so that it reaches him without scooping.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: i.e., like one grasping at water, who has nothing in his grip. He said: The Arabs make a proverb of one who strives for what he cannot attain, using the image of one grasping water. Sībawayh cited:

*"So she became, in what had been between me and her of affection,*
*like the one who grips water in his hand."*

And another said:

*"And I, and you, and longing for you,*
*am like one who grips water which his fingers cannot hold."*

It has also been said: the disbelievers, in their calling upon their idols in time of need, are likened to a thirsty man who cannot reach water, who sits at the edge of a well calling upon the water to quench his thirst; he neither reaches the bottom of the well to the water, nor does the water rise up to him, because it is inanimate and does not perceive his thirst or his call. Likewise, what the disbelievers call upon of idols is inanimate and does not perceive their call, cannot answer them, and cannot benefit them, end of quote.

The *kāf* (in *ka-*) is in the position of an accusative (naṣb), i.e., "like the answer (*mithla istijābah*)." The noun *istijābah* is, in estimate, annexed to *bāsiṭ* ("one who stretches out"), and this is the annexation of a verbal noun to its object. The agent of the verbal noun is omitted; its estimate is: "like the answer of water to one who stretches out his two palms to it." When it was omitted, it was made explicit in His words "to the water." Had it been pronounced, the pronoun would have returned to it, and the construction would have been: "his two palms to it." This is what is estimated from al-Zamakhsharī's statement regarding this simile, and Abū al-Baqāʾ followed him.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: The meaning of the speech is that the disbelievers call upon [their idols] for their needs and benefits, and they do not answer. Then God gave an example of their answering with one who stretches his palms to the water and beckons to it with approach; it never reaches his mouth. Likewise the answering of these [idols] and the benefit from them never occurs, end of quote.

The subject of *li-yabluġa* ("so that it may reach") is the pronoun referring to *al-mā'* ("the water"), and *li-yabluġa* is related to *bāsiṭ*. ﴿وما هو﴾ ("and it is not") means: "and the water is not one who reaches it," i.e., one who reaches the mouth. It is also possible that *huwa* refers to the mouth, and the *hā'* in *bi-bālighihi* refers to the water, i.e., "and the mouth is not one who reaches the water," because each of them does not reach the other in this condition.

It is also read as *ka-bāsiṭin kaffayhi* with *tanwīn* on *bāsiṭin*.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Where are those you used to call upon besides God? They will say: they have vanished from us﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:37].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Only in a loss in which there is no benefit," because if they call upon God, He does not answer them, and if they call upon the gods, they are not able to answer them.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: the voices of the disbelievers are veiled from God, so their call is not heard.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Aʿraj read *al-maḥāl* with a fatḥah on the *mīm*. From Ibn ʿAbbās: power/strength (*al-ḥawl*). From ʿUbaydah: stratagem (*al-ḥīlah*). It is said: *al-maḥāl* and *al-maḥālah*, which is stratagem; and from it is the Arab proverb: "The man is helpless, not the stratagem (*al-maḥālah*)."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also possible that the meaning is "severe in punishment," and that it is a figure of speech for strength and power, as in the saying: "The arm of God is stronger, and His cutting is sharper," because an animal that is extremely strong is described as possessing intense strength and the ability to undertake what others cannot. Do you not see their saying: "The calamities broke his backbone (*faqarathu al-fawāqir*)"? That is because the *fiqār* is the spine of the back and its support.

The pronoun in *lahu* ("to Him") refers to God, exalted is He. "The call of truth" (*da'wat al-ḥaqq*): Ibn ʿAbbās said: the call of truth is "There is no god but God," and whatever is in the Sharīʿah in its meaning. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: the call of truth is monotheism (*al-tawḥīd*). al-Ḥasan said: God is the Truth (*al-Ḥaqq*), so calling upon Him is the call of truth. It has also been said: the call of truth is supplication to Him at the time of fear, for in that state none is called upon except Him, as He said: ﴿Those whom you call upon vanish, except Him﴾ [al-Isrā' 17:67]. al-Māwardī said: this is more fitting to the context of the verse.

It has been said: "the call of truth" means the call of seeking, the true one, i.e., the one whose answer is hoped for, whereas calling upon other than God is not answered.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: In it there are two aspects. The first: the call is attributed to *al-ḥaqq*, which is the opposite of falsehood, just as the word is attributed to it in His saying: "the word of truth" (*kalimat al-ḥaqq*), to indicate that the call is associated with truth and specific to it, and that it is far from falsehood. The meaning is that God, glorified is He, is called upon, and He answers the call and gives the caller his request if it is in his interest; so His call is associated with the truth because He is worthy that supplication be directed to Him, for in calling upon Him there is benefit and advantage, unlike what does not benefit and whose call is of no use. The second: that it is attributed to *al-ḥaqq*, who is God, mighty and majestic, in the sense of "the call to the Truth who hears and answers."

On the authority of al-Ḥasan, may God have mercy on him: the Truth is God the Exalted, and every call to Him is the call of truth, end of quote. This second aspect that al-Zamakhsharī mentioned does not appear sound, because its end result is the estimate: "To God is a call to God," just as you say: "To Zayd is the call of Zayd," and this construction is not valid. What appears to be the case is that this idafah is of the type of attributing a noun to its adjective, as in His saying: ﴿and the home of the Hereafter﴾ [Yūsuf 12:109] according to one of the two views, and the estimate is: "To God belongs the true call" (*al-da'wah al-ḥaqq*), in contrast to others, for their calling is false. The meaning is that the call to God, exalted is He, is the true call.

When God mentioned the disputing of the disbelievers about God, and their dispute was about establishing gods alongside Him, He mentioned that to Him belongs the true call, i.e., whoever calls upon Him, his call is the truth, unlike their idols for whose sake they disputed about God, for calling upon them is false and nothing comes of it. So He said: ﴿And those who call upon﴾.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The gods whom the disbelievers call upon besides God do not answer them with anything of their requests except with an answer like that of (*bāsiṭ kaffayhi*, "one who stretches out his two palms"), i.e., like the answer of water to one who stretches out his two palms to it, asking it to reach his mouth. Water is an inanimate thing that does not perceive his stretching out his palms, nor his thirst and need for it, and cannot answer his call and reach his mouth. Likewise, what they call upon is an inanimate thing that does not perceive their call, cannot answer them, and cannot benefit them.

It has also been said: they were likened, in the futility of their call to their gods, to one who wants to scoop water with his hands in order to drink it, so he spreads them, extending his fingers, but his palms retain none of it, and he does not reach his goal of drinking, end of quote.

So the pronoun in *yad'ūna* ("they call") refers to the disbelievers, and the returning pronoun for *alladhīna* is omitted, i.e., *yad'ūnahum* ("they call upon them"). This is supported by the reading of those who read *tad'ūna* with a *tā'*, which is the reading of al-Yazīdī from Abū ʿAmr.

It has also been said: *alladhīna* means the disbelievers who call upon, and the object of *yad'ūna* is omitted, i.e., they call upon the idols. The returning pronoun for *alladhīna* is the *wāw* in *yad'ūna*, and the *wāw* in *lā yastajībūna* ("they do not answer") refers in this view to the omitted object of *yad'ūna*, while in the first view it refers to *alladhīna*.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: [the disbeliever is] like one who looks at his reflection in the water, wanting to take hold of it; so too the one in need imagines in his need the image of his need.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: like one who stretches his hands out to the water so that it reaches him without scooping.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: i.e., like one grasping at water, who has nothing in his grip. He said: The Arabs make a proverb of one who strives for what he cannot attain, using the image of one grasping water. Sībawayh cited:

*"So she became, in what had been between me and her of affection,*
*like the one who grips water in his hand."*

And another said:

*"And I, and you, and longing for you,*
*am like one who grips water which his fingers cannot hold."*

It has also been said: the disbelievers, in their calling upon their idols in time of need, are likened to a thirsty man who cannot reach water, who sits at the edge of a well calling upon the water to quench his thirst; he neither reaches the bottom of the well to the water, nor does the water rise up to him, because it is inanimate and does not perceive his thirst or his call. Likewise, what the disbelievers call upon of idols is inanimate and does not perceive their call, cannot answer them, and cannot benefit them, end of quote.

The *kāf* (in *ka-*) is in the position of an accusative (naṣb), i.e., "like the answer (*mithla istijābah*)." The noun *istijābah* is, in estimate, annexed to *bāsiṭ* ("one who stretches out"), and this is the annexation of a verbal noun to its object. The agent of the verbal noun is omitted; its estimate is: "like the answer of water to one who stretches out his two palms to it." When it was omitted, it was made explicit in His words "to the water." Had it been pronounced, the pronoun would have returned to it, and the construction would have been: "his two palms to it." This is what is estimated from al-Zamakhsharī's statement regarding this simile, and Abū al-Baqāʾ followed him.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: The meaning of the speech is that the disbelievers call upon [their idols] for their needs and benefits, and they do not answer. Then God gave an example of their answering with one who stretches his palms to the water and beckons to it with approach; it never reaches his mouth. Likewise the answering of these [idols] and the benefit from them never occurs, end of quote.

The subject of *li-yabluġa* ("so that it may reach") is the pronoun referring to *al-mā'* ("the water"), and *li-yabluġa* is related to *bāsiṭ*. ﴿وما هو﴾ ("and it is not") means: "and the water is not one who reaches it," i.e., one who reaches the mouth. It is also possible that *huwa* refers to the mouth, and the *hā'* in *bi-bālighihi* refers to the water, i.e., "and the mouth is not one who reaches the water," because each of them does not reach the other in this condition.

It is also read as *ka-bāsiṭin kaffayhi* with *tanwīn* on *bāsiṭin*.

﴿وما دُعاءُ الكافِرِينَ إلّا في ضَلالٍ﴾ ("And the call of the disbelievers is only in error"), i.e., in bewilderment, or in vanishing, because it benefits nothing and is of no use; that call has gone astray from them just as the ones called upon have gone astray. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Where are those you used to call upon besides God? They will say: they have vanished from us﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:37].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Only in a loss in which there is no benefit," because if they call upon God, He does not answer them, and if they call upon the gods, they are not able to answer them.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: the voices of the disbelievers are veiled from God, so their call is not heard.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verses 12–14 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿He it is who shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and produces the heavy clouds.﴾ ﴿The thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and so do the angels, out of awe of Him. He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whomever He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength.﴾ ﴿To Him is the true call. Those they call upon besides Him do not respond to them with anything, except like one who stretches his hands out to water so that it may reach his mouth, but it does not reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ (p-374) When the Exalted lliminated the servants with His saying: ﴿And when God wills evil for a people, there is no turning it back﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], He followed it with what includes matters indicating the power and wisdom of God the Exalted, which resemble blessings in one respect and punishments in another. The discussion of the lightning, the thunder, the thunderbolts and the clouds has already appeared in al-Baqara.

Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: "a fear of the thunderbolts, and a hope for the rain." Qatada said: "a fear for travelers of the harm of rain, and a hope for the resident of its benefit." Close to this is what al-Zajjaj mentioned: "a fear for the land that fears the harm of rain upon it, and a hope for one who hopes to benefit from it." Al-Mawardi mentioned: "a fear of punishment, and a hope for reward."

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and others that he used "the lightning" as a metonym for the water, since rain usually accompanies it, and this is of the type of applying a thing figuratively to what usually accompanies it. Al-Hawfi said: "fear and hope" are two verbal nouns (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun of address. Al-Zamakhshari permitted this, meaning: "fearing and hoping." He said: "The meaning of fear and hope is that the falling of thunderbolts causes fear at the flash of lightning, and gives hope of the rain." Abu al-Tayyib said:

*A youth like the dark cloud: he is feared and hoped for;*
*the rain is hoped for from him, and the thunderbolts are feared.*

It has been said: whoever has harm from it fears the lightning and the rain, like the traveler, and whoever has dates and raisins drying in his threshing-floor, and whoever has a house that leaks. Some lands do not benefit their people from rain, like the people of Egypt. End of quotation.

As for his first statement on the explanation of fear and hope, it is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan that preceded. As for his saying "like the people of Egypt," it is not as he mentioned. Rather, they benefit from rain during many periods of the growth of crops, and by it the crops grow and flourish. Indeed, periods pass over the crops when they are harmed and their growth is diminished by the withholding of rain.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the two words be in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative from the lightning, as if it in itself is fear and hope, or as "possessing fear and hope." Abu al-Baqa said: ﴿fear and hope﴾ is an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is not valid for them to be an object of purpose, because they are not the act of the agent in the causative verb, except by assuming an elided genitive (muḍāf), meaning 'the will of fear and hope,' or in the sense of 'causing fear and causing hope.'" End of quotation. The reason they are not taken at face value is that the agent of the causative verb is not the agent of the fear and hope: the will is God's act, while the fear and the hope are an act of those addressed. So the agent does not unite in the verb with the verbal noun. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that the agent must be the same in both, is not agreed upon; rather, some grammarians do not stipulate this, and this is the view of Ibn Kharuf.

The word ﴿al-saḥāb﴾ (the clouds) is a collective noun which may be masculine or feminine, singular or plural. He said: ﴿and the palm trees, tall with fruit﴾ [Qaf: 10]. For this reason it was made plural in His saying ﴿al-thiqāl﴾ (the heavy), meaning "with water." It is the plural of *thaqīla* (heavy). Mujahid and Qatada said: its meaning is that they bear the water, and the Arabs describe them with this. Qays ibn Akhtam said:

*How many a garden of the sand-grouse's gardens,*
*whose blossoms are like lamps,*
*is none more beautiful than it, nor a cloud*
*or a sheet that uncovers its valleys.*

The heavy buckets are those laden (with water). The apparent sense is that the glorifying (tasbīḥ) is attributed to the thunder. If the thunder can truly glorify, the attribution is literal; if it cannot, the attribution is figurative. His indefinite use of it in His saying ﴿in it are darknesses, thunder and lightning﴾ [al-Baqara: 19] denies that it is the proper name of an angel. Ibn al-Anbari said: the reporting of the sound as glorification is figurative, as when one says, "your speech has grieved me."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And the hearers of the thunder among the servants, who hope for rain, glorify, praising Him": that is, they cry out "Glory be to God" and "Praise be to God." In a hadith: "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise." And from ʿAli: "Glory be to Him for whom it glorifies." When the thunder grew intense, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O God, do not kill us with Your anger, do not destroy us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that." Among the innovations of the Sufis is: the thunder is the shrieks of the angels, the lightning is the sighs of their hearts, and the rain is their weeping. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it has been said regarding the thunder that it is a wind choking between the clouds, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. But in my view this is not valid, because this is the babble of the naturalists and other atheists. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: Know that the investigating philosophers mention that these upper phenomena are only completed by spiritual, celestial powers; the cloud has a particular spirit from the celestial spirits that directs it, and likewise with the winds and all upper phenomena. This is exactly what we have said: that the thunder is the name of an angel among the angels who glorifies God the Exalted. So what the commentators said in this expression is exactly what the investigating philosophers mentioned, so how can an intelligent person deny it? End of quotation.

This man's aim is to make what the philosophers adopt fit the paths of the Sharia, and that never happens. The sayings of the commentators on the thunder were already mentioned in al-Baqara, and they did not agree that the thunder is the name of an angel. Even supposing it were the name of an angel, it does not follow that this angel directs the cloud or anything else, since such knowledge is not derived except from the Prophet (ﷺ), who is attested to be protected from error, not from the misguided philosophers.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in His saying ﴿out of His awe﴾ (*min khīfatihi*) is to God the Exalted, just as it refers to Him in ﴿with His praise﴾ (*bi-ḥamdihi*). The meaning of *khīfatihi* is "out of His dread and majesty." It has been said that it refers to the thunder. The angels are His helpers; God made this (awe) for them, so they are fearful, submissive, and obedient to Him. And although the thunder falls under the term "the angels," this is generalization after specification. End of quotation. This is a weak view.

The word ﴿man﴾ (whomever) is the object of ﴿fa-yuṣību﴾ (so He strikes). This is a case of operation (*iʿmāl*) of competing verbs: the second verb operates on it, since ﴿yursilu﴾ (He sends) also seeks ﴿man﴾, and ﴿fa-yuṣību﴾ seeks it as well. If the first verb had operated, the construction would have been: "He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them upon whomever He wills." But it came in the common usage of the Arabic tongue, and this is the preferred form according to the Basrans: the operation of the second verb.

The object of ﴿yashāʾu﴾ (He wills) is elided, its estimated meaning being: "whomever He wills to strike." In a report: the Messenger (ﷺ) sent to a tyrant among the Arabs to invite him to Islam. He said: "Tell me about the God of Muhammad: is He made of pearl or of gold?" Then a thunderbolt fell upon him, and the verse was revealed concerning him. Mujahid said: a Jew debated with the Messenger (ﷺ), and while he was in that state, a thunderbolt fell and took the top of his skull, so the verse was revealed concerning him. Ibn Jurayj said: the occasion of its revelation was the story of Arbad ibn Rabiʿa and ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl, and he mentioned their well-known story, the gist of which is: ʿAmir threatened the Messenger (ﷺ) if he did not respond to what he requested, and he and Arbad intended to assassinate him, but God the Exalted protected him. ʿAmir was struck with a plague-boil and died in a foreign land, and Arbad was struck by a thunderbolt and killed. His brother Labid has several verses about him, among them:

*I fear for Arbad the calamities of death,*
*and I do not dread the star-rising of al-Simak or of al-Asad.*

*The lightning and the thunderbolts have bereaved me of the horsemen*
*on the day of the disaster, the brave ones.*
