The subject of *li-yabluġa* ("so that it may reach") is the pronoun referring to *al-mā'* ("the water"), and *li-yabluġa* is related to *bāsiṭ*. ﴿وما هو﴾ ("and it is not") means: "and the water is not one who reaches it," i.e., one who reaches the mouth. It is also possible that *huwa* refers to the mouth, and the *hā'* in *bi-bālighihi* refers to the water, i.e., "and the mouth is not one who reaches the water," because each of them does not reach the other in this condition.

It is also read as *ka-bāsiṭin kaffayhi* with *tanwīn* on *bāsiṭin*.

﴿وما دُعاءُ الكافِرِينَ إلّا في ضَلالٍ﴾ ("And the call of the disbelievers is only in error"), i.e., in bewilderment, or in vanishing, because it benefits nothing and is of no use; that call has gone astray from them just as the ones called upon have gone astray. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Where are those you used to call upon besides God? They will say: they have vanished from us﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:37].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Only in a loss in which there is no benefit," because if they call upon God, He does not answer them, and if they call upon the gods, they are not able to answer them.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: the voices of the disbelievers are veiled from God, so their call is not heard.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verses 15–16:

﴿To Allah prostrate, willingly or unwillingly, all who are in the heavens and the earth, and their shadows too, morning and evening.﴾ ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" Say: "Allah." Say: "Have you then taken, apart from Him, protectors who have no power to benefit or harm even themselves?" Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are the darknesses and the light equal? Or have they set up for Allah partners who created the like of His creation, so that the creation seemed alike to them?" Say: "Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Subduer.">: If prostration (sujud) is taken in the sense of submission and compliance (al-khudu' wa al-inqiyad), then by its generality all of them submit to what He wills for them, whether they like it or not, and their shadows submit to Him, in their extension and contraction, their shifting and their vanishing, in accordance with His will. If prostration is taken to mean the specific bodily form, namely placing the forehead on the ground at the place where the one placing it stands, then the statement is general but specified, since whoever does not prostrate is excluded from it. In that case, "willingly" (taw') expresses the prostration of the angels and the believers, and "unwillingly" (karh) expresses the prostration of those whom the sword brought into Islam, as Qatadah said: they prostrate unwillingly, and perhaps out of hypocrisy; or unwillingness is their initial state, and the description remains upon them even if their faith is later sound. It has been said: "willingly" means prostration is not burdensome for them, and "unwillingly" means it is burdensome for them, because imposing obligations is a hardship. It has been said: whoever's period of Islam is long, so that he has grown accustomed to prostration, and "unwillingly" refers to one who is new to Islam until he becomes accustomed to prostration; this was said by Ibn al-Anbari. It has been said: it is general on the assumption that prostration is an expression for the specific bodily form, by which the verb "yasjudu" has the form of a report while its meaning is an effect; or its meaning is: every one in the heavens and the earth must prostrate to Him, and so obligation is expressed by actuality. What appears is that the context of this verse is that the entire world is subdued to Allah, submissive to what He wills of it, restricted to His will, so that nothing proceeds from it except what Allah, the Exalted, has decreed. Thus those you worship, whatever they are, are included under this subjugation. This meaning is supported by the association of the shadows in the prostration. The shadows are not persons of whom prostration in the specific form can be conceived, but they fall under His will, the Exalted, who directs them as He wills, since they are part of the world; the world, its substances and accidents, falls under His will, as the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows turn from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah?﴾ [an-Nahl: 48]. That the word "shadows" is meant to denote persons, as some have said, is weak, and weaker than it is the statement of Ibn al-Anbari: that He, the Exalted, gave the shadows intellects by which they prostrate and humble themselves, just as He gave the mountains understanding so that they addressed and were addressed; for a mountain may possess intellect on the condition of supposing life, but a shadow is an accident in which life cannot be conceived to subsist. Rather, the meaning of the shadows' prostration is their inclination from side to side as He, the Exalted, wills. Al-Farra' said: "al-zill" is a verbal noun, meaning originally [the shade], then it was applied to the image that appears for a body and its length, due to the descent of the sun, and its shortness due to its height; so it is submissive to Allah, the Exalted, in its length, its shortness, and its inclination from side to side. These two times were singled out for mention because shadows are magnified and multiply at them. The explanation of "al-ghuduww" and "al-asal" has preceded at the end of al-A'raf. It is narrated that when the disbelievers prostrate to their idol, their shadow prostrates to Allah at that time.

Abu Mijlaz read: "wa al-iysal." Ibn Jinni said: it is a verbal noun of asala, meaning he entered the afternoon (al-asil), just as one says asbaha, meaning he entered the morning. And since the question concerns a matter so clear that no one can deny it, the answer came from the questioner. Thus precedence in answering was more eloquent in argument against them and quicker in cutting them off, as they awaited an answer from them, since there is no answer except this one which was hastened to, as the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?" Say: "Allah."﴾ [Saba': 24]. What Makki said is remote, that they did not know the answer and so asked the questioner, who informed them of it; because He, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ [Luqman: 25]. If they acknowledge that the originator and inventor of the heavens and the earth is Allah, how can it be said that they did not know the answer and asked the questioner?

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Say: Allah" is a report of their acknowledgment and an affirmation of it against them; for if it is said to them, "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?", they have no choice but to say, "Allah," as in His saying: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 86] ﴿They will say: "Allah."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 87]. This is like the debater saying to his companion, "Is this your statement?" If he says, "This is my statement," he says, "This is your statement," reporting his acknowledgment as a confirmation upon him and a beginning from him; then he says to him, "It will then bind you, according to this statement, to such and such." It may also be an instruction, i.e., if they hold back from answering, He instructs them, and they will take the instruction and cannot deny it. Al-Kirmani said: say, O Muhammad, to the disbelievers: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" It is a question of affirmation and eliciting, that they will say, "Allah"; so when they say it, "Say: Allah," meaning: He is as you have said. It has also been said: if they answer you, well; otherwise, "Say: Allah," since there is no answer other than this. End of quotation. This is a summary of the two opinions that al-Zamakhshari stated. Al-Baghawi said: it is narrated that when he said this to the polytheists, they turned to him and said, "You answer," so Allah commanded him and he said, "Say: Allah." End of quotation.

He used the interrogative in His saying: ﴿Say: Have you then taken...?﴾ as rebuke and denunciation; that is: after you have known that He, the Exalted, is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, you take protectors apart from Him and abandon Him; so you made what should have been a cause of monotheism, your knowledge and acknowledgment, a cause of association. Then He described those protectors by the attribute of incapacity, namely that they have no power to benefit or harm themselves; and one who is in this condition, how can he possess benefit or harm for them? Then He illustrated this by the state of the disbeliever and the believer, and then the state of disbelief and faith, presenting this in the form of a question to which the addressee hastens to answer without thought or reflection, by His saying: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ Then He moved to the question about the two attributes, "the darknesses," which belong to the disbeliever, and "the light," which belongs to the believer.

The discussion of the plural "darknesses" and the singular "light" has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-Akhawan and Abu Bakr read: ﴿Am hal tastawi﴾ with the yā' (yastawi), while the majority read it with the tā' (tastawi). The "am" in His saying "am hal" is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and it is estimated as "bal" (rather); the hamzah is, according to the preferred view, [implicit], and the estimate is: "Rather, is it that the ... are equal?" As for "hal": although it may stand in place of the interrogative hamzah in many places, it has been combined with it in the poet's words:

Ahal ra'unā bi-wādī al-qafri dhī al-ukam
("Did they see us in the barren valley of the dunes?")

And if it is combined with it while the hamzah is explicit, then combining it with "am," which implies it, is more fitting. And "hal" after disjunctive "am" may or may not be used, since it resembles the nominal interrogative particles in non-originality of interrogation, as in His saying: ﴿Or who controls hearing and sight?﴾ [Yunus: 31]. It is also permissible not to use it after disjunctive "am," since "am" implies it, so they would not combine "am" and the hamzah for that reason. The poet said regarding omitting "hal" after "am" and using it:

Hal ma 'alimta wa mā istawda'ta maktūm
Am ḥablahā idh nata'ka al-yawma maṣrūm

Am hal kabīr bakā lam yaqḍi 'abratahu
Ithra al-aḥibbah yawma al-bayni mashkūm

Then He shifted from addressing them to speaking of them in the third person, turning away from them, alerting to their rebuke for setting up partners with Allah, marveling at them, and denouncing them. This interrogation includes mockery of them, since it is known by necessity that these idols, and what they took as protectors apart from Allah and made partners, are not able to create an atom or bring anything into existence at all. The meaning is: these partners do not create anything, so that they would deserve worship. He made them partners of Allah, that is: they made for Allah partners described as creators, like the creation of Allah, so that this resembled them, and they worshipped them. It is known that they do not create anything, and they themselves are created; how then can they share in worship? ﴿Is He who creates like He who creates not?﴾ [an-Nahl: 17]. Then He commanded him, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Say: Allah is the Creator of all things﴾, that is: the Originator of all things, their objects of worship and others; and they too acknowledge this: ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ [Luqman: 25]. It is possible that His saying ﴿and He is the One, the Subduer﴾ falls under the command "Say," so that He commanded him to inform them that He, the Exalted, is the One, singular in divinity, the Subduer under whose power and dominion all things are. It is also possible that it is a new statement, in which it is said that He is characterized by these two attributes, unity and subjugation. He, the Exalted, cannot be overcome, and all else is subdued and under His lordship, mighty and majestic.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verse 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their capacity, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from that which they heat in the fire, seeking ornament or goods, there is a foam like it. Thus does Allah strike the parables of truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it passes away as scum; but as for that which benefits mankind, it remains upon the earth. Thus does Allah strike the parables.﴾ ﴿For those who respond to their Lord is the best (reward). But those who do not respond to Him—if they had everything on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom. Those will have a terrible reckoning, and their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting-place.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is a parable that Allah struck for the truth and its people, and for falsehood and its party, just as He struck the parables of the blind and the seeing, and the darkness and the light, as parables for them both. So He likened the truth (p-381) and its people to the water that descends from the sky, whereby valleys flow for people, and they live by it and it benefits them in various kinds of benefit; and to the metal (filiz) from which they benefit in making ornaments and in fashioning vessels and various tools. Even if there were only iron, which has mighty strength, it would suffice. That (truth) remains upon the earth, enduring with a manifest endurance, as water persists in its benefits, and its traces remain in springs, wells, grains and fruits that grow by it, which are stored and multiply. Likewise, precious substances remain for lengthy periods. And He likened falsehood, in the swiftness of its dissolution, the imminence of its disappearance and its stripping away from benefit, to the foam of the torrent that is cast off, and to the foam of the metal that floats atop it when it is melted.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The beginning of this verse is a reminder of the power of Allah the Exalted and an establishment of proof against the disbelievers in Him. When the mention of that was complete, He made it an example of truth and falsehood, of faith and disbelief, and of doubt regarding the law and certainty in it. End of quote. It has also been said: This is a parable that Allah the Exalted struck for the Qur'an, the hearts, and truth and falsehood. So the water is like the Qur'an, because of what is in it of the life of hearts and the persistence of the Law (shar') and religion. The valleys are a parable for hearts, and the meaning of (according to their capacity) is according to the breadth and narrowness of hearts. Some of them are receptive to it, so they preserve it, retain it, and reflect upon it, and its fruit appears and they grasp its interpretation and meaning. Some are a level below that, and some are several levels below. The foam is like doubts, suspicions, and the denial of the disbelievers that it is the speech of Allah, and their repelling it with falsehood. The pure water that benefits is like the truth. End of quote.

There is a sound hadith that supports this interpretation, which is his ﷺ saying: "The likeness of that with which I have been sent of guidance and knowledge is like a rain that fell upon a land. A portion of it was good, which accepted the water and produced grass and abundant herbage. And there was a portion of it that was hard, which held the water, so people benefited from it: they drank, watered (their animals) and pastured. And there were portions of it that were barren flats which hold no water and produce no grass. That is the likeness of what I have brought of knowledge and guidance, and the likeness of one who does not accept the guidance of Allah with which I have been sent."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: His saying the Exalted, ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾, means by it the Law and religion; ﴿and the valleys flow﴾ means the hearts; i.e., the noble takes his share, and the dull takes his share. This is a statement that is not sound—Allah knows best—from Ibn 'Abbas, because it inclines toward the sayings of the people of symbols (rumuz), and al-Ghazali and the people of that path have relied upon it, and there is no justification for taking the word out of the understanding of Arabic speech without a reason that calls for it. And Allah is the one who grants success to what is right. Even if this saying is sound from Ibn 'Abbas, he intended only that His saying the Exalted, ﴿Thus does Allah strike the parables of truth and falsehood﴾, means: the truth that becomes settled in hearts, and the falsehood that likewise befalls them. End of quote.

The word "ma'" (water) means rain. The word "awdiyah" (valleys) is indefinite because rain indicates a manner of alternation, so some valleys flow and others do not. The meaning of "bi-qadarihā" is: according to their size and their magnitude, or according to what was decreed for them of water, by reason of the benefit of the rain to those upon whom it falls, not their harm. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And as for that which benefits mankind﴾? So the rain is a parable for the truth, for it is beneficial and free of harm.

Al-Jumhur read (bi-qadarihā) with a fatha on the dal. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Abu 'Amr in one narration read it with a sukun. Al-Hawfi said: (bi-qadarihā) is connected to (sālat, flowed). Abu al-Baqa' said: (bi-qadarihā) is a complement (silah) to (awdiyah). He made (al-sayl, the torrent) definite because he meant by it what is understood from the verb, and what the verb includes of the verbal noun is indefinite; but when the apparent noun refers back to it, it becomes definite, just as it would be if it were stated explicitly as indefinite. For this reason, when what the verb indicates of the verbal noun is referred back to, it is included, as in: "Whoever denies (man kadhdhaba) it is worse for him," i.e., denial (al-kadhib) is worse for him. Had it come here as a pronoun, it would also be permissible, referring back to the verbal noun understood from (sālat). (Ihtamala) is in the sense of (hamala, to carry); there came in it the form (iftaʿala) in the sense of the unaugmented form, like (iqtadara) and (qadara).

(Rabiyan) means swelling, elevated over the surface of the torrent, and from it comes (rabwah, a hillock). "And from that which you heat (tūqidūna) upon it": i.e., from the things upon which you heat fire, which are gold, silver, iron, copper, lead, tin, and the like, of that which is heated and which has foam. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Ibn Muhaysin, Mujahid, Talhah, Yahya, and the people of Kufa read (yūqidūna) with the yā' in the third person, meaning "people heat." The rest of the seven, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, and Shaybah read it with the tā' in the second person (p-382), and (ʿalayhi) is connected to (tūqidūna), and (fī al-nār, in the fire) as well. Abu 'Ali and al-Hawfi said: it is connected to (tūqidūna). Abu 'Ali said: One may heat upon anything, and it need not be in the fire, as in His saying: ﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, upon the clay﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]; that construction which he was commanded to build is heated upon, yet it is not in the fire, but its flame reaches it. Makki and others said: (fī al-nār) is connected to an omitted element whose estimate is: existing or established. They prohibited connecting it to (tūqidūna), because they claimed that one does not heat upon something except that it is in the fire; and connecting the prepositional phrase to (tūqidūna) entails specifying one state from another state. End of quote. If we say that one does not heat upon something except that it is in the fire, it would be permissible for it to be connected to (tūqidūna), and that is permissible by way of emphasis, as they said regarding His saying: ﴿flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38].

(Ibtighā'a) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), and the conditions of the object of purpose are present in it. Al-Hawfi said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal), i.e., "seeking an ornament." Mentioning the complement of (ibtighā'a) is an indication of the benefit of what they heat upon. "Ḥilyah" means what is made for women, of what is adorned with, from gold and silver. "Matā'" means what is made of iron and copper and the like of tools which are the mainstay of life, such as vessels, shovels, implements of war, tree-cutters, plows, and other things.

(Zabad, foam) is nominative as the subject, and its predicate is in His saying (wa-mimmā tūqidūna). It is evident that the preposition (min) here is partitive, because that foam is a part of what is heated from those metals. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that (min) be for the starting point of the extent, i.e., from it arises foam like the foam of water; and the similarity lies in both being generated from filth and turbidity, and the truth and falsehood are in the sense of the omitted noun: like the truth and falsehood. He likened the truth to what is purified from the substance of these metals of dross and impurity and its continuing benefit, and likened falsehood to the foam and the scum gathered from the filth and dirt, which has no permanence and no value. He detailed what had been previously mentioned of what benefits and of the foam, beginning with the foam, since it is the one mentioned later in His saying: ﴿swelling foam﴾, and in His saying: ﴿foam like it﴾. Since falsehood is a metaphor for it, it has a later description, and this is an eloquent method: in division, one begins with what was mentioned last, as in His saying: ﴿On the day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black; as for those whose faces turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. Beginning with what came first is also eloquent, as in His saying: ﴿Among them is the wretched and the blessed﴾ [Hud: 105], ﴿as for those who are wretched, they are in the Fire﴾ [Hud: 106]. It seems—Allah knows best—that in the detailing he begins with what is more important to mention.

(Juffa'an) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal): i.e., dissolved and scattered, having no benefit in it and no permanence for it. The foam is meant to include what the torrent carried and what came out from the metals. He mentioned (zabad) in the singular and did not use the dual, even though two kinds of foam were previously mentioned, because they share the general quality of being foam, so they are one with respect to the common aspect. Ru'bah read (juffālan) with lām in place of the hamzah, from their saying: "jaffalat al-rih al-sahāb," when the wind carries the clouds and scatters them. From Abu Hatim: this reading of Ru'bah is not to be followed, because he used to eat mice—meaning he was a rustic, coarse Bedouin. Also from Abu Hatim: the readings of the Bedouins are not to be considered in the Qur'an.

﴿As for that which benefits mankind﴾: i.e., of the pure water, free of foam, and of the pure metallic substance, free of dross. That is, the likeness of that manner is like the truth and falsehood. ﴿Thus does Allah strike the parables.﴾

The apparent meaning is that, after He struck this parable for truth and falsehood, He moved on to what belongs to the people of truth in reward and to the people of falsehood in punishment, and said: ﴿For those who responded to their Lord is the best (reward)﴾, i.e., those whom Allah called through His Messenger ﷺ, and who answered by following His religion, will have the best state, which is victory in this world and what they were singled out with of Allah's blessing, and entry into Paradise in the Hereafter. So (al-ḥusnā, the best) is the subject, and its predicate is in (li-lladhīna, for those who). ﴿And those who did not respond﴾ is a subject whose predicate is what follows. He varied between the two initial clauses because of what the fronting of the prepositional phrase indicates of care and concern, and according to al-Zamakhshari's view, of exclusivity: i.e., the best is for these, not for others. Also because the recitation of our shaykhs is to stop at His saying (al-amthāl) and begin with (li-lladhīna).

Upon this understanding al-Hawfi parsed (al-ḥusnā) as the subject and (li-lladhīna) as its predicate. Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted it and the early scholars understood it likewise. Ibn 'Abbas said: the reward of the best (al-ḥusnā), which is "There is no god but Allah." Mujahid said: the good life is what is in goodness. It was said: Paradise, because it is the utmost of the best. It was said: the recompense multiplied many times over. Al-Zamakhshari connected (li-lladhīna) to His saying (yaḍrib, strikes), saying: ﴿For those who responded﴾ is connected to (yaḍrib), i.e., thus does Allah strike the parables for the believers who responded, and for the disbelievers who did not respond; i.e., these two are the likenesses of the two groups.

(Al-ḥusnā) is an attribute of the verbal noun of (istajābū), i.e., they responded with the best response. And their saying: ﴿Had they that...﴾ is a new sentence, mentioning what is prepared for those who do not respond. End of quote.

The first explanation is the better one, because it covers the striking of parables in general and is not restricted to these two examples. God has struck many parables in these two verses and elsewhere. Also, it mentions the reward of those who respond, unlike al-Zamakhshari's view. Just as it mentions the punishment for those who do not respond, it mentions the reward for those who do. Furthermore, his estimate of the phrase "the good response" implies that the response is restricted. Its opposite is not a total denial of response; its opposite is the denial of the good response. Yet God has denied response absolutely. Also, on his view, His saying ﴿Even if they had everything on earth, all of it⦈ becomes a statement detached from what precedes it, or almost detached, since the meaning becomes: thus God strikes the parables for the believers and the disbelievers, [saying] "even if they had everything on earth." If the construction had been connected by a particle linking "even if" (law) to what precedes it, the detachment would disappear. Moreover, it creates the appearance of shared reference in the pronoun, although restricting this to the disbelievers is known to them. Also, this construction has occurred before, and the explanation of similar wording has already been given, in His saying ﴿Even if they had everything on earth, and the like of it with it, they would ransom themselves with it⦈. As for ﴿the evil reckoning⦈, Ibn Abbas said: that their good deeds are not accepted and their evil deeds are not forgiven. Al-Nakha'i and Farqad said: that they are called to account for all their sins, and are called to account and held responsible for them without any of them being forgiven. Abu al-Jawza' said: it is al-munaqasha (close, detailed scrutiny). It was also said: it is a rebuke and reproach at the time of reckoning. The explanation of similar wording has already been given, in His saying ﴿Their refuge is Hell, and what an evil resting-place it is⦈.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verse 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their capacity, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from that which they heat in the fire, seeking ornament or goods, there is a foam like it. Thus does Allah strike the parables of truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it passes away as scum; but as for that which benefits mankind, it remains upon the earth. Thus does Allah strike the parables.﴾ ﴿For those who respond to their Lord is the best (reward). But those who do not respond to Him—if they had everything on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom. Those will have a terrible reckoning, and their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting-place.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is a parable that Allah struck for the truth and its people, and for falsehood and its party, just as He struck the parables of the blind and the seeing, and the darkness and the light, as parables for them both. So He likened the truth (p-381) and its people to the water that descends from the sky, whereby valleys flow for people, and they live by it and it benefits them in various kinds of benefit; and to the metal (filiz) from which they benefit in making ornaments and in fashioning vessels and various tools. Even if there were only iron, which has mighty strength, it would suffice. That (truth) remains upon the earth, enduring with a manifest endurance, as water persists in its benefits, and its traces remain in springs, wells, grains and fruits that grow by it, which are stored and multiply. Likewise, precious substances remain for lengthy periods. And He likened falsehood, in the swiftness of its dissolution, the imminence of its disappearance and its stripping away from benefit, to the foam of the torrent that is cast off, and to the foam of the metal that floats atop it when it is melted.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The beginning of this verse is a reminder of the power of Allah the Exalted and an establishment of proof against the disbelievers in Him. When the mention of that was complete, He made it an example of truth and falsehood, of faith and disbelief, and of doubt regarding the law and certainty in it. End of quote. It has also been said: This is a parable that Allah the Exalted struck for the Qur'an, the hearts, and truth and falsehood. So the water is like the Qur'an, because of what is in it of the life of hearts and the persistence of the Law (shar') and religion. The valleys are a parable for hearts, and the meaning of (according to their capacity) is according to the breadth and narrowness of hearts. Some of them are receptive to it, so they preserve it, retain it, and reflect upon it, and its fruit appears and they grasp its interpretation and meaning. Some are a level below that, and some are several levels below. The foam is like doubts, suspicions, and the denial of the disbelievers that it is the speech of Allah, and their repelling it with falsehood. The pure water that benefits is like the truth. End of quote.

There is a sound hadith that supports this interpretation, which is his ﷺ saying: "The likeness of that with which I have been sent of guidance and knowledge is like a rain that fell upon a land. A portion of it was good, which accepted the water and produced grass and abundant herbage. And there was a portion of it that was hard, which held the water, so people benefited from it: they drank, watered (their animals) and pastured. And there were portions of it that were barren flats which hold no water and produce no grass. That is the likeness of what I have brought of knowledge and guidance, and the likeness of one who does not accept the guidance of Allah with which I have been sent."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: His saying the Exalted, ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾, means by it the Law and religion; ﴿and the valleys flow﴾ means the hearts; i.e., the noble takes his share, and the dull takes his share. This is a statement that is not sound—Allah knows best—from Ibn 'Abbas, because it inclines toward the sayings of the people of symbols (rumuz), and al-Ghazali and the people of that path have relied upon it, and there is no justification for taking the word out of the understanding of Arabic speech without a reason that calls for it. And Allah is the one who grants success to what is right. Even if this saying is sound from Ibn 'Abbas, he intended only that His saying the Exalted, ﴿Thus does Allah strike the parables of truth and falsehood﴾, means: the truth that becomes settled in hearts, and the falsehood that likewise befalls them. End of quote.

The word "ma'" (water) means rain. The word "awdiyah" (valleys) is indefinite because rain indicates a manner of alternation, so some valleys flow and others do not. The meaning of "bi-qadarihā" is: according to their size and their magnitude, or according to what was decreed for them of water, by reason of the benefit of the rain to those upon whom it falls, not their harm. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And as for that which benefits mankind﴾? So the rain is a parable for the truth, for it is beneficial and free of harm.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verses 19–26 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Is one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only people of understanding are reminded.﴾ ﴿Those who fulfill the covenant of Allah and do not break the agreement.﴾ ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined, fear their Lord, and dread a terrible reckoning.﴾ ﴿And those who patiently seek the countenance of their Lord, establish the prayer, spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good; for them is the good outcome of the home.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence they will enter, along with whoever was righteous among their fathers, spouses, and offspring; and the angels will enter upon them from every gate.﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final home!"﴾ 

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Is one who knows﴾ was revealed concerning Hamza and Abu Jahl. It was also said: concerning ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Abu Jahl. And it was said: concerning ʿAmmar ibn Yasir and Abu Jahl.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read (ʾawa man) with a waw in place of the fa', and (unzila) in the active voice.

When Allah Most High mentioned the parable of the believer and the disbeliever, and mentioned the reward for the believer and the punishment for the disbeliever, He then expressed disapproval of those who consider the two equal, and denied this, saying: ﴿Is one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ That is: the two are not alike, because one who knows a thing sees it, while one who is ignorant of it is like the blind. The intended blindness is blindness of insight, and for this reason it is contrasted with knowledge. The hamza is an interrogative particle, meaning a denial that any confusion could arise after the parable has been given, since the state of one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth and responds to it is far removed from the state of the ignorant one who has not gained insight and therefore does not respond, like the distance between foam and water, or between dross and pure gold. Then He stated that only people of intellect are reminded by admonition and the striking of parables.

The fa' is conjunctive, and the interrogative hamza has been placed first because it begins the sentence; the implied construction is: "Then is one who knows...". What rules out that there is a verb omitted between the hamza and the fa', with the fa' coordinating what follows with that verb, is what al-Zamakhshari supposed in His saying ﴿Have they not traveled?﴾ [Yusuf: 109] and His saying ﴿Do they not then reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 68].

They permitted that (alladhina) be a substitute for (ulu, "people of") or an attribute of it, and an attribute of (man) in His saying ﴿Is one who knows...﴾. (Wa-innama yatadhakkaru, "only are reminded") is a parenthetical clause. The subject whose predicate is ﴿for them is the good outcome of the home﴾ is like His saying ﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah﴾, followed by ﴿for them is the curse﴾.

The apparent meaning is that "covenant" is general. It was also said that it is specific. As-Suddi said: it is what He covenanted with them in the Qur'an. Qatadah said: it refers to the first covenant, which is His saying ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 172]. Al-Qaffal said: it is what is within their reasoning and intellect of the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God) and prophethood. It was also said: it is in the earlier scriptures and the Qur'an. It was also said: it is what was taken through the tongues of the messengers. It was also said: it is faith in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day.

The apparent meaning is that "covenant" is attributed to the agent, that is: what Allah has covenanted. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿and do not break the agreement﴾ is an emphatic clause for His saying ﴿fulfill the covenant of Allah﴾, since the covenant is the agreement, and fulfilling the covenant necessarily entails the absence of its opposite.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The covenant of Allah is what they bound themselves to by testifying to His lordship. He made them bear witness against themselves: ‘Am I not your Lord?’ They said: ‘Yes.’ ﴿And do not break the agreement﴾: they do not break any pact they bound themselves to and accepted, of faith in Allah Most High, and other agreements between them and Allah Most High and between the servants." This is a generalization after a specification. He attributed the covenant to the object, and distinguished the two clauses by making the second a generalization after a specification, since the taking of the agreement is general among them, between them and Allah, and between the servants.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "The phrase ‘the covenant of Allah’ is a noun of genus, meaning all of Allah's covenants, including His commands and prohibitions which He enjoined upon His servants. Included in these expressions is the commitment to all obligations and the avoidance of all sins. His saying ﴿and do not break the agreement﴾ means: when they have made a covenant in obedience to Allah, they do not break it." Qatadah said: Allah's warning to His servants about breaking the agreement has preceded, and He forbade it in about twenty-some verses. It is possible that it refers to a specific agreement, namely the one that Allah Most High took from the back of their father Adam, peace be upon him.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "Among the greatest of covenants mentioned is that one should not ask anyone other than Him." He mentioned the story of Abu Hamza al-Khurasani and his falling into a well, and people passing by him and covering the well while he did not ask them to bring him out, until someone came and brought him out without being asked, and he did not see who brought him out, and a voice called out to him: "How did you find the fruit of trust in God?" Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "This is a man who made a covenant with Allah and found its fulfillment in full. So follow his example." Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi, however, denied this act of Abu Hamza and explained its error, and that reliance on God does not contradict seeking help in such a situation. He mentioned that Sufyan al-Thawri and others said: if a person became hungry and did not ask until he died, he would enter the Fire. It cannot be denied that Allah Most High may have shown kindness to Abu Hamza in his ignorance.

﴿That which Allah has commanded to be joined﴾: its apparent meaning is general to everything He has commanded in His Book and through the tongue of His Prophet. Al-Hasan said: what is meant is joining oneself to the Messenger ﷺ through faith in him. Ibn Jubayr said something similar. Qatadah said: it is the ties of kinship. It was also said: joining faith with action. It was also said: joining the bond of Islamic brotherhood through spreading the greeting of peace, visiting the sick, attending funerals, observing the rights of neighbors, companions, friends, and servants. It was also said: supporting the believers.

(Amara, "commanded") takes two objects with a preposition, which is (bihi, "with it"), and the first object is omitted, its implied form being: "what Allah commanded them with." ﴿That it be joined﴾ is in a position of genitive as a substitute for the pronoun, meaning: "with its joining."

﴿And fear their Lord﴾: that is, all His threats. ﴿And dread a terrible reckoning﴾: that is, scrutiny, so that they reckon with themselves before they are reckoned with. It was also said: ﴿they fear their Lord﴾ means they glorify Him. It was also said: concerning severing kinship. It was also said: concerning all sins. It was also said: concerning what He commanded them to join.

(Sabaru, "they patiently endured") is unrestricted, applying to what one must endure of afflictions in the self and in wealth, and of the covenant of obligation.

The relative clause here comes in the past tense, while in the earlier clauses describing those who join it came in the present tense, in His saying ﴿those who fulfill﴾ and ﴿those who join﴾, with (ma, "what") coordinated to them for the sake of stylistic variety in eloquence. The subject here carries the meaning of a conditional noun in the past tense, like the present tense in a conditional noun. For this reason the grammarians said: when a past-tense verb is a relative clause or an attribute of a general indefinite noun, it may be intended to refer to the past, or it may be intended to refer to the future. Among its uses referring to the past in a relative clause is ﴿those to whom the people said﴾ [Al ʿImran: 173], and among its uses referring to the future is ﴿except those who repent before you overpower them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 34].

It also appears that the restriction of this relative clause to the past tense and of those two clauses to the present tense is because those two clauses are meant to express continuity and constancy, whereas this clause is meant to express that it precedes those two clauses. (Ma, "what") is coordinated to them, because the occurrence of those relative clauses follows from the occurrence of patience and its precedence over them. For this reason no relative clause in the Qur'an comes except in the past tense, since it is a condition for the occurrence and fulfillment of obligations. And Allah knows best.

(Ibtigha'an, "seeking") is in the accusative. It was said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative. The better view is that it is an object of purpose, meaning: their patience is for the sake of seeking the face of Allah sincerely, not for the hope that people will say, "How patient he is!" nor out of fear of being blamed for complaining, or of the enemies rejoicing at them, as the poet said:

*And my endurance before the scorners, that I may show them*
*That I do not yield to the misfortunes of time.*

(Here the commentary continues in part 2.)

Because impatience (jaza') achieves nothing, or because he knows that there is no way to reverse what has passed or what has occurred. The apparent meaning of "the face" (al-wajh) here is the direction of God, that is, the direction intended with good deeds seeking His reward, as you say: "He went out for the sake of such-and-such."

He draws attention to these two qualities: bodily worship and financial worship, for they are the pillar of the religion. Patience in them is the greatest patience, because of the repetition of the prayers and because souls are attached to the love of acquiring wealth. He also draws attention to the two states of spending. Secret giving is the best state of voluntary charity, as came in the report about the seven whom God shelters in His shade on the day when there is no shade but His, including "a man who gave charity and concealed it." Open giving is the best state of obligatory charity, because making it public is better in that case.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿From what We have provided them﴾ means from what is lawful, because what is unlawful cannot be a provision and cannot be attributed to God," end of quote. This is the way of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school).

Regarding patience, the early generations (al-Salaf) have closely related statements. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They were patient in obeying God's command." Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: "They were patient in their religion." 'Ata' said: "They were patient in calamities and misfortunes." Ibn Zayd said: "They were patient in obedience and in refraining from disobedience."

(Yadra'una): they repel. Ibn Zayd said: they repel evil with good. Qatadah said: they returned kindness to them, as in His saying: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63]. Al-Hasan said: when they are deprived, they give; when they are wronged, they pardon; when they are cut off, they keep ties. Al-Qutabi said: when they are belittled, they show forbearance. Ibn Jubayr said: they repel wrongdoing with what is right. Ibn Kaysan said: when they sin, they repent, and when they flee, they turn back in repentance, so that they repel from themselves the harm of sin through repentance. This meaning is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of al-Dahhak from him. It was also said: they repel their polytheism by saying "There is no god but God." It was said: they repel the hostilities of people with peace. It was said: whoever they see doing something hateful to them, they respond with what is best. It was said: they repel an evil deed with a good deed. This is supported by what is reported in a hadith that Mu'adh said: "O Messenger of God, advise me." He said: "When you do an evil deed, follow it with a good deed that will erase it." Secret with secret, and open with open. It was said: the punishment is repelled by charity. It was said: when they intend an evil deed, they stop, turn back from it, and seek forgiveness. All these statements are figurative. In summary, they do not repay evil with evil, as the poet said:

They repay the injustice of the unjust with forgiveness,
and the offense of the offensive with kindness.

This is contrary to the character of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam), as he said:

Bold is the one who, when wronged, punishes with a wrong,
swiftly; and if he is not wronged first, he will wrong.

It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning the Ansar (the Medinan helpers), and then it became general for everyone who possesses these qualities. ﴿The final abode﴾ ('uqba al-dar) is the outcome of the worldly life, and it is Paradise, because it is the one that God intended to be the outcome of the world and the place of its people. ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is an apposition (badal) to ﴿the final abode﴾. It is also possible that what is meant is the final outcome of the abode of the Hereafter, as opposed to the abode of this world, for the good outcome in the Hereafter is theirs. It is also possible that "gardens" is the predicate of an omitted subject.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read "jannatu" (plural). Al-Nakha'i read "jannatu" in the singular. [p. 387] It is reported from Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr that "yudkhaluna" is in the passive voice. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿wa man salaha﴾ with a damma on the lam, while al-Jumhur read it with a fatha, which is more eloquent. 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "wa dhurriyyatihim" in the singular, while al-Jumhur read it in the plural. Ibn Ya'mar read "fa-ni'ma" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the 'ayn, which is the original form, as the rajiz (rajaz poet) said:

They were blessed, those who strive on the day of the Shutur.

Ibn Wththab read "fa-na'ma" with a fatha on the nun, a sukun on the 'ayn, and the mim lightened, a Tamimi dialect form. Al-Jumhur read "ni'ma" with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the 'ayn, which is more common in usage.

Mujahid and others said: ﴿whoever is righteous﴾ means: whoever does righteous deeds and believes. This indicates that mere lineage from the righteous does not benefit, only righteous deeds benefit. It was said: the phrase ﴿whoever is righteous﴾ may mean: by God's decree and His foreknowledge. Ibn 'Abbas said: this righteousness is faith in God and in the Messenger (ﷺ). This is good news of the blessing of their gathering together with their relatives in Paradise. The apparent reading is that "man" (whoever) is conjoined to the pronoun in "yadkhuluna" (they enter), and it has been separated from it by the object. It was said it may be an object "with" (maf'ul ma'ahu), meaning: they enter it along with whoever is righteous. The phrase ﴿from their fathers﴾ includes the father and mother of each one, and the males predominate over the females, so it is as if it were said: whoever is righteous among their fathers and their mothers.

﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾, meaning: with gifts and presents from God, honoring them. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: these are eight deeds pointing to the eight gates of Paradise, and whoever does them enters through whichever gate he wishes. Al-Asamm said something similar: "from every gate" means the gate of prayer, the gate of zakah, the gate of patience, and so on.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi has a strange discourse about the angels. He mentioned that the angels are groups; among them are spiritual beings and among them are cherubic beings. When the servant trains his soul with various disciplines, such as patience, gratitude, watchfulness, and self-accounting, then each of these stations has a sacred essence and a heavenly spirit that is preserved for that quality with greater specificity. At death, when those sacred essences shine, there is manifested in them from each heavenly spirit what suits them of the specific quality, so that from the angels of patience there flows upon them specific psychological perfections that appear only in the station of patience, and from the angels of gratitude spiritual perfections that are revealed only in the station of gratitude, and so on for all the stations, end of quote. This is a philosophical discourse that the Arabs do not understand, and the prophets did not bring it. It is a discourse to be rejected, to which the Muslims do not turn. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Tabari (may God have mercy on him) related, concerning the manner of the angels' entry, hadiths which we have not elaborated on because their chains are weak, end of quote.

﴿Peace be upon you﴾ (salamun) is in the nominative as the subject, and ('alaykum) is the predicate, and the clause is quoted with an omitted verb: "they say, 'Peace be upon you.'" The apparent meaning is that the words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ are the greeting of the angels to them. ﴿For what you patiently endured﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this reward is because of your patience in the world through hardships. Or the particle "bi" (with) means "in exchange for": in exchange for your patience, that is, in exchange for what you endured of the hardships of patience, these delights and blessings. It was said: "salam" is a plural of "salamah" (safety), meaning: God has saved you from the terrors of the Day of Resurrection because of your patience in the world. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible for it to be connected to "salam": that is, He greets you and honors you because of your patience. The object of praise is omitted, meaning: "How excellent is the final abode, the Garden, from Hell." The word "al-dar" (abode) may mean this world or the Hereafter. A group said: the meaning is that they have been given the Garden as a consequence after Hell. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this interpretation is based on a hadith which states that every man in Paradise had a known place in the Fire, but God diverted him from it to bliss, so it is shown to him and it is said to him: "This is the place of your seat; God has exchanged it for Paradise for you, because of your faith, obedience, and patience," end of quote. Since patience is what produced those prior acts of obedience, the angels mention that eternal bliss is attained only through patience. The construction did not come with "fulfillment of the covenant" or anything else.

﴿And those who break the covenant of God after its ratification and sever what God has commanded to be joined and cause corruption on the earth - those will have the curse, and they will have the evil abode﴾. ﴿God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts [it], and they rejoice in the worldly life, while the worldly life compared to the Hereafter is but a brief enjoyment﴾.

[p. 388] Muqatil said: ﴿And those who break﴾ was revealed concerning the People of the Book. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿God extends﴾ was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah. When God mentioned the state of the blessed and what was due to them of noble and honorable matters, He mentioned the state of the wretched and what was due to them of disgraceful matters. The explanation of ﴿Those who break the covenant of God after its ratification and sever what God has commanded to be joined﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27] was given earlier, at the beginning of al-Baqarah. There, for the blessed, was mentioned explicitly ﴿the final abode﴾, which is Paradise, and the honoring of them by the angels with peace, which is the utmost nearness and intimacy. Here, for the wretched, is due distance from God's mercy. ﴿The evil abode﴾ means the abode of evil, which is Hell, and "evil" qualifies the outcome of the abode, which may be this world.

Since many of the wretched were granted the blessings and pleasures of this world, God informed that He is the One who extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it, and disbelief and faith have no connection with provision. He may restrict provision for the believer so that his reward is magnified, and He may extend it to the disbeliever as a respite, so that his sins increase. ("Yaqdiru," restricts) is the opposite of ("yabsutu," extends), meaning constriction, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], and on this is understood ﴿And he thought that We would not decide against him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87], and the saying of that man who was burned and scattered into the sea: "If God restricts [His power] over me," meaning: if He constricts me. It was also said: "yaqdiru" means He gives according to what is sufficient. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa yaqdur" with a damma on the dal wherever it occurs.

The pronoun in ﴿they rejoice﴾ refers to ﴿Those who break﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27]. This is a resumed statement informing of their ignorance concerning the abundance of worldly provision bestowed upon them. Their rejoicing is the rejoicing of arrogance and expansion, not the joy of happiness at God's grace and bounty upon them, and they did not respond to it with gratitude, so as to deserve the bliss of the Hereafter through God's grace. He deems them ignorant through this rejoicing, since it is joy in what will soon pass away and end. The view that it is conjoined to the relative clauses is far-fetched.

﴿And those who break﴾, meaning: they cause corruption on the earth.

﴿And they rejoice in the worldly life.﴾ There is inversion and reordering in the speech. ("Mata'" enjoyment) means something going away and perishing, which one enjoys briefly and then it vanishes, as the poet said:

Enjoy yourself, O disheveled one, for a thing
you have passed beyond death is the only enjoyment.

Another said:

You would be a fine enjoyment if you could remain,
but there is no remaining for a human being.

Another said:

Enjoy the world, for you are perishing,
of intoxications and beautiful women.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it was hidden from them that the bliss of this world, in comparison with the bliss of the Hereafter, is nothing but a meager thing, enjoyed like the provision of a traveler, which is what he takes quickly of dates, or a sip of gruel, or something else, end of quote. This is the meaning of the statement of al-Hasan: God informed His Prophet that the worldly life, compared to what God has prepared for His friends in the Hereafter, is a meager provision, not enjoyed except like the quick provision of a traveler, which is what he takes of dates, or a sip of gruel, or something else. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is provision like the provision of a herder. Mujahid said: it is a little that goes away, of the enjoyments of the day when it rises, so it must inevitably pass away.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verses 19–26 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Is one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only people of understanding are reminded.﴾ ﴿Those who fulfill the covenant of Allah and do not break the agreement.﴾ ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined, fear their Lord, and dread a terrible reckoning.﴾ ﴿And those who patiently seek the countenance of their Lord, establish the prayer, spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good; for them is the good outcome of the home.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence they will enter, along with whoever was righteous among their fathers, spouses, and offspring; and the angels will enter upon them from every gate.﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final home!"﴾ 

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Is one who knows﴾ was revealed concerning Hamza and Abu Jahl. It was also said: concerning ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Abu Jahl. And it was said: concerning ʿAmmar ibn Yasir and Abu Jahl.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read (ʾawa man) with a waw in place of the fa', and (unzila) in the active voice.

When Allah Most High mentioned the parable of the believer and the disbeliever, and mentioned the reward for the believer and the punishment for the disbeliever, He then expressed disapproval of those who consider the two equal, and denied this, saying: ﴿Is one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ That is: the two are not alike, because one who knows a thing sees it, while one who is ignorant of it is like the blind. The intended blindness is blindness of insight, and for this reason it is contrasted with knowledge. The hamza is an interrogative particle, meaning a denial that any confusion could arise after the parable has been given, since the state of one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth and responds to it is far removed from the state of the ignorant one who has not gained insight and therefore does not respond, like the distance between foam and water, or between dross and pure gold. Then He stated that only people of intellect are reminded by admonition and the striking of parables.

The fa' is conjunctive, and the interrogative hamza has been placed first because it begins the sentence; the implied construction is: "Then is one who knows...". What rules out that there is a verb omitted between the hamza and the fa', with the fa' coordinating what follows with that verb, is what al-Zamakhshari supposed in His saying ﴿Have they not traveled?﴾ [Yusuf: 109] and His saying ﴿Do they not then reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 68].

They permitted that (alladhina) be a substitute for (ulu, "people of") or an attribute of it, and an attribute of (man) in His saying ﴿Is one who knows...﴾. (Wa-innama yatadhakkaru, "only are reminded") is a parenthetical clause. The subject whose predicate is ﴿for them is the good outcome of the home﴾ is like His saying ﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah﴾, followed by ﴿for them is the curse﴾.

The apparent meaning is that "covenant" is general. It was also said that it is specific. As-Suddi said: it is what He covenanted with them in the Qur'an. Qatadah said: it refers to the first covenant, which is His saying ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 172]. Al-Qaffal said: it is what is within their reasoning and intellect of the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God) and prophethood. It was also said: it is in the earlier scriptures and the Qur'an. It was also said: it is what was taken through the tongues of the messengers. It was also said: it is faith in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day.

The apparent meaning is that "covenant" is attributed to the agent, that is: what Allah has covenanted. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿and do not break the agreement﴾ is an emphatic clause for His saying ﴿fulfill the covenant of Allah﴾, since the covenant is the agreement, and fulfilling the covenant necessarily entails the absence of its opposite.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The covenant of Allah is what they bound themselves to by testifying to His lordship. He made them bear witness against themselves: ‘Am I not your Lord?’ They said: ‘Yes.’ ﴿And do not break the agreement﴾: they do not break any pact they bound themselves to and accepted, of faith in Allah Most High, and other agreements between them and Allah Most High and between the servants." This is a generalization after a specification. He attributed the covenant to the object, and distinguished the two clauses by making the second a generalization after a specification, since the taking of the agreement is general among them, between them and Allah, and between the servants.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "The phrase ‘the covenant of Allah’ is a noun of genus, meaning all of Allah's covenants, including His commands and prohibitions which He enjoined upon His servants. Included in these expressions is the commitment to all obligations and the avoidance of all sins. His saying ﴿and do not break the agreement﴾ means: when they have made a covenant in obedience to Allah, they do not break it." Qatadah said: Allah's warning to His servants about breaking the agreement has preceded, and He forbade it in about twenty-some verses. It is possible that it refers to a specific agreement, namely the one that Allah Most High took from the back of their father Adam, peace be upon him.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "Among the greatest of covenants mentioned is that one should not ask anyone other than Him." He mentioned the story of Abu Hamza al-Khurasani and his falling into a well, and people passing by him and covering the well while he did not ask them to bring him out, until someone came and brought him out without being asked, and he did not see who brought him out, and a voice called out to him: "How did you find the fruit of trust in God?" Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "This is a man who made a covenant with Allah and found its fulfillment in full. So follow his example." Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi, however, denied this act of Abu Hamza and explained its error, and that reliance on God does not contradict seeking help in such a situation. He mentioned that Sufyan al-Thawri and others said: if a person became hungry and did not ask until he died, he would enter the Fire. It cannot be denied that Allah Most High may have shown kindness to Abu Hamza in his ignorance.
