The disbelievers (*al-kuffar*) is general to all disbelievers, and this matter continues among them until the Day of Resurrection, as al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sa'ib said, or it is the apparent wording. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the disbelievers of Quraysh; and the Arabs will not cease to be struck by calamities from the expeditions (*saraya*) and campaigns (*ghazawat*) of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Muqatil and al-Zamakhshari said: the disbelievers of Makkah. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿a calamity will strike them for what they have done﴾, for their disbelief and evil deeds, a calamity, a disaster that strikes them with what God causes to descend upon them at every time of the various afflictions and disasters in their own persons, their children and their wealth; or ﴿it will alight close to their dwellings﴾, so they will be frightened and disturbed, and its sparks will fly toward them, and its evils will reach them, until ﴿the promise of God comes﴾, which is their death or the Resurrection. End of quote.

Al-Hasan said: the state of the disbelievers is always thus, and God promised the establishment of the Hour. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *tahullu* ("alights") refers to *qari'a* (calamity). This is what al-Hasan said. A group said: the *ta'* is for address, and the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ); or "you (O Muhammad) alight close to their dwellings with your army," as he alighted at al-Hudaybiyyah. Al-Tabari attributed this to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah, and 'Ikrimah said it. The "promise of God" would then be the conquest of Makkah, which God had promised him, and this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr read *aw yahullu* with *ya'* in the third person. It is possible that it refers to the meaning of *qari'a*, taking the masculine into account because it means "affliction"; or the *ha'* in *qari'a* is for emphasis, so it is masculine. It is also possible that it refers to the Messenger (ﷺ); that is, "the Messenger alights close." Mujahid also read *min diyarihim* in the plural. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-qari'a* is punishment from heaven. 'Ikrimah said: the expeditions and the advance guards.

In His saying ﴿And messengers were certainly mocked﴾ and so on, there is consolation for the Messenger, upon whom be prayer and peace, that your situation is the situation of those Messengers who came before you, and that those who mock are given respite, that is, they are granted time and then seized. It is also a warning that the state of whoever mocks you, though he is given respite, is like the state of those (earlier mockers) in their being seized, and it is a threat to them. In His saying ﴿So how was My punishment?﴾, it is an interrogative whose meaning is amazement at what befell them, and within it is a threat to the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿أفَمَن هو قائِمٌ عَلى كُلِّ نَفْسٍ بِما كَسَبَتْ وجَعَلُوا لِلَّهِ شُرَكاءَ قُلْ سَمُّوهم أمْ تُنَبِّئُونَهُ بِما لا يَعْلَمُ في الأرْضِ أمْ بِظاهِرٍ مِنَ القَوْلِ بَلْ زُيِّنَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مَكْرُهم وصُدُّوا عَنِ السَّبِيلِ ومَن يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَما لَهُ مِن هادٍ﴾ ﴿لَهم عَذابٌ في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا ولَعَذابُ الآخِرَةِ أشَقُّ وما لَهم مِنَ اللَّهِ مِن واقٍ﴾

(p-394) "Man" (مَن) is a relative pronoun whose clause is what follows it, and it is the subject (mubtada'), while the predicate is omitted. Its estimated form is: "like one who despairs in this way of their partners, which neither harm nor benefit," just as it is omitted in His saying: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 22], whose estimated form is: "like one whose heart is hard, who is in darkness." What indicates it is His saying: ﴿and they have set up partners for Allah﴾, just as what indicates the hard-hearted one is ﴿so woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾ [al-Zumar: 22]. The omission of this predicate is made fitting by the fact that the subject has as its counterpart the omitted predicate, and it has come explicitly many times, such as His saying: ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], ﴿Is one who knows...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19], then He said: ﴿like one who is blind?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19]. The apparent view is that His saying ﴿and they have set up partners for Allah﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) informing about their evil conduct and that they associated with Allah what is not fit for divinity. He censured them for this ugly act. Yet the Bari' (the Creator), exalted is He, is the One who encompasses the states of souls, the manifest and the hidden. He drew attention to one of their states, which is acquisition (kasb), so that man may reflect on what he acquires of good and evil, and what follows from that acquisition in recompense. He expressed by "qa'im" (standing over) the encompassing and watchfulness from which He is never heedless.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible to estimate what occurs as the predicate of the subject and to connect it by conjunction. ﴿and they have set up for Allah﴾, that is: "and they have set up"; and its illustration: ﴿Is one who is He﴾ with this attribute (they did not affirm His unity and set up partners for Him), while He is Allah, who alone deserves worship, end of quotation. In this reading there is the placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun in His saying ﴿for Allah﴾, meaning "for Him," and in it is the omission of the predicate in correspondence, and most of what has come with this predicate is as a counterpart.

In the tafsir of Abu Abd Allah al-Razi, he said: The stern companion of the covenant: the waw in His saying "and they have set up" (wa ja'alu) is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the estimated form is: "Is one who is standing over every soul for what it has earned existent?" while the situation is that they have set up partners for Him. Then the apparent noun, "for Allah," was placed in the position of the pronoun, estimating His divinity and declaring it explicitly, just as you say: "The giver to people and their enricher exists, and someone like me is deprived?" End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyya said: "Is one who is standing over every soul for what it has earned more deserving of worship, or lifeless things which neither harm nor benefit?" This is an interpretation. It appears that the statement is linked to His saying "and they have set up partners for Allah," as if the meaning were: "Is one who possesses power and oneness, and to whom a partner is set up, would He take vengeance and punish or not?" He is far removed who went to the view that His saying "Is one who is standing" means the angels appointed over the children of Adam; al-Qurtubi related this from al-Dahhak. The predicate is also omitted, its estimated form being "like others among the created beings." He is also far removed who went to the view that His saying "and they have set up" is conjoined to "was mocked" (istuhzi'a), meaning: "they mocked and they set up," then He commanded him to say to them: "Name them" (sammuhum), meaning mention them by their names, and the meaning is that they are not of those who are mentioned and named; only one who benefits and harms is mentioned and named. This is like someone who mentions to you that a person is honored and magnified, while in your view he does not deserve that, so you say to the one who mentions him: "Name him so that I may show you his falsity and that he is not as you mention." Close to this is the view of one who said regarding His saying "Name them": this is said only of a thing so despised that it is not mentioned and no name is given to it; then it is said to it: "Name it if you wish," that is, it is too lowly to be mentioned and named. But if you wish to give it a name, do so. It is as if He said: "Name them as gods," by way of threat. The meaning is: whether you name them with this name or do not name them, they are so base that the intellect should not turn to them. It was said: "Name them" when they made and caused death and life, so that the partnership would be valid. It was said: "Demand of them proof that they are gods." It was said: "Describe them and look whether they deserve divinity." Al-Zamakhshari said: You set up partners for Him, so name them for Him: who are they, and make them clear by their names? It was said: this is a threat, as you say to one whom you threaten over drinking wine: "Name the wine after this!"

The "am" (أم) in His saying "or do you inform Him" is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and it is an interrogation of rebuke. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Rather, do you inform Him of partners whom He does not know (p-395) on the earth, while He is the Knower of what is in the heavens and the earth? So when He does not know them, it is known that they are not anything that knowledge could relate to. The intent is the negation that He has partners, and similar to it is: ﴿Say: Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or in the earth?﴾ [Yunus: 18]," end of quotation. So the subject in His saying "of what He does not know" is made to refer to Allah, and the returning pronoun to "what" (ma) is omitted, meaning "of what Allah does not know." We had already construed that verse with the subject in "of what He does not know" referring to "what" (ma), and we established that there; it is established here too, meaning: "Do you inform Allah of the partnership of idols which do not possess any knowledge at all?" He mentioned the negation of knowledge "on the earth," since the earth is the abode of those idols, so if their knowledge is negated in the place where they are, its negation in the heavens is all the more fitting. Al-Hasan read: "tunbi'unahu" from "anba'a." It was said: the intent is "you suppose you can inform Him of a matter you know and He does not know it." He specified the earth for the negation of a partner because it was not that He had any partner at all, since they claimed that Allah has a partner on the earth, not elsewhere.

The apparent view regarding "am" in His saying "or with an apparent word" is that it is also disjunctive, meaning: "Rather, do you name them partners with an apparent word, without there being any reality to it?" That is, you utter those names and call them gods, and there is no reality to them, since you do not know that they possess none of the attributes of divinity, like His saying: ﴿You worship besides Him only names which you have named﴾ [Yusuf: 40]. Mujahid said: "or with an apparent word" means so. Qatada said: "with a false word, having no inner reality." From this is the saying of the poet:

"You taunt us for their milk and their flesh, and that is a clear shame, O son of Rayta."

That is, false. It was said: "am" is conjunctive, and the estimate is: "or do you inform Him with an apparent word having no reality," like His saying: ﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30]. Then after this argument, He said, in a manner of belittling what they are upon: ﴿Rather, their scheme has been made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾.

Al-Wahidi said: When He mentioned the proofs of the corruption of their saying, He said: "Leave that proof, for they do not benefit from it, because their scheme has been made attractive to them." Mujahid read: "Bal zayyana" (with the active verb) and "makrahum" (with the accusative). The majority read "zuyyina" (passive) with "makruhum" (nominative), meaning: their plotting against Islam through their polytheism, and what they intended by their sayings and actions of contradicting the Sharia. The Kufans read "wa-suddu" here and in (Ghafir) with a dammah on the sad, passive, so the verb is transitive. The rest of the seven read it with a fathah, which allows both transitive and intransitive senses: they turned themselves away or turned others away. Ibn Wathhab read "wa-siddu" with a kasrah on the sad, like the reading of ﴿it has been returned to us﴾ [Yusuf: 65] with a kasrah on the ra'. In al-Lawami' (it is said): al-Kisa'i (read) for Ibn Ya'mar "wa-siddu" with kasrah as a dialect form, and with the dammah he applied it with the preposition like "qablu"; as for in (al-Mu'min) it is with kasrah for Ibn Wathhab, end of quotation. Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wa-saddun" with tanwin, conjoined to "makruhum." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray﴾, whoever He forsakes, you know that he will not be guided. ﴿So he has no guide﴾: so he has no one who is able to guide him, end of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (I'tizal, the rationalist school).

The punishment in this world is what befalls them because of their disbelief: killing, captivity, plunder, humiliation, wars, and afflictions upon their bodies, and other things by which the disbelievers are tested. The punishment of the Hereafter is more severe upon souls, since it is burning with fire forever: ﴿Every time their skins are burned through, We replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa': 56]. (And there is no protector against Allah for them) "min waqin": from one who shields them from the punishment and protects them. When He mentioned what is prepared for the disbelievers in the Hereafter, He mentioned what is prepared for the believers, saying:

﴿The likeness of the Garden which the righteous have been promised: beneath it rivers flow; its food is perpetual and its shade. That is the end of those who have been righteous, and the end of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾

﴿The likeness of the Garden﴾: that is, its description, which is in the strangeness of a parable. "Mathal" (likeness) is in the nominative as the subject (ibtida') in the school of Sibawayh, and its predicate is omitted, meaning: in what We have related to you is the likeness of the Garden. And ﴿beneath it rivers flow﴾ is an explanation of that likeness. You say: "I likened the thing" when you described it and brought it near to understanding, and there is no striking of a parable here for it, so it is like His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾ [al-Rum: 27], meaning the highest attribute. Abu Ali denied that "mathal" could mean attribute, saying: its meaning is only alerting (tanbih). Al-Farra' said: that is, its attribute is that rivers flow beneath it, and similar to this exists in Arabic speech, end of quotation. It is not possible to omit "annaha" (that), and he only explained the meaning without mentioning the grammatical analysis (i'rab). Some people interpreted the Qur'an as having an inserted "mathal," and that the estimate is: "the Garden which the righteous have been promised flows," but inserting nouns is not permissible. They related from al-Farra' that the Arabs insert "mathal" and "mithl" frequently, and he took His saying ﴿There is nothing like His likeness﴾ [al-Shura: 11] as meaning "as He is, there is nothing." Others said the predicate is "flows," as you say: "the attribute of Zayd is dark-complexioned." This also cannot be correct, since "flows" cannot be a predicate of the attribute; rather "flows" is interpreted as dropping "an" (that) and raising the verb, and the estimate is: "that flows" (an tajri), with a second predicate: "the rivers." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: the likeness of the Garden is a Garden that flows, by omitting the qualified noun, as a representation of what is absent from us by what we witness, end of quotation.

Abu Ali said: what al-Zajjaj said is not correct, neither in the sense of attribute nor in the sense of resemblance, because the Garden he estimated is a Garden, and it cannot be the attribute; and because resemblance is an expression of the likeness that exists between two like things, and it is an event, whereas the Garden is a Garden, so there is no likeness. Ali and Ibn Mas'ud read: "mithal al-Jannah" in the plural, meaning its attributes. In al-Lawami', on the authority of al-Sulami: "amthal al-Jannah" is a plural whose meaning is the attributes of the Garden; that is because they are differing attributes, so it is put in the plural, like "al-hulqum" and "al-is'al." "Its food" (al-ukul) is what is eaten in it, and its perpetuity means that it never ceases, as He said: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 33]. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: that is, its pleasures are lasting; they are not increased by hunger nor wearied by satiety. "Its shade" means: lasting in continuance and comfort, not dispersed by the sun, nor inclined by cold as in this world. That is, that Garden is the end of those who have been righteous, that is, those who avoided polytheism.

﴿The likeness of the Garden which the righteous have been promised: beneath it rivers flow; its food is perpetual and its shade. That is the end of those who have been righteous, and the end of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾

﴿The likeness of the Garden﴾: that is, its description, which is in the strangeness of a parable. "Mathal" (likeness) is in the nominative as the subject (ibtida') in the school of Sibawayh, and its predicate is omitted, meaning: in what We have related to you is the likeness of the Garden. And ﴿beneath it rivers flow﴾ is an explanation of that likeness. You say: "I likened the thing" when you described it and brought it near to understanding, and there is no striking of a parable here for it, so it is like His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾ [al-Rum: 27], meaning the highest attribute. Abu Ali denied that "mathal" could mean attribute, saying: its meaning is only alerting (tanbih). Al-Farra' said: that is, its attribute is that rivers flow beneath it, and similar to this exists in Arabic speech, end of quotation. It is not possible to omit "annaha" (that), and he only explained the meaning without mentioning the grammatical analysis (i'rab). Some people interpreted the Qur'an as having an inserted "mathal," and that the estimate is: "the Garden which the righteous have been promised flows," but inserting nouns is not permissible. They related from al-Farra' that the Arabs insert "mathal" and "mithl" frequently, and he took His saying ﴿There is nothing like His likeness﴾ [al-Shura: 11] as meaning "as He is, there is nothing." Others said the predicate is "flows," as you say: "the attribute of Zayd is dark-complexioned." This also cannot be correct, since "flows" cannot be a predicate of the attribute; rather "flows" is interpreted as dropping "an" (that) and raising the verb, and the estimate is: "that flows" (an tajri), with a second predicate: "the rivers." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: the likeness of the Garden is a Garden that flows, by omitting the qualified noun, as a representation of what is absent from us by what we witness, end of quotation.

Abu Ali said: what al-Zajjaj said is not correct, neither in the sense of attribute nor in the sense of resemblance, because the Garden he estimated is a Garden, and it cannot be the attribute; and because resemblance is an expression of the likeness that exists between two like things, and it is an event, whereas the Garden is a Garden, so there is no likeness. Ali and Ibn Mas'ud read: "mithal al-Jannah" in the plural, meaning its attributes. In al-Lawami', on the authority of al-Sulami: "amthal al-Jannah" is a plural whose meaning is the attributes of the Garden; that is because they are differing attributes, so it is put in the plural, like "al-hulqum" and "al-is'al." "Its food" (al-ukul) is what is eaten in it, and its perpetuity means that it never ceases, as He said: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 33]. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: that is, its pleasures are lasting; they are not increased by hunger nor wearied by satiety. "Its shade" means: lasting in continuance and comfort, not dispersed by the sun, nor inclined by cold as in this world. That is, that Garden is the end of those who have been righteous, that is, those who avoided polytheism.

﴿أفَمَن هو قائِمٌ عَلى كُلِّ نَفْسٍ بِما كَسَبَتْ وجَعَلُوا لِلَّهِ شُرَكاءَ قُلْ سَمُّوهم أمْ تُنَبِّئُونَهُ بِما لا يَعْلَمُ في الأرْضِ أمْ بِظاهِرٍ مِنَ القَوْلِ بَلْ زُيِّنَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مَكْرُهم وصُدُّوا عَنِ السَّبِيلِ ومَن يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَما لَهُ مِن هادٍ﴾ ﴿لَهم عَذابٌ في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا ولَعَذابُ الآخِرَةِ أشَقُّ وما لَهم مِنَ اللَّهِ مِن واقٍ﴾

(p-394) "Man" (مَن) is a relative pronoun whose clause is what follows it, and it is the subject (mubtada'), while the predicate is omitted. Its estimated form is: "like one who despairs in this way of their partners, which neither harm nor benefit," just as it is omitted in His saying: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 22], whose estimated form is: "like one whose heart is hard, who is in darkness." What indicates it is His saying: ﴿and they have set up partners for Allah﴾, just as what indicates the hard-hearted one is ﴿so woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾ [al-Zumar: 22]. The omission of this predicate is made fitting by the fact that the subject has as its counterpart the omitted predicate, and it has come explicitly many times, such as His saying: ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], ﴿Is one who knows...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19], then He said: ﴿like one who is blind?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19]. The apparent view is that His saying ﴿and they have set up partners for Allah﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) informing about their evil conduct and that they associated with Allah what is not fit for divinity. He censured them for this ugly act. Yet the Bari' (the Creator), exalted is He, is the One who encompasses the states of souls, the manifest and the hidden. He drew attention to one of their states, which is acquisition (kasb), so that man may reflect on what he acquires of good and evil, and what follows from that acquisition in recompense. He expressed by "qa'im" (standing over) the encompassing and watchfulness from which He is never heedless.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible to estimate what occurs as the predicate of the subject and to connect it by conjunction. ﴿and they have set up for Allah﴾, that is: "and they have set up"; and its illustration: ﴿Is one who is He﴾ with this attribute (they did not affirm His unity and set up partners for Him), while He is Allah, who alone deserves worship, end of quotation. In this reading there is the placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun in His saying ﴿for Allah﴾, meaning "for Him," and in it is the omission of the predicate in correspondence, and most of what has come with this predicate is as a counterpart.

In the tafsir of Abu Abd Allah al-Razi, he said: The stern companion of the covenant: the waw in His saying "and they have set up" (wa ja'alu) is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the estimated form is: "Is one who is standing over every soul for what it has earned existent?" while the situation is that they have set up partners for Him. Then the apparent noun, "for Allah," was placed in the position of the pronoun, estimating His divinity and declaring it explicitly, just as you say: "The giver to people and their enricher exists, and someone like me is deprived?" End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyya said: "Is one who is standing over every soul for what it has earned more deserving of worship, or lifeless things which neither harm nor benefit?" This is an interpretation. It appears that the statement is linked to His saying "and they have set up partners for Allah," as if the meaning were: "Is one who possesses power and oneness, and to whom a partner is set up, would He take vengeance and punish or not?" He is far removed who went to the view that His saying "Is one who is standing" means the angels appointed over the children of Adam; al-Qurtubi related this from al-Dahhak. The predicate is also omitted, its estimated form being "like others among the created beings." He is also far removed who went to the view that His saying "and they have set up" is conjoined to "was mocked" (istuhzi'a), meaning: "they mocked and they set up," then He commanded him to say to them: "Name them" (sammuhum), meaning mention them by their names, and the meaning is that they are not of those who are mentioned and named; only one who benefits and harms is mentioned and named. This is like someone who mentions to you that a person is honored and magnified, while in your view he does not deserve that, so you say to the one who mentions him: "Name him so that I may show you his falsity and that he is not as you mention." Close to this is the view of one who said regarding His saying "Name them": this is said only of a thing so despised that it is not mentioned and no name is given to it; then it is said to it: "Name it if you wish," that is, it is too lowly to be mentioned and named. But if you wish to give it a name, do so. It is as if He said: "Name them as gods," by way of threat. The meaning is: whether you name them with this name or do not name them, they are so base that the intellect should not turn to them. It was said: "Name them" when they made and caused death and life, so that the partnership would be valid. It was said: "Demand of them proof that they are gods." It was said: "Describe them and look whether they deserve divinity." Al-Zamakhshari said: You set up partners for Him, so name them for Him: who are they, and make them clear by their names? It was said: this is a threat, as you say to one whom you threaten over drinking wine: "Name the wine after this!"

The "am" (أم) in His saying "or do you inform Him" is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and it is an interrogation of rebuke. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Rather, do you inform Him of partners whom He does not know (p-395) on the earth, while He is the Knower of what is in the heavens and the earth? So when He does not know them, it is known that they are not anything that knowledge could relate to. The intent is the negation that He has partners, and similar to it is: ﴿Say: Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or in the earth?﴾ [Yunus: 18]," end of quotation. So the subject in His saying "of what He does not know" is made to refer to Allah, and the returning pronoun to "what" (ma) is omitted, meaning "of what Allah does not know." We had already construed that verse with the subject in "of what He does not know" referring to "what" (ma), and we established that there; it is established here too, meaning: "Do you inform Allah of the partnership of idols which do not possess any knowledge at all?" He mentioned the negation of knowledge "on the earth," since the earth is the abode of those idols, so if their knowledge is negated in the place where they are, its negation in the heavens is all the more fitting. Al-Hasan read: "tunbi'unahu" from "anba'a." It was said: the intent is "you suppose you can inform Him of a matter you know and He does not know it." He specified the earth for the negation of a partner because it was not that He had any partner at all, since they claimed that Allah has a partner on the earth, not elsewhere.

The apparent view regarding "am" in His saying "or with an apparent word" is that it is also disjunctive, meaning: "Rather, do you name them partners with an apparent word, without there being any reality to it?" That is, you utter those names and call them gods, and there is no reality to them, since you do not know that they possess none of the attributes of divinity, like His saying: ﴿You worship besides Him only names which you have named﴾ [Yusuf: 40]. Mujahid said: "or with an apparent word" means so. Qatada said: "with a false word, having no inner reality." From this is the saying of the poet:

"You taunt us for their milk and their flesh, and that is a clear shame, O son of Rayta."

That is, false. It was said: "am" is conjunctive, and the estimate is: "or do you inform Him with an apparent word having no reality," like His saying: ﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30]. Then after this argument, He said, in a manner of belittling what they are upon: ﴿Rather, their scheme has been made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾.

Al-Wahidi said: When He mentioned the proofs of the corruption of their saying, He said: "Leave that proof, for they do not benefit from it, because their scheme has been made attractive to them." Mujahid read: "Bal zayyana" (with the active verb) and "makrahum" (with the accusative). The majority read "zuyyina" (passive) with "makruhum" (nominative), meaning: their plotting against Islam through their polytheism, and what they intended by their sayings and actions of contradicting the Sharia. The Kufans read "wa-suddu" here and in (Ghafir) with a dammah on the sad, passive, so the verb is transitive. The rest of the seven read it with a fathah, which allows both transitive and intransitive senses: they turned themselves away or turned others away. Ibn Wathhab read "wa-siddu" with a kasrah on the sad, like the reading of ﴿it has been returned to us﴾ [Yusuf: 65] with a kasrah on the ra'. In al-Lawami' (it is said): al-Kisa'i (read) for Ibn Ya'mar "wa-siddu" with kasrah as a dialect form, and with the dammah he applied it with the preposition like "qablu"; as for in (al-Mu'min) it is with kasrah for Ibn Wathhab, end of quotation. Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wa-saddun" with tanwin, conjoined to "makruhum." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray﴾, whoever He forsakes, you know that he will not be guided. ﴿So he has no guide﴾: so he has no one who is able to guide him, end of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (I'tizal, the rationalist school).

The punishment in this world is what befalls them because of their disbelief: killing, captivity, plunder, humiliation, wars, and afflictions upon their bodies, and other things by which the disbelievers are tested. The punishment of the Hereafter is more severe upon souls, since it is burning with fire forever: ﴿Every time their skins are burned through, We replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa': 56]. (And there is no protector against Allah for them) "min waqin": from one who shields them from the punishment and protects them. When He mentioned what is prepared for the disbelievers in the Hereafter, He mentioned what is prepared for the believers, saying:

﴿The likeness of the Garden which the righteous have been promised: beneath it rivers flow; its food is perpetual and its shade. That is the end of those who have been righteous, and the end of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾

The verses (36–37) of Surah al-Ra'd are cited in the commentary's opening, but the translation below follows the passage as it stands:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book rejoice at what has been sent down to you, and among the factions are those who deny part of it. Say: "I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not to associate anything with Him. To Him I call, and to Him is my return."﴾ ﴿And thus We sent it down as an Arabic judgment. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have no protector or defender against Allah.﴾

It was revealed concerning the believers among the People of the Book. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi, and al-Zamakhshari (a grammarian and exegete) preferred it, saying: "Those among the Jews who embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Ka'b, and their companions, and those among the Christians who embraced Islam, who were eighty men: forty from Najran, eight from Yemen, and thirty-two from Abyssinia (al-Habasha)."

﴿And among the factions﴾ means: and among their factions, namely their disbelievers, who united against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in enmity, such as Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and al-Sayyid and al-'Aqib, the two bishops (usquffayn) of Najran, and their partisans.

﴿who deny part of it﴾ because they did not deny the narratives, some of the rulings, and the meanings that are established in their books without alteration. However, they denied what described Islam and the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which they had distorted and altered. End of quotation. And from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd: it was revealed concerning the believing Jews, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. And from Qatadah: it was revealed concerning the companions of the Messenger (ﷺ), whom Allah praised for rejoicing at what was sent down to you of the matter of religion. And from Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Qatadah: the intended meaning of the People of the Book is all of them, who rejoice at what has been sent down of the Qur'an, since in it is confirmation of their books and praise of their prophets and of their rabbis and monks, who were upon the religion of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both. This view is weak, on the grounds that their concern with it is greater than their joy, so their joy is not counted. Also, the Jews and Christians deny part of it, and Allah has set a contrast between those who deny part of it and those to whom We gave the Book.

As for "the factions," Mujahid said: they are the Jews, the Christians, and the Magians. Another group said: they are the factions of the Arabs of the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance). Muqatil said: the factions are the Banu Umayyah, the Banu al-Mughirah, and the family of Abu Talhah.

Since what was sent down to him includes the worship of Allah and the negation of partners, he was commanded to respond to those who deny it, and it was said to him: ﴿Say: "I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not to associate anything with Him."﴾ So your denial of part of the Qur'an, which was revealed for the worship and unity of Allah, while you yourselves claim the obligation of worship and the negation of partners with Him, I call to His law and His religion, and to Him is my return at the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment, in all my circumstances in this world and the Hereafter.

Abu Julayd reported from Nafi' a reading of ﴿wa-la ushrika﴾ with a nominative ending (raf') by way of resumption (al-qat', meaning starting a new clause, not dependent on the previous verb); that is: "and I do not associate." It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal, an accusative describing the state of the subject): that I worship Allah without associating anything with Him.

﴿And thus﴾ means: like Our sending down the Book upon the prophets before you, because His saying ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾ implies His sending down the Book. And this which We sent down is in the tongue of the Arabs, just as the earlier books were in the tongue of those to whom they were sent down: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people, to make [the message] clear to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 4]. By "judgment" he meant that it distinguishes between truth and falsehood and rules between them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying "and thus" means: just as We made it easy for these people to rejoice and for those people to deny part of it, so We sent it down as an Arabic judgment. End of quotation.

"Judgment" (hukman) is placed in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of object in "anzalnahu" (We sent it down), and the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. "Judgment" means what the Qur'an includes of meanings. Since its expression is in the tongue of the Arabs, he attributed it to them.

﴿And if you were to follow﴾: the address is to someone other than the Messenger (ﷺ), because he is protected from following their desires. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is from the mode of stirring, provoking, and urging the hearers to steadfastness in the religion and firmness in it, so that no one who holds fast to the proof slips when faced with doubts. Otherwise, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because of his great firmness of character, would be in a position [of never slipping].

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 13, verses 38–40:**

﴿And We had already sent messengers before you, and We gave them wives and offspring. And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of God. For every term there is a Book.﴾ ﴿God erases what He wills and establishes [what He wills], and with Him is the Mother of the Book.﴾ ﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We take you [in death], your duty is only to convey [the message], and upon Us is the reckoning.﴾

Al-Kalbi said: The Jews reproached the Messenger (ﷺ) and said: "We see no concern in this man except women and marriage. If he were a prophet, as he claims, the matter of prophethood would have occupied him away from women." So this verse was revealed. It was said: They used to demand signs from him and deny abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another). So God, exalted is He, answered them that the messengers before him were like him, having wives and offspring, and it was not for them to bring signs of their own choosing, nor did they bring what was demanded of them. Among the sacred laws (shara'i') are benefits that vary according to circumstances and times, so for every time there is a ruling that is "written" upon the servants, meaning that what He wills is imposed upon them.

His saying ﴿for every term there is a Book﴾ is a general expression concerning things that have terms (ajal), because there is nothing among them except that it has a term at its beginning and at its end, and that term is written and determined. Al-Dahhak and al-Farra' said: the meaning is "for every book there is a term," and it is not permissible to claim inversion (al-qalb, the reversal of the order of words in a sentence) except in cases of poetic necessity. As for its being the answer to the first condition, this is not apparent, because it does not follow from it, for the meaning would become: "Whether We show you some of the punishment We promise them, your duty is only to convey." As for its being the answer to the second condition, namely "or We take you," the same objection applies, because the meaning would become: "If We take you, your duty is only to convey," and the obligation to convey does not follow from his death, peace be upon him, since obligation ends after death. Therefore it requires interpretation, namely that for each of the two conditions there should be supposed an appropriate consequence that follows from it. The sense, God knows best, is: "Whether We show you some of what We promise them of punishment, that will be a cure for you against your enemies and a proof of your truthfulness when you report what will befall them." He did not specify the time of its befalling them, so it is possible that it occurs during your lifetime, and it is possible that it occurs to them after your death.

﴿or We take you﴾: that is, or that We take you before its befalling them, so there is no blame or reproach upon you, since some of what God promised through your tongue of their punishment has already befallen them. ﴿your duty is only to convey﴾, not the descent of punishment upon them, for that belongs to Me; and upon Us is their recompense for their denial of you and their disbelief in what you brought.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 13, verses 41–43:**

﴿Have they not seen that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts? And Allah judges; there is none to repel His judgment, and He is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿And those before them had already plotted, but to Allah belongs all plotting. He knows what every soul earns, and the disbelievers will come to know to whom belongs the final abode.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Allah suffices as a witness between me and you, and so does whoever has knowledge of the Book."﴾

[p. 400] The pronoun in ﴿Have they not seen﴾ refers to those who were promised (the threat), and in this there is an admonition for whoever takes heed. They are alerted to look at parts of the land from its outlying regions. "(We come)" means with command and power, as in His saying: ﴿So Allah came upon their structures﴾ [al-Nahl: 26]. The land is the land of the disbelievers mentioned, and by "reducing it from its outlying parts" for the Muslims is meant: from its sides. The Muslims used to raid the areas around the lands of the disbelievers on the side nearest to Madinah, and they would prevail over the edges of the land of Makkah. The "outlying parts" (al-atraf) are the sides. It has been said: the tarf (edge, choice part) of every thing is its best, and from this is the saying of Ali ibn Abi Talib: "The sciences are valleys; whichever valley you take from them, you have lost; so take from every thing a tarf," meaning: its best. This is what Ibn Atiyya said. What appears to be correct is that the meaning of tarfan (a part) is a side and a portion, as if he were indicating that a person participates in some parts of the sciences, because he cannot master all of them, and he did not indicate that he spends his whole life on a single science.

Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: "We come to the land of these people" with victory for you, so You diminish it by what enters your religion from the tribes and the lands adjacent to them. What secures them from Him enabling him over them? This interpretation is only possible if this verse is assumed to have been revealed in Madinah. It has been said: "the land" (al-ard) is a generic noun, and the diminishing from the outlying parts is by the ruin of the habitation which Allah brings upon the disbelievers. This is also reported from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. And from both of them also: the diminishing is by the death of people, the destruction of fruits, and the loss of blessing. And from Ibn Abbas also: the death of its nobles and its great ones, and the departure of the righteous and the good; according to this, the "outlying parts" here are the nobles. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-tarf and al-taraf: the noble man. From Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: the departure of its jurists and the best of its people. From Mujahid: the death of the jurists and the scholars. Ikrima and al-Sha'bi said: it is the diminishing of souls. It has been said: the destruction of those among the nations whom He destroyed before Quraysh, and the destruction of their land after them. The most suitable of these sayings is the first. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention except what is close to it; he said: "We come to the land" the land of disbelief, "reducing it from its outlying parts" by what is opened to the Muslims of their lands, so the abode of war is diminished and the abode of Islam increased, and this is among the signs of dominance and victory. Similar to it is: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts? Are they the victors?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 44] and ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. The meaning is: upon you is delivering what you have been entrusted with; do not concern yourself with what lies beyond that, for We will suffice you in it, and We will complete what We promised you of triumph; let not its delay distress you, for that is due to the wisdom which We know and you do not know. Then He consoled him and relieved his soul by what He mentioned of the early signs of triumph. The saying of those who said that the diminishing is by the death of the nobles, the scholars and the best people is also sound, and its explanation is: Have they not seen that We bring about in the world, through differences, ruin after building, death after life, humiliation after honor, and deficiency after perfection? These are changes perceived by the senses. So what secures them from Allah reversing the matter against them, so that they become humbled after having been dominant?

Al-Dahhak recited (nunaqqisuha) with a doubled consonant, from naqqasa, which makes transitive the intransitive naqasa with the doubling. The mu'aqqib (one who repels) is the one who turns back upon a thing and nullifies it; its real sense is the one who follows it up, i.e., by repelling and nullifying. From this it is said of the owner of a right: mu'aqqib, because he pursues his debtor with demand and claim. Labid said:

*The pursuit of the mu'aqqib of his right by the wronged one*

The meaning is that He has decreed for Islam dominance and advance, and against disbelief reversal and downfall. It has also been said: His judgments are followed up, i.e., one looks at their consequences to see whether it is a calamity or not. The clause ﴿there is none to repel His judgment﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), i.e., His judgment is executed.

﴿And He is swift in reckoning﴾: the discussion of this clause has already preceded. Then the Most High informed that the earlier nations used to plot against their prophets, just as Quraysh did, and that this is the habit of those who deny the messengers: Nimrod plotted against Ibrahim, Pharaoh against Musa, and the Jews against Isa. The Most High made their plotting as if it were no plotting, since He attributed all plotting to Himself. The meaning of His plotting is His punishment of them; He named it plotting because it arose from plotting, and this is by way of reciprocity, like His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]. Then He explained His saying ﴿to Allah belongs all plotting﴾ by His saying: ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾ [p. 401], and the meaning is: He recompenses every soul for what it has earned. Then He threatened the disbeliever with His saying: ﴿and the disbelievers will come to know to whom belongs the final abode﴾, for the punishment will come to him from where he is heedless of it, and then he will know to whom the praiseworthy outcome belongs. Jinah ibn Hubaysh recited (wa-sa-yu'lamu al-kafiru), in the passive from a'lama, i.e., "and he will be informed." The two Harams (Makki and Madani) and Abu Amr recited (al-kafiru) in the singular, meaning the genus; the rest of the seven recited (al-kuffar) in the broken plural. Ibn Mas'ud recited (al-kafirun) in the sound plural, and Ubayy recited (alladhina kafaru). Ata' interpreted "al-kafir" as the mockers, who were five, and the partitioners (al-muqtasimin), who were twenty-eight. Ibn Abbas said: by al-kafir he means Abu Jahl. It is fitting that Ata's interpretation be taken as an example, because the information about the disbeliever's knowledge of the final abode is a meaning that encompasses all disbelievers.

When the disbelievers said ﴿You are not a messenger﴾, meaning: you are merely a claimant to what is not yours, He commanded him to suffice with the witness of Allah between them, since He had manifested through his hands proofs of his messengership, some of which are sufficient for whoever is granted success. "The Book" here is the Qur'an, and the meaning is: whoever recognizes what it contains of sound meanings and of inimitable composition that exceeds the capacity of human beings, bears witness to this. It has also been said: "the Book" is the Torah and the Gospel, and "the one who has the knowledge of the Book" is whoever among their scholars has embraced Islam, because they recognize his description (peace be upon him) in their books. Qatada said: such as Abd Allah ibn Salam, Tamim al-Dari and Salman al-Farisi. Mujahid said: he means Abd Allah ibn Salam specifically. These two sayings are only sound if the verse is Madani, while the majority hold that it is Makki. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and al-Baqir said: he is Ali ibn Abi Talib. It has also been said: it is Jibril, and "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet. It has also been said: it is Allah the Most High; this was said by al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and al-Zajjaj. From al-Hasan: "No, by Allah, He means only Allah," and the meaning is: sufficient is He who deserves worship, and He who knows what is in the Tablet alone, as a witness between me and you. Ibn Atiyya said: this view is objected to on the ground that it involves the coordination (atf) of an attribute upon the thing described, which is not permitted, since attributes are only coordinated with one another. (Abu Hayyan responds:) This is not as he claimed, for "man" (man) is not described by such, nor by any relative pronoun except alladhi, allati and their derivatives, and dhu and dhawat al-Ta'iyyatayn. His saying "attributes are only coordinated with one another" is not absolute, but has a condition, namely that their referents differ. Ibn Atiyya means: you do not say "I passed by Zayd and the scholar," coordinating "the scholar" to the proper name, which has no sense of attribute in it; likewise "Allah" is a proper name. When he sensed this objection to making it coordinated with Allah, he supposed the phrase "who deserves worship," so that it would be coordination of attributes with one another, not of an attribute upon a proper name. The "man" in the recitation of the majority is in the genitive position by coordination with the wording "Allah," or in the nominative position by coordination with the place of "Allah," since in the view of those who consider the preposition (ba') superfluous it is the subject of "kafa." Ibn Atiyya said: it may also be in the nominative position as an inchoative, with the predicate omitted, its estimated form being: "more just and more effective in speech," and the like of this, which the word "witness" (shahidan) indicates; and by this is meant Allah the Most High. It was also read (wa-bi-man), with the preposition ba' entering upon "man," coordinated with "bi-Allah." Ali, Ubayy, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Ibn Jubayr, Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra, al-Dahhak, Salim ibn Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn Abi Ishaq, Mujahid, al-Hakam and al-A'mash read: (wa-min 'indihi 'ilmu al-kitab), making "min" a preposition, the following word governed by it, and "ilm" nominative as an inchoative, with the prepositional phrase in the position of the genitive. Ali also read thus, as did Ibn al-Sumayqa and al-Hasan, with a variant from him.

(wa-man 'indahu) with "min" as a preposition, (ilmu al-kitab) with "'ulima" as a verb in the passive, and "al-kitab" raised as its subject. It was also read (wa-man 'indahu) with a preposition, (ilmu al-kitab) with doubled consonant in the passive; the pronoun in "'indihi" in these three readings refers to Allah the Most High.

Al-Zamakhshari said, concerning the reading in which "'indahu" is a relative clause: "ilm" is raised by the implied element in the adverbial phrase, so it becomes the agent; for when an adverbial phrase falls as a relative clause it draws closer to the resemblance of a verb through its dependence upon the relative pronoun, so it governs like a verb, as in your saying: "I passed by the one who is in the house, his brother," where "his brother" is the agent, as you say: "by the one who is settled in the house, his brother." This is based on the active participle: just as this is permitted with the active participle, though it is better to govern the apparent noun, so it is permitted in what takes its place of adverbial phrase or prepositional phrase. Sibawayh explicitly permitted this in such a case as: "I passed by a man, handsome his face," allowing "handsome his face" with "handsome" raised as a fronted predicate. Thus we received this question from our teachers. Some beginners in grammar may imagine that when the active participle depends upon any of the things we have mentioned, its governing of the apparent noun becomes obligatory, and this is not so. Al-Hawfi parsed ﴿with him is the knowledge of the Book﴾ as an inchoative and predicate within the relative clause of "man." Abu al-Baqa said: "it may also be that it is the predicate: that is, 'with him,' and the inchoative is: 'the knowledge of the Book.'" As for whoever reads ﴿and whoever has﴾ with "'indahu" as a preposition, then "the Book" in his reading is the Qur'an, and the meaning is that He, the Most High, by His bounty and kindness, has given knowledge of the Book, or the Book has been known, according to the two readings; i.e., I have known its meanings, and that it is the greatest of miracles remaining through the passage of ages. The honor of the servant through the sciences of the Qur'an is thus from the kindness of Allah the Most High toward him and His granting him success in its being inimitable, and His granting him success in comprehending that.

They are alerted to look at parts of the land from its outlying regions. "(We come)" means with command and power, as in His saying: ﴿So Allah came upon their structures﴾ [al-Nahl: 26]. The land is the land of the disbelievers mentioned, and by "reducing it from its outlying parts" for the Muslims is meant: from its sides. The Muslims used to raid the areas around the lands of the disbelievers on the side nearest to Madinah, and they would prevail over the edges of the land of Makkah. The "outlying parts" (al-atraf) are the sides. It has been said: the tarf (edge, choice part) of every thing is its best, and from this is the saying of Ali ibn Abi Talib: "The sciences are valleys; whichever valley you take from them, you have lost; so take from every thing a tarf," meaning: its best. This is what Ibn Atiyya said. What appears to be correct is that the meaning of tarfan (a part) is a side and a portion, as if he were indicating that a person participates in some parts of the sciences, because he cannot master all of them, and he did not indicate that he spends his whole life on a single science.

Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: "We come to the land of these people" with victory for you, so You diminish it by what enters your religion from the tribes and the lands adjacent to them. What secures them from Him enabling him over them? This interpretation is only possible if this verse is assumed to have been revealed in Madinah. It has been said: "the land" (al-ard) is a generic noun, and the diminishing from the outlying parts is by the ruin of the habitation which Allah brings upon the disbelievers. This is also reported from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. And from both of them also: the diminishing is by the death of people, the destruction of fruits, and the loss of blessing. And from Ibn Abbas also: the death of its nobles and its great ones, and the departure of the righteous and the good; according to this, the "outlying parts" here are the nobles. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-tarf and al-taraf: the noble man. From Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: the departure of its jurists and the best of its people. From Mujahid: the death of the jurists and the scholars. Ikrima and al-Sha'bi said: it is the diminishing of souls. It has been said: the destruction of those among the nations whom He destroyed before Quraysh, and the destruction of their land after them. The most suitable of these sayings is the first. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention except what is close to it; he said: "We come to the land" the land of disbelief, "reducing it from its outlying parts" by what is opened to the Muslims of their lands, so the abode of war is diminished and the abode of Islam increased, and this is among the signs of dominance and victory. Similar to it is: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts? Are they the victors?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 44] and ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. The meaning is: upon you is delivering what you have been entrusted with; do not concern yourself with what lies beyond that, for We will suffice you in it, and We will complete what We promised you of triumph; let not its delay distress you, for that is due to the wisdom which We know and you do not know. Then He consoled him and relieved his soul by what He mentioned of the early signs of triumph. The saying of those who said that the diminishing is by the death of the nobles, the scholars and the best people is also sound, and its explanation is: Have they not seen that We bring about in the world, through differences, ruin after building, death after life, humiliation after honor, and deficiency after perfection? These are changes perceived by the senses. So what secures them from Allah reversing the matter against them, so that they become humbled after having been dominant?

Al-Dahhak recited (nunaqqisuha) with a doubled consonant, from naqqasa, which makes transitive the intransitive naqasa with the doubling. The mu'aqqib (one who repels) is the one who turns back upon a thing and nullifies it; its real sense is the one who follows it up, i.e., by repelling and nullifying. From this it is said of the owner of a right: mu'aqqib, because he pursues his debtor with demand and claim. Labid said:

*The pursuit of the mu'aqqib of his right by the wronged one*

The meaning is that He has decreed for Islam dominance and advance, and against disbelief reversal and downfall. It has also been said: His judgments are followed up, i.e., one looks at their consequences to see whether it is a calamity or not. The clause ﴿there is none to repel His judgment﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), i.e., His judgment is executed.

﴿And He is swift in reckoning﴾: the discussion of this clause has already preceded. Then the Most High informed that the earlier nations used to plot against their prophets, just as Quraysh did, and that this is the habit of those who deny the messengers: Nimrod plotted against Ibrahim, Pharaoh against Musa, and the Jews against Isa. The Most High made their plotting as if it were no plotting, since He attributed all plotting to Himself. The meaning of His plotting is His punishment of them; He named it plotting because it arose from plotting, and this is by way of reciprocity, like His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]. Then He explained His saying ﴿to Allah belongs all plotting﴾ by His saying: ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾ [p. 401], and the meaning is: He recompenses every soul for what it has earned. Then He threatened the disbeliever with His saying: ﴿and the disbelievers will come to know to whom belongs the final abode﴾, for the punishment will come to him from where he is heedless of it, and then he will know to whom the praiseworthy outcome belongs. Jinah ibn Hubaysh recited (wa-sa-yu'lamu al-kafiru), in the passive from a'lama, i.e., "and he will be informed." The two Harams (Makki and Madani) and Abu Amr recited (al-kafiru) in the singular, meaning the genus; the rest of the seven recited (al-kuffar) in the broken plural. Ibn Mas'ud recited (al-kafirun) in the sound plural, and Ubayy recited (alladhina kafaru). Ata' interpreted "al-kafir" as the mockers, who were five, and the partitioners (al-muqtasimin), who were twenty-eight. Ibn Abbas said: by al-kafir he means Abu Jahl. It is fitting that Ata's interpretation be taken as an example, because the information about the disbeliever's knowledge of the final abode is a meaning that encompasses all disbelievers.

When the disbelievers said ﴿You are not a messenger﴾, meaning: you are merely a claimant to what is not yours, He commanded him to suffice with the witness of Allah between them, since He had manifested through his hands proofs of his messengership, some of which are sufficient for whoever is granted success. Then He followed the witness of Allah with the witness of whoever has the knowledge of the Book. "The Book" here is the Qur'an, and the meaning is: whoever recognizes what it contains of sound meanings and of inimitable composition that exceeds the capacity of human beings, bears witness to this. It has also been said: "the Book" is the Torah and the Gospel, and "the one who has the knowledge of the Book" is whoever among their scholars has embraced Islam, because they recognize his description (peace be upon him) in their books. Qatada said: such as Abd Allah ibn Salam, Tamim al-Dari and Salman al-Farisi. Mujahid said: he means Abd Allah ibn Salam specifically. These two sayings are only sound if the verse is Madani, while the majority hold that it is Makki. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and al-Baqir said: he is Ali ibn Abi Talib. It has also been said: it is Jibril, and "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet. It has also been said: it is Allah the Most High; this was said by al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and al-Zajjaj. From al-Hasan: "No, by Allah, He means only Allah," and the meaning is: sufficient is He who deserves worship, and He who knows what is in the Tablet alone, as a witness between me and you. Ibn Atiyya said: this view is objected to on the ground that it involves the coordination (atf) of an attribute upon the thing described, which is not permitted, since attributes are only coordinated with one another. (Abu Hayyan responds:) This is not as he claimed, for "man" (man) is not described by such, nor by any relative pronoun except alladhi, allati and their derivatives, and dhu and dhawat al-Ta'iyyatayn. His saying "attributes are only coordinated with one another" is not absolute, but has a condition, namely that their referents differ. Ibn Atiyya means: you do not say "I passed by Zayd and the scholar," coordinating "the scholar" to the proper name, which has no sense of attribute in it; likewise "Allah" is a proper name. When he sensed this objection to making it coordinated with Allah, he supposed the phrase "who deserves worship," so that it would be coordination of attributes with one another, not of an attribute upon a proper name. The "man" in the recitation of the majority is in the genitive position by coordination with the wording "Allah," or in the nominative position by coordination with the place of "Allah," since in the view of those who consider the preposition (ba') superfluous it is the subject of "kafa." Ibn Atiyya said: it may also be in the nominative position as an inchoative, with the predicate omitted, its estimated form being: "more just and more effective in speech," and the like of this, which the word "witness" (shahidan) indicates; and by this is meant Allah the Most High. It was also read (wa-bi-man), with the preposition ba' entering upon "man," coordinated with "bi-Allah." Ali, Ubayy, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Ibn Jubayr, Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra, al-Dahhak, Salim ibn Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn Abi Ishaq, Mujahid, al-Hakam and al-A'mash read: (wa-min 'indihi 'ilmu al-kitab), making "min" a preposition, the following word governed by it, and "ilm" nominative as an inchoative, with the prepositional phrase in the position of the genitive. Ali also read thus, as did Ibn al-Sumayqa and al-Hasan, with a variant from him.

(wa-man 'indahu) with "min" as a preposition, (ilmu al-kitab) with "'ulima" as a verb in the passive, and "al-kitab" raised as its subject. It was also read (wa-man 'indahu) with a preposition, (ilmu al-kitab) with doubled consonant in the passive; the pronoun in "'indihi" in these three readings refers to Allah the Most High.

Al-Zamakhshari said, concerning the reading in which "'indahu" is a relative clause: "ilm" is raised by the implied element in the adverbial phrase, so it becomes the agent; for when an adverbial phrase falls as a relative clause it draws closer to the resemblance of a verb through its dependence upon the relative pronoun, so it governs like a verb, as in your saying: "I passed by the one who is in the house, his brother," where "his brother" is the agent, as you say: "by the one who is settled in the house, his brother." What al-Zamakhshari said is not a binding rule; for the adverbial phrase and the prepositional phrase, when they fall as relative clauses, circumstantial clauses, or predicates, either originally or through substitution, or when a negative particle or interrogative particle precedes them, then the apparent noun following them may be raised as the agent, which is the better option, and that raised noun may also be an inchoative, with the adverbial phrase or prepositional phrase in the position of the nominative as its predicate, and the whole nominal sentence then serves as a relative clause, qualifier, circumstantial clause, or predicate. This is based on the active participle: just as this is permitted with the active participle, though it is better to govern the apparent noun, so it is permitted in what takes its place of adverbial phrase or prepositional phrase. Sibawayh explicitly permitted this in such a case as: "I passed by a man, handsome his face," allowing "handsome his face" with "handsome" raised as a fronted predicate. Thus we received this question from our teachers. Some beginners in grammar may imagine that when the active participle depends upon any of the things we have mentioned, its governing of the apparent noun becomes obligatory, and this is not so. Al-Hawfi parsed ﴿with him is the knowledge of the Book﴾ as an inchoative and predicate within the relative clause of "man." Abu al-Baqa said: "it may also be that it is the predicate: that is, 'with him,' and the inchoative is: 'the knowledge of the Book.'" As for whoever reads ﴿and whoever has﴾ with "'indahu" as a preposition, then "the Book" in his reading is the Qur'an, and the meaning is that He, the Most High, by His bounty and kindness, has given knowledge of the Book, or the Book has been known, according to the two readings; i.e., I have known its meanings, and that it is the greatest of miracles remaining through the passage of ages. The honor of the servant through the sciences of the Qur'an is thus from the kindness of Allah the Most High toward him and His granting him success in its being inimitable, and His granting him success in comprehending that.
